7.2.3	Deferred System Information Acquisition in EC operation and for PEO

In order to reduce energy consumption in packet idle mode, the network may broadcast information to assist the MS to apply deferred system information acquisition.

To this purpose it reconfigures EC System Information type 2 for a cell to include an Idle Mode Mobility cell group description comprising cells, geographically adjacent or close to each other, with shared cell parameters related to cell (re)selection, Routing Area assignment, paging monitoring, DL Coverage class selection, mobility support and cell barring and assigns it a broadcast frequency list containing BCCH carriers allocated in these cells. To better match cell deployments, some cell parameters may deviate from the common values and are separately indicated on a per cell basis.

To allow for different settings of shared cell parameters in geographic adjacent areas, different Idle Mode Mobility cell groups are defined with an identifier to distinguish one from the other, thus providing a spatially definite assignment of cells to Idle Mode Mobility cell groups. Since values of shared or non-shared cell parameters in a particular Idle Mode Mobility cell group are subject to change in time, a change mark is assigned to the Idle Mode Mobility cell group. An increment of the change mark for a particular Idle Mode Mobility cell group hence indicates to the MS to acquire the complete EC SI in the serving cell.

To enable fast detection if a cell is part of a specific Idle Mode Mobility cell group or not, the MS identifies from EC-SCH reception the Idle Mode Mobility cell group identifier and the related change mark. Thus, an MS reselecting to a cell in the same IMM cell group as the last serving cell has read the EC-SCH and decoded both the IMM cell group identifier and the IMM cell group change mark. If both values match with those of the last serving cell, it will not need to read the EC-BCCH for this cell prior to the decision for cell reselection, neither after cell reselection to this cell for subsequent cell reselections and for paging monitoring in packet idle mode. Only in case a valid page is received, that requires to send a paging response, or the MS needs to perform an uplink data transmission, or a timeout since the last reading of the complete EC SI in a different than the current serving cell is expired, the MS is required to read the complete EC System Information in the current serving cell.

The network may choose to deactivate deferred SI acquisition in network deployments for which EC System Information needs to be reconfigured more frequently or for which adjacent cells' idle mode mobility parameters differ too much. The support of deferred system information acquisition is broadcasted in EC System Information.

For PEO devices, that operate in normal coverage, a similar concept was designed, that includes the PEO IMM Cell Group definition in the System Information type 13 (SI 13) message and reuses cell parameters broadcasted in SI 2 and SI 3. For fast detection if a neighbour cell belongs to the same PEO IMM Cell Group or not, the MS monitors paging request and immediate assignment messages on downlink CCCH, where the PEO IMM cell group identifier and the PEO IMM change mark are sent and evaluates whether they are identical to those of the current serving cell. In this case it defers reading of system information for that cell, similar to a device in EC operation. Power savings up to around 20% related to the radio module power consumption of the device have been estimated.

question: How is the subscriber registered in the VLR?
passage:
In the context of mobile networks, a subscriber is registered in the Visitor Location Register (VLR) when they roam into a different Public Land Mobile Network (PLMN) area. The process begins when the subscriber's mobile device connects to the network, prompting the VLR to create a temporary record for the subscriber. This record includes the International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) and other relevant information necessary for managing the subscriber's services while they are in the VLR's coverage area. 

When a home subscriber (HPLMN) trace is activated, the trace request is forwarded to the VLR where the subscriber is registered via a Mobile Application Part (MAP) message (MAP-ACTIVATE-TRACE-MODE). This allows the VLR to monitor and manage the subscriber's activities, ensuring that the necessary trace records are created when specific events occur, such as calls or messages. If the subscriber roams into a foreign PLMN, the trace request is stored in the HLR, but the trace is not active in the VLR until the subscriber is located within its area.

question: which one create a trace record?
passage: In the context of subscriber tracing as defined by the 3GPP specifications, trace records are created when a trace is activated for a home subscriber (IMSI) within the Home Public Land Mobile Network (HPLMN). This activation can be initiated by the operator through the management function "Activate Home Subscriber Trace" in the Home Location Register (HLR). Once activated, trace records are generated by various network elements such as the Mobile Switching Center (MSC) and Base Station System (BSS) when specific invoking events occur, including mobile originated calls (MOC), mobile terminated calls (MTC), SMS messages, and location updates. The trace records are then forwarded to the Operations Support Function (OSF) as defined by the trace parameters. Additionally, similar processes apply for tracing foreign subscribers, although trace records for foreign subscribers are only produced in the Visitor Location Register (VLR) and not in the HLR.

question: What is NB-LTE?
passage: NB-LTE, or Narrow Band LTE, is a variation of the LTE (Long Term Evolution) technology specifically designed to support low throughput applications, particularly for the Internet of Things (IoT). It operates using a narrower bandwidth of 200 kHz (1 Resource Block), which allows it to utilize existing GSM/GPRS spectrum and cater to the needs of low-cost, low-power devices. The design of NB-LTE retains many fundamental aspects of legacy LTE while modifying certain parameters to optimize performance for IoT applications. This includes the ability to deploy NB-LTE in various modes, such as inband, guardband, and standalone, allowing for flexible integration with existing LTE networks. The development of NB-LTE reflects the industry's recognition of the need for efficient solutions tailored to the unique requirements of massive IoT connectivity.

When I first heard of a variation of LTE (NB-LTE) with using only 200 Khz (1 RB), I thought like this : "OK, I think I can understand the motivation is 200 Khz. It is same as basic channel bandwidth of GSM. So if we use this in LTE, we may be able to use GSM/GPRS spectrum for NB-LTE. Also, even the smallest bandwidth of the current LTE (1.4 Mhz) might be too much for such a super
low throughput application like IoT. OK, so far so good. Then a question popped up in my mind.

OK.. I think 200 Khz (more accurately 180 Khz) is to utilize 1RB of legacy LTE as it is. Also, it is not difficult think of how we utilize this single RB because data transmission and reception in the single RB is possible even in legacy LTE. However, there are somethings that cannot be reduced to single RB bandwidth in legacy LTE. So you may have following questions.

I would not give you answers to any of these questions in this page. It is just my way of studying anything new. Coming up with my own question before jumping into textbook or specification documents.

The first impression that I got while I was reading Release 13 LTE-NB specification is that it is almost a new design except a few very fundamental factors/parameters.

Followings are some of parameters that remains same in LTE-NB comparing to normal (legacy) LTE

Followings are some of parameters that are different from legacy LTE. I would just put down a high level descriptions of the difference here. For the details, I would recommend you to each separate pages that I listed at the top.

In short, there is no changes at all in Downlink and small changes in Uplink as follows.

As you know, LTE is originally designed to provide very high data rate. So it might sound ironic that we are trying to provide very low throughput service like IoT. However, as far as I experienced.. in engineering there is no such a thing like ironic.. engineers are always to try to come up with a solution when there is need. Even though LTE is originally designed for high throughput,
there has been continuous effort for low throughput (low cost) solution for the past couple of years. This is why you start seeing UE Category running backward. Most of initial LTE implementation was implemented as Category 3 and kept incrementing the numbers. However, we started seeing backward numbers like Category 1 and Category 0. However, all of exisiting LTE categories still keep the lowest boundary of LTE specification as follows :

However, the industry realized that there would be limitation to make LTE perfectaly suitable for IoT / MTC crieteria (super simple, untra cheap, extremly low energy consumption). Finally the industry tried to break at least one of the LTE boundary. It is to break frequency domain boundary and decide to make it narrower.

Then the question is how narrow it should be. Probably the most practical answer they found seems to be the bandwidth of 1RB because 1 RB is the minimum scheduling unit of current (legacy) LTE in frequency domain. They might have tried to pick narrower bandwidth (e.g, 6 subcarriers etc). However, in this case it would require too much redesign from the legacy LTE.

The industry decided to time domain boundary as it is, meaning that we can use the most of time domain design of the legacy LTE as it is.

With 1RB Bandwidth selected, we can utilize(deploy) this system in various situation as illustrated below.

Inband Mode : In this mode, we can deploy LTE NB within a legacy LTE if you just reserve only 1 RB anywhere in the legacy LTE band.

Guardband Mode : As you know, every LTE band has at least 100 Khz guardband on each end of the band. It means that you can easily have around 200 Khz space between any two non-contiguous band even if they are sitting in the closest possible locations. Guardband mode is
to deply LTE-NB in the space that are reserved for the guardband of legacy LTE band.

Standalone Mod : In previous two modes, LTE-NB coexists with an existing legacy LTE band. But we can think of another case where it is deployed completely independent from any legacy LTE. In an extreme case, we may deploy it in completely free space in the spectrum. However,
in practical sense this mode of operation is intended to reserve (free up) a GSM channel and deploy LTE-NB in that space.

Followings are some of parameters that are different from legacy LTE. I would just put down a high level descriptions of the difference here. For the details, I would recommend you to each separate pages that I listed at the top.

In short, there is no changes at all in Downlink and small changes in Uplink as follows.

As you know, LTE is originally designed to provide very high data rate. So it might sound ironic that we are trying to provide very low throughput service like IoT. However, as far as I experienced.. in engineering there is no such a thing like ironic.. engineers are always to try to come up with a solution when there is need. Even though LTE is originally designed for high throughput,
there has been continuous effort for low throughput (low cost) solution for the past couple of years. This is why you start seeing UE Category running backward. Most of initial LTE implementation was implemented as Category 3 and kept incrementing the numbers. However, we started seeing backward numbers like Category 1 and Category 0. However, all of exisiting LTE categories still keep the lowest boundary of LTE specification as follows :

However, the industry realized that there would be limitation to make LTE perfectaly suitable for IoT / MTC crieteria (super simple, untra cheap, extremly low energy consumption). Finally the industry tried to break at least one of the LTE boundary. It is to break frequency domain boundary and decide to make it narrower.

Then the question is how narrow it should be. Probably the most practical answer they found seems to be the bandwidth of 1RB because 1 RB is the minimum scheduling unit of current (legacy) LTE in frequency domain. They might have tried to pick narrower bandwidth (e.g, 6 subcarriers etc). However, in this case it would require too much redesign from the legacy LTE.

The industry decided to time domain boundary as it is, meaning that we can use the most of time domain design of the legacy LTE as it is.

With 1RB Bandwidth selected, we can utilize(deploy) this system in various situation as illustrated below.

Inband Mode : In this mode, we can deploy LTE NB within a legacy LTE if you just reserve only 1 RB anywhere in the legacy LTE band.

Guardband Mode : As you know, every LTE band has at least 100 Khz guardband on each end of the band. It means that you can easily have around 200 Khz space between any two non-contiguous band even if they are sitting in the closest possible locations. Guardband mode is
to deply LTE-NB in the space that are reserved for the guardband of legacy LTE band.

Standalone Mod : In previous two modes, LTE-NB coexists with an existing legacy LTE band. But we can think of another case where it is deployed completely independent from any legacy LTE. In an extreme case, we may deploy it in completely free space in the spectrum. However,
in practical sense this mode of operation is intended to reserve (free up) a GSM channel and deploy LTE-NB in that space.

question: How is the UE position estimated in the WLAN positioning method?
gold_answer: the UE position is estimated with the knowledge of geographical coordinate of reference WLAN access points
passage: In the WLAN positioning method, the User Equipment (UE) position is estimated by utilizing the geographical coordinates of reference WLAN access points. This process involves collecting measurements from the UE's WLAN receivers and applying a location determination algorithm that leverages databases containing the locations of these reference points. The UE can operate in three positioning modes: standalone, UE-assisted, and UE-based. In standalone mode, the UE reports its estimated position, including latitude, longitude, and altitude, along with location uncertainty. In UE-assisted and UE-based modes, the UE also provides similar location information while indicating the use of the WLAN method for position calculation. This collaborative approach between the UE and the Location Management Function (LMF) ensures accurate positioning based on the available WLAN infrastructure.

8.5.1	General

This clause defines the information that may be transferred between LMF and UE.

8.5.2.1.4	WLAN AP Location

This assistance data provides the location (possibly including altitude information) of the access point [21].

8.5.2.2	Information that may be transferred from the UE to LMF

The information that may be signalled from the UE to the LMF is summarized in Table 8.5.2.2-1.

In Standalone mode, the UE reports the latitude, longitude and possibly altitude, together with an estimate of the location uncertainty, if available.

8.5.3	WLAN Positioning Procedures

8.5.3.1	Capability Transfer Procedure

The Capability Transfer procedure for WLAN positioning is described in clause 7.1.2.1.

8.5.3.2	Assistance Data Transfer Procedure

The purpose of this procedure is to enable the UE to request assistance data from the LMF (e.g., as part of a positioning procedure) and the LMF to provide assistance data to the UE (e.g., as part of a positioning procedure).

8.5.3.2.1	LMF initiated Assistance Data Delivery

Figure 8.5.3.2.1-1 shows the Assistance Data Delivery operations for the network-assisted WLAN method when the procedure is initiated by the LMF.

8.5.3.2.2	UE initiated Assistance Data Transfer

Figure 8.5.3.2.2-1 shows the Assistance Data Transfer operations for the network-assisted WLAN method when the procedure is initiated by the UE.

(1)	The UE determines that certain WLAN assistance data is desired (e.g., as part of a positioning procedure when the LMF provided assistance data are not sufficient for the UE to fulfil the request) and sends a LPP Request Assistance Data message to the LMF. This request includes an indication of which specific WLAN assistance data is requested.

(2)	The LMF provides the requested assistance data in a LPP Provide Assistance Data message, if available at the LMF. The entire set of assistance data may be delivered in one or several LPP messages. In this case, this step may be repeated by the LMF several times. If any of the UE requested assistance data in step (1) are not provided in step 2, the UE shall assume that the requested assistance data are not supported, or currently not available at the LMF. 5.3.3.15	MBMS Indicator Channel (MICH)

The MBMS Indicator Channel (MICH) is a fixed rate (SF=256) physical channel used to carry the MBMS notification indicators. The MICH is always associated with an S-CCPCH to which a FACH transport channel is mapped.

Figure 26D illustrates the frame structure of the MICH. One MICH radio frame of length 10 ms consists of 300 bits (b0, b1, …, b299). Of these, 288 bits (b0, b1, …, b287) are used to carry notification indicators. The remaining 12 bits are not formally part of the MICH and shall not be transmitted (DTX).

In each MICH frame, Nn notification indicators {N0, …, NNn-1} are transmitted, where Nn=18, 36, 72, or 144.

question: What is LMF selection?
gold_answer: used by the AMF to determine an LMF for location estimation of the target UE
passage: LMF selection refers to the process used by the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) to identify a Location Management Function (LMF) for estimating the location of a target User Equipment (UE). The selection process begins by checking if an LMF ID is available in the UE's location context or provided by the UE itself. If such an ID exists, the AMF evaluates whether the identified LMF can be utilized for the current location estimation task. Additionally, the LMF may indicate its unsuitability for the current UE's access network or serving cell, prompting the AMF to select a different LMF if necessary, especially in cases of UE mobility. The selection can be based on locally configured LMF profiles at either the AMF or LMF, or by querying the Network Repository Function (NRF) for available options. Factors such as the current network conditions and the specific requirements of the location estimation process are considered during LMF selection.

question: What is DASH?
passage: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) is a streaming protocol that enables high-quality streaming of media content over the internet. It allows for adaptive bitrate streaming, which means that the quality of the video can adjust in real-time based on the user's network conditions, ensuring a smooth viewing experience. DASH is designed to optimize the delivery of multimedia content by breaking it into smaller segments, which can be delivered and played back as needed. This technology is particularly beneficial for mobile networks, as it helps manage bandwidth and improve the Quality of Experience (QoE) for users. The enhancements related to QoE for DASH, as specified in the 3GPP standards, allow operators to collect and analyze quality-related metrics from media clients, enabling better network optimization and user experience management.

12.2	Quality of Experience (QoE) related Features

Summary based on the input provided by Ericsson LM in SP-180037.

QoE reporting is a functionality which allows quality-related metrics feedback from a media client in the UE. In a previous Rel-14 work item IQoE [1], this QoE functionality was enhanced for the DASH streaming specification TS 26.247 [2], giving the operator better possibilities to control such metrics feedback. The current Rel-15 work item EQoE_MTSI [3] introduced the same enhancements also to the MTSI specification TS 26.114 [4], keeping the QoE functionalities for DASH and MTSI services aligned.

The enhancements introduced by EQoE_MTSI in TS 26.114 are:

Summary based on the input provided by China Unicom, Huawei, China Telecom in RP-172192 revised in RP-181821.

The benefit of understanding customers' experience, e.g. throughput, data loss, latency, for streaming services has attracted operators' attention. ITU-T P.NATS has released the standards on the model and evaluation of MOS models for streaming services in December 2016. SA4 has specified information about Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, DASH, services to be collected from the DASH application on the UE and agreed to support MDT enhancement option for both QoE metrics configuration and QoE metrics reporting [1].A WI on QoE Measurement Collection for streaming services in UTRAN was approved at RAN#73 and a 'container based solution' has been specified [2]. SA5 has studied the management solution for collection of QoE information and proposed use cases, potential requirements and possible solutions. A WI was approved to specify the function Management of QoE measurement collection [3].

Based on the work above, the operators can collect and utilize the QoE measurement information of streaming services to better understand the user experience and optimize their network in E-UTRAN. This work item specified the core requirement for Quality of Experience (QoE) Measurement Collection for streaming services in E-UTRAN [4].

This feature enables the network to collect QoE measurement information from the UE. The feature is activated by Trace Function from the MDT framework. Both signalling based and management based initiation cases are allowed. For the signalling based case, the QoE Measurement Collection is initiated towards a specific UE from CN nodes using the MDT mechanism; for the management based case, the QoE Measurement Collection is initiated from OAM targeting an area (without targeting a specific UE).

The QoE measurement configuration from OAM or CN in E-UTRAN is included in a container of RRCConnectionReconfiguration message and forwarded to the UE similar to in UTRAN. For transferring the QoE measurement report, a new SRB4 and a new uplink RRC message "application layer measurement report" are introduced. SRB4 is configured via RRCConnectionReconfiguration meassage. A container in the new message is defined to send the QoE measurement report.

The QoE measurement configuration and measurement reporting are supported in RRC_CONNECTED state only. E-UTRAN can release the QoE measurement configuration towards the UE at any time. If not explicitly released by the eNB, QoE measurement will be continued in case of intra-eNB HO and inter-eNB HO and both source and target cell belong to defined same measurement reporting area.

question: Which initiation cases are allowed?
gold_answer: Both signalling based and management based initiation cases
passage: The initiation cases allowed for Quality of Experience (QoE) measurement collection in E-UTRAN include both signaling-based and management-based approaches. In the signaling-based case, the QoE Measurement Collection is initiated towards a specific User Equipment (UE) from Core Network (CN) nodes using the Measurement Data Traffic (MDT) mechanism. Conversely, in the management-based case, the initiation comes from Operations, Administration, and Management (OAM) targeting a broader area without specifying a particular UE. This dual approach enables operators to effectively gather and utilize QoE metrics to enhance user experience and optimize network performance.

question: How does MSCA request a Handover number?
passage: To request a Handover Number, the Mobile Switching Center A (MSCA) initiates a MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request. This request includes an A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST and is sent over the established MAP connection. For speech calls, MSCA must also provide the Iu Supported Codecs List to facilitate subsequent handovers. Upon receiving the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request, the Mobile Switching Center B (MSCB) performs the assignment operation and retrieves a Handover Number from the Visitor Location Register B (VLR-B). If there are issues with the assignment or Handover Number allocation, MSCB will indicate this in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER response, which may include either the outcomes of the procedures or an error message. If the request is successful, MSCA will proceed to establish a circuit connection to MSCB.
context:
13.1	GSM handover

If a circuit connection has to be set up (for example for a Mobile Originated or Mobile Terminated Call Establishment) after an Inter-MSC handover without circuit connection, MSCA shall request a Handover Number using a MAPPREPARE-HANDOVER request, containing the A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST, on the established MAP connection. For speech calls, MSC-A shall also include the Iu Supported Codecs List to be used by MSC-B for subsequent intra-MSC-B intersystem handover to UMTS and intra-MSC-B SRNS relocation. If MSCB indicates to MSCB and to MSCA that at least one of two procedures assignment or Handover Number allocation can not be completed, then MSCA shall terminate the circuit establishment attempt. The existing connection to the MS shall be maintained, if possible.
Upon receipt of the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request MSCB shall perform the requested assignment operation towards the BSS. In addition it shall retrieve a Handover Number from VLR-B. If a failure occurs in the assignment or Handover Number allocation then it shall be reflected in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER response that at least one of these two procedures has not been completed (i.e. either by a MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER result with the assignment procedure outcome and the Handover Number allocation outcome or by a MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER error).

If MSC-A supports A interface over IP, then for speech calls MSC-A may include the AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor) in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request.
If the BSS-B supports A over IP then MSC-B shall include a Codec List (MSC preferred) in the A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST message to BSS-B. MSC-B may select the codecs for the Codec List (MSC preferred) from the channel type information and the AoIPSupported Codecs List (Anchor), if this list was provided by 3G_MSC-A in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request. For a detailed description of the handling of these codec lists by MSC-A and MSC-B see 3GPP TS 23.153. If the AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor) was not provided or MSC-B does not support the selection of codecs from the AoIP-Supported Codecs List, then MSC-B shall create the Codec List (MSC preferred) using the channel type information received from 3G_MSC-A in the A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST message included in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request.

If MSC-A provided an AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor) in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request and MSCB selected the codecs for the Codec List (MSC preferred) from the AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor), MSCB may include the AoIP-Selected Codec (Target) and AoIP-Available Codecs List (MAP) in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER response.
When MSCA receives a successful MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER response it shall establish a circuit connection to MSCB by using the appropriate network supported procedures. In figure 36 this is indicated by the IAM (Initial Address Message) and ACM (Address Complete Message). MSCB shall also send the Answer message if appropriate to the signalling system. Upon receipt of the Answer MSCA shall consider the circuit connection establishment phase complete. If a failure occurs during the cirucit establishment phase then the existing connection to the MS shall be maintained, if possible.

question: What project helped propel 2G evolution into 3G?
passage: The project that helped propel the evolution from 2G to 3G was the establishment of the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) in 1998. By uniting these diverse markets, 3GPP facilitated the transition from the original GSM-based 2G technology to the more advanced 3G capabilities, paving the way for a global market for equipment, handsets, and roaming services. question: What may the UE while connected to a gNB require to perform OTDOA measurements from E-UTRA TPs?
passage: While connected to a gNB, the User Equipment (UE) may require measurement gaps to perform OTDOA (Observed Time Difference of Arrival) measurements from E-UTRA (Evolved Universal Terrestrial Radio Access) TPs (Transmission Points). These measurement gaps are necessary for the UE to accurately measure downlink radio signals from multiple E-UTRA TPs, which is essential for estimating its position. The UE can request these measurement gaps from the gNB using the specified procedures in the relevant 3GPP clauses. Additionally, if the UE is not aware of the System Frame Number (SFN) of at least one E-UTRA TP in the OTDOA assistance data, it may utilize autonomous gaps to acquire the SFN of the E-UTRA OTDOA reference cell before proceeding with the measurement gap request.

8.2	OTDOA positioning

8.2.1	General

In this version of the specification, only OTDOA based on LTE signals is supported.

In the OTDOA positioning method, the UE position is estimated based on measurements taken at the UE of downlink radio signals from multiple E-UTRA TPs (possibly including PRS-only E-UTRA TPs from a PRS-based TBS), along with knowledge of the geographical coordinates of the measured TPs and their relative downlink timing.

The UE while connected to a gNB may require measurement gaps to perform the OTDOA measurements from E-UTRA TPs. The UE may request measurement gaps from a gNB using the procedure described in clause 7.4.1.1. If the UE is not aware of the SFN of at least one E-UTRA TP in the OTDOA assistance data, the UE may use autonomous gaps to acquire SFN of the E-UTRA OTDOA reference cell prior to requesting measurement gaps for performing the requested E-UTRA RSTD measurements.

The UE while connected to a ng-eNB may require measurement gaps to perform inter-frequency RSTD measurements for OTDOA from E-UTRA TPs (see TS 38.133 [32]). The UE may request measurement gaps from a ng-eNB using the procedure described in clause 7.4.2.1.

The specific positioning techniques used to estimate the UE's location from this information are beyond the scope of this specification.

question: Why may the UE while connected to a ng-eNB require measurement gaps?
gold_answer: to perform inter-frequency RSTD measurements for OTDOA from E-UTRA TPs
passage: The User Equipment (UE) connected to a ng-eNB may require measurement gaps to perform specific tasks related to positioning, particularly for OTDOA (Observed Time Difference of Arrival) measurements. These measurement gaps are necessary for the UE to accurately measure downlink radio signals from multiple E-UTRA Transmission Points (TPs). The UE can request these gaps from the ng-eNB to facilitate inter-frequency RSTD (Reference Signal Time Difference) measurements, which are essential for determining its location based on the timing of signals received from different TPs. If the UE lacks knowledge of the System Frame Number (SFN) of at least one E-UTRA TP, it may utilize autonomous gaps to acquire the SFN of the OTDOA reference cell before proceeding with the measurement requests. This process ensures that the UE can effectively gather the necessary data for accurate positioning.

question: Why does the UE require measurement gaps to perform OTDOA?
gold_answer: The UE may request measurement gaps from a gNB using the procedure described in clause 7.4.1.1.
passage: In the context of OTDOA (Observed Time Difference of Arrival) positioning, the User Equipment (UE) requires measurement gaps to perform accurate measurements of downlink radio signals from multiple E-UTRA Transmission Points (TPs). These measurement gaps are essential because they allow the UE to temporarily suspend its ongoing communication with the gNB (gNodeB) to focus on gathering the necessary signal measurements without interference. During these gaps, the UE can also acquire the System Frame Number (SFN) of the E-UTRA TPs, which is crucial for determining the relative timing of the signals being measured. This process ensures that the UE can effectively estimate its position based on the timing differences of the signals received from various TPs, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the OTDOA positioning method.

question: How can the delivery of assistance data to the SLP be viewed?
passage: The delivery of assistance data to the SLP (Service Location Protocol) can be viewed as an independent external process. This is particularly relevant in scenarios such as UE-assisted OTDOA (User Equipment-assisted Observed Time Difference of Arrival), where the SLP requires assistance data from the NG-RAN (Next Generation Radio Access Network). The SLP can communicate with the LMF (Location Management Function) via the SPC (Service Provider Connection), allowing for the transfer of assistance data that was initially delivered to the LMF through NRPPa (Next Generation Radio Protocol for Positioning). This process is designed to be transparent to the UE and the SUPL session, meaning that the retrieval of assistance data does not interfere with the ongoing positioning transaction. Thus, while the SLP plays a crucial role in the positioning operation, the actual delivery of assistance data occurs through established control-plane mechanisms, ensuring a seamless integration of data from external sources.

3GPP-Specs#38305-f70#72

A.4	Procedures combining C-plane and U-plane operations

Since SUPL by definition is carried over the user plane, it is not applicable to operations terminating at the NG-RAN. SUPL operations must take place in combination with control-plane procedures over NRPPa.

This situation could arise in the case of UE-assisted OTDOA, for example, in which the SLP needs to provide the UE (in a SUPL session) with assistance data supplied by the NG-RAN. This clause uses a UE-assisted OTDOA positioning operation as an example.

Although the positioning server in this operation is the SLP, the existence of an interface to the LMF means that the SLP can communicate with the LMF via the SPC. In particular, this means that assistance data that was delivered to the LMF via NRPPa can be transferred over to the SLP for delivery to the UE via LPP over SUPL.

There are several ways to realise this general behaviour. In the simplest case, the LMF could be supplied with the necessary assistance data in advance, so that it can be supplied to the SLP without any actual NRPPa procedures taking place in real time (and possibly even before the positioning transaction begins).

In the event that the LMF does not have the required assistance data available, it would need to retrieve them from the NG-RAN once it was made aware that they were needed.

In both cases, it should be noted that the retrieval of the assistance data is transparent to the UE and to the actual SUPL session. This model is parallel to the approach used with A-GNSS, in which assistance data such as satellite ephemerides are retrieved from sources entirely external to the cellular network. For purposes of LPP over SUPL, the delivery of assistance data to the SLP can be viewed as an independent external process.

The delivery of assistance data to the UE, however, takes place through the same mechanisms as control-plane LPP, transported through SUPL.

In scenarios such as UE-assisted OTDOA (User Equipment-assisted Observed Time Difference of Arrival), the SLP requires assistance data from the NG-RAN (Next Generation Radio Access Network) to provide to the UE during a SUPL (Secure User Plane Location) session. The LMF can supply this assistance data to the SLP, which is then delivered to the UE using LPP (Location Positioning Protocol) over SUPL. 

There are two primary methods for this communication: the LMF may have the necessary assistance data pre-provided, allowing it to transfer the data to the SLP without real-time NRPPa (NR Protocol for Positioning Assistance) procedures. Alternatively, if the LMF lacks the required data, it can retrieve it from the NG-RAN when notified of the need. This process is designed to be transparent to the UE and the SUPL session, ensuring that the delivery of assistance data occurs seamlessly alongside control-plane operations.

Although the positioning server in this operation is the SLP, the existence of an interface to the LMF means that the SLP can communicate with the LMF via the SPC. In particular, this means that assistance data that was delivered to the LMF via NRPPa can be transferred over to the SLP for delivery to the UE via LPP over SUPL.

There are several ways to realise this general behaviour. In the simplest case, the LMF could be supplied with the necessary assistance data in advance, so that it can be supplied to the SLP without any actual NRPPa procedures taking place in real time (and possibly even before the positioning transaction begins).

In the event that the LMF does not have the required assistance data available, it would need to retrieve them from the NG-RAN once it was made aware that they were needed.

In both cases, it should be noted that the retrieval of the assistance data is transparent to the UE and to the actual SUPL session. This model is parallel to the approach used with A-GNSS, in which assistance data such as satellite ephemerides are retrieved from sources entirely external to the cellular network. For purposes of LPP over SUPL, the delivery of assistance data to the SLP can be viewed as an independent external process.

The delivery of assistance data to the UE, however, takes place through the same mechanisms as control-plane LPP, transported through SUPL.

question: During a basic inter-system GSM to UMTS handover, what does 3G_MSCA initiate and control?
passage: During a basic inter-system GSM to UMTS handover, the 3G_MSCA initiates and controls all aspects of the handover procedure. This process begins with the reception of a Handover Required message from the BSS-A on the A-interface and continues until the completion of the handover, which is confirmed by the reception of a Handover Complete message from the 3G_MSCB on the E-interface. Throughout this procedure, 3G_MSCA is responsible for managing the call and mobility of the user equipment (UE), ensuring that all necessary signaling and resource allocation tasks are executed effectively to maintain service continuity during the transition from GSM to UMTS.

question: Why does UE request assistance data from the LMF?
gold_answer: as part of a positioning procedure
passage: The User Equipment (UE) requests assistance data from the Location Management Function (LMF) primarily to enhance the accuracy of its positioning procedures. 5.5.4.3	Initial access and mobility

The mobile phones synchronise to the mobile network by "listening" to the Primary and Secondary Synchronization Signals (PSS and SSS), shown in respectively blue and orange on the figure below (note that the figure shows an "NR-" prefix which is omitted in the text). The vertical separations are the Ressource Blocks (RB), as defined in the previous section, i.e. a group of 12 subcarriers. The horizontal separations are the OFDM symbols. Four OFDM symbols together with 20 RBs form a so-called "SS/PBCH (Synchronization Signals/ Physical Broadcast Channel) block".

The PSS and NSS are transmitted over 127 subcarriers, i.e. about 10.5 RBs. (They are designed to carry the Physical Cell ID (PCID) selected from 1008 candidates.)
 Once synchronised with the PSS and NSS, the mobiles can retrieve the full SS/PBCH structure, and thus "listen" to the Physical Broadcast Channel (PBCH) and its associated Demodulation reference signals (DM-RS).

The PBCH carries only the minimum system information necessary for initial access, such as system frame number (SFN), initial configurations for PDCCH, PDSCH and DM-RS, and information required to determine the frame timing such as SS/PBCH block index and half-frame index. These are referred to as "System Information Block 1 (SIB1)".

One or multiple SS/PBCH blocks can be transmitted by using transmission beamforming within a half frame, with configurable periodicity from 5 ms to 160 ms. The maximum number of SS/PBCH blocks and the applicable subcarrier spacing for SS/PBCH block transmission are dependent on the frequency range, as shown in Table 5.5.4.3-1. SIB1 and other system information (SIB2 and onwards) are carried by PDSCH which is scheduled by PDCCH. SIB1 contains necessary information to perform random access procedure for initial access.

Paging message is carried by PDSCH which is scheduled by PDCCH. Numerology used for SIB1 transmission on a NR cell is indicated in master information block (MIB) carried by PBCH and is commonly applied to transmissions for other system information (SIB2 and onwards), Paging, Msg.2 ("Message 2", as explained below) and Msg.4 transmissions on the same cell.

Four different PRACH preamble formats based on the long ZC sequence are defined and corresponding numerology is defined for each PRACH preamble format as shown in Table 5.5.4.3-2.

In addition, nine different PRACH preamble formats based on the short ZC sequence are defined and corresponding numerology is defined for each PRACH preamble format as shown in Table 5.5.4.3-3.

Msg.2 and Msg.4 for random access are carried by PDSCH that are scheduled by PDCCH.

Msg.3 for random access is carried by PUSCH which is scheduled by random access response (RAR) in Msg.2 or PDCCH in case of retransmission.

For mobility measurement, SS/PBCH block and/or CSI-RS can be utilized in NR. SS/PBCH block based reference signal received power (RSRP), reference signal received quality (RSRQ) and signal-to-noise and interference ratio (SINR) are defined, and CSI-RS based RSRP, RSRQ and SINR are also defined. question: What does the UE trigger with the two new events?
passage: The UE triggers two new events, H1 and H2, to report its altitude in relation to an eNB-configured threshold. Specifically, H1 is triggered when the UE's altitude is above the threshold, while H2 is triggered when it is below. These events enable the eNB to determine if the UE is flying and to assess potential interference issues. Additionally, the enhancements allow the UE to provide information about its planned flight path to the eNB, which can aid in optimizing mobility and handover decisions.

13.9	Enhanced LTE Support for Aerial Vehicles

Summary based on the input provided by Ericsson in RP-181045 revised in RP-181644.

Enhancements according to those identified in TR 36.777 [1] to support aerial UE functions in LTE were introduced in this WI [2].

An aerial UE which is flying has a higher likelihood of having line-of-sight to eNBs which terrestrial UEs normally do not have line-of-sight to. This could result in interference and issues with mobility. This WI aimed to address such issues. Below is a description of the enhancements introduced as part of this WI.

TS 36.331 was extended with two reporting events H1 and H2. With these two new events, the UE triggers a height report when the UE's altitude is above(H1) or below(H2) of an eNB-configured threshold. Further, the RRM measurement framework was extended such that the UE can be configured to trigger a measurement report if an event condition is met for a configurable number of cells. Events applicable for this enhancement are A3, A4 and A5. These enhancements help the eNB to determine that a UE is flying and/or allow to detect that the UE may be causing or experiencing interference.

To improve mobility performance, RRC signalling was added to allow the UE to indicate to the eNB the planned flight path. More specifically, the UE can indicate where the UE is planned to be in the future which could be taken into account by the eNB for mobility purposes, e.g. the eNB may be able to use this information to know in advance which cell would be suitable for the UE to be handed over to and if a new X2 connection is beneficial to be established.

In some countries it may not be allowed to fly drones which are connected to LTE network without authorization. 13.9	Enhanced LTE Support for Aerial Vehicles

Summary based on the input provided by Ericsson in RP-181045 revised in RP-181644.

Enhancements according to those identified in TR 36.777 [1] to support aerial UE functions in LTE were introduced in this WI [2].

An aerial UE which is flying has a higher likelihood of having line-of-sight to eNBs which terrestrial UEs normally do not have line-of-sight to. This could result in interference and issues with mobility. This WI aimed to address such issues. Below is a description of the enhancements introduced as part of this WI.

TS 36.331 was extended with two reporting events H1 and H2. With these two new events, the UE triggers a height report when the UE's altitude is above(H1) or below(H2) of an eNB-configured threshold. Further, the RRM measurement framework was extended such that the UE can be configured to trigger a measurement report if an event condition is met for a configurable number of cells. Events applicable for this enhancement are A3, A4 and A5. These enhancements help the eNB to determine that a UE is flying and/or allow to detect that the UE may be causing or experiencing interference.

To improve mobility performance, RRC signalling was added to allow the UE to indicate to the eNB the planned flight path. More specifically, the UE can indicate where the UE is planned to be in the future which could be taken into account by the eNB for mobility purposes, e.g. the eNB may be able to use this information to know in advance which cell would be suitable for the UE to be handed over to and if a new X2 connection is beneficial to be established.

In some countries it may not be allowed to fly drones which are connected to LTE network without authorization. In order for the network to know if the user of the UE has a suitable subscription, a signalling from the CN to the eNB was introduced with information about whether the subscription supports Aerial UE function. How the eNB uses this information was left for implementation.

To reduce possible uplink interference, UL power control enhancements were specified allowing for UE-specific fractional pathloss compensation factor, and the range of the UE specific P0 parameter was also extended.

For more details please refer to the status report [3] and associated CRs [4-5].

question: What happens to the cell layout and locations of the BSs over a series of D drops?
passage: Over a series of D drops in system-level simulations, the cell layout and locations of the base stations (BSs) remain fixed. However, the locations of the mobile stations (MSs) are randomly varied at the beginning of each drop. This approach allows for the assessment of performance metrics such as throughput and delay while maintaining a consistent environment for the BSs, which simplifies the simulation process. The BSs are assumed to transmit with full power, while only a subset of them is actively simulated during each drop.

5	Spatial channel model for simulations

The spatial channel model for use in the system-level simulations is described in this clause. As in the link level simulations, the description is in the context of a downlink system where the BS transmits to a MS; however the material in this clause (with the exception of Clause 5.7 on Ioc modelling) can be applied to the uplink as well.

As opposed to link simulations which simply consider a single BS transmitting to a single MS, the system simulations typically consist of multiple cells/sectors, BSs, and MSs. Performance metrics such as throughput and delay are collected over D drops, where a "drop" is defined as a simulation run for a given number of cells/sectors, BSs, and MSs, over a specified number of frames. During a drop, the channel undergoes fast fading according to the motion of the MSs. Channel state information is fed back from the MSs to the BSs, and the BSs use schedulers to determine which user(s) to transmit to. Typically, over a series of D drops, the cell layout and locations of the BSs are fixed, but the locations of the MSs are randomly varied at the beginning of each drop. To simplify the simulation, only a subset of BSs will actually be simulated while the remaining BSs are assumed to transmit with full power.  The goal of this clause is to define the methodology and parameters for generating the spatial and temporal channel coefficients between a given base and mobile for use in system level simulations. For an S element BS array and a U element MS array, the channel coefficients for one of N multipath components (note that these components are not necessarily time resolvable, meaning that the time difference between successive paths may be less than a chip period) are given by an S -by- U  matrix of complex amplitudes. We denote the channel matrix for the nth multipath component (n = 1,…,N) as . It is a function of time t because the complex amplitudes are undergoing fast fading governed by the movement of the MS. Clauses 5.2, 5.3, and 5.4 give the details for the general procedure. Figure 5.1 below provides a roadmap for generating the channel coefficients. Clause 5.5 specifies optional cases that modify the general procedure. Clause 5.6 describes the procedure for generating correlated log normal user parameters used in Clause 5.3. Clause 5.7 describes the method for accounting for intercell interference. Clause 5.8 presents calibration results.

question: What is considered by link simulations?
gold_answer: a single BS transmitting to a single MS

In contrast, spatial channel models for system-level simulations consider a more complex scenario involving multiple cells, sectors, BSs, and MSs. These simulations evaluate performance metrics such as throughput and delay over multiple simulation runs, known as "drops." The methodology for generating channel coefficients involves defining parameters and procedures that account for the spatial and temporal characteristics of the channel, including the effects of intercell interference and the random variation of MS locations across simulation runs. This comprehensive approach allows for a more realistic assessment of network performance in dynamic environments.

7.8.2	Call Hold (HOLD)

Call Hold can be provisioned per subscriber or per profile.
If Call Hold is provisioned per subscriber and Call Hold is active, it will be active for all profiles. Data for the Call Hold Supplementary Service will be stored in the HLR, and if appropriate in the VLR, in the usual manner. Call Hold will function as specified in 3G TS 23.083 and will not distinguish between MSP and non-MSP subscribers.
If Call Hold is provisioned per profile then the HOLD_flag shall be set in the HLR (see subclause 6.3: HOLD_flag). On receipt of an Initial_DP message for an MO or MT call, the gsmSCF will check the subscription information for the profile in use for that call. If HOLD is not active and operative, then the SII2 will be included in the Connect message with the HOLD Treatment Indicator set to Reject HOLD Request.

question: What is HOLD?
passage: Call Hold (HOLD) is a supplementary service that can be provisioned either per subscriber or per profile in telecommunications systems. When provisioned per subscriber, Call Hold is active for all profiles associated with that subscriber. The service's data is stored in the Home Location Register (HLR) and, if necessary, in the Visitor Location Register (VLR). Call Hold operates according to the specifications outlined in 3G TS 23.083 and applies uniformly to both Managed Service Provider (MSP) and non-MSP subscribers. If provisioned per profile, the HOLD_flag is set in the HLR, and upon receiving an Initial_DP message for a mobile-originated (MO) or mobile-terminated (MT) call, the gsmSCF checks the subscription information. If Call Hold is not active, the system will reject any HOLD requests by including the HOLD Treatment Indicator set to Reject in the Connect message.

question: What is the downside of using FEC?
gold_answer: it can recover the error up to only a certain level, if there is more errors exceeding the specific level it is impossible to recover error.
passage: The downside of using Forward Error Correction (FEC) is that it can only recover errors up to a certain level. If the amount of errors exceeds this threshold, recovery becomes impossible. Additionally, to enhance the capability of error correction, more redundancy bits must be added to the transmitted data, which increases the overhead. This added complexity can lead to inefficiencies in data transmission, especially in scenarios where the error rate is high, as the system may require significant additional resources to maintain effective communication.

You would realize that most of digital data processing or communication would have not be realized if there is no mechism for error handling (error detection and correction)

First let's think of the definition of 'Error'. What is 'Error' ? It is simple. Error can be defined as 'any difference between the transmitted data and received data'. Once Error happened, we need to have some mechanism to figure out 'whether there exists any error' or 'exactly where is the error occured'. This mechanism of finding the existence of error is called 'Error Detection'. If we know the exact contents of transmitted data, it would be very simple to find out the location of errors. Just simply by comparing the transmitted data
and received data, we can easily find the location of errors. However in realty, we don't know what is the transmitted data (original data). So we have to figure out the location of errors only from the received data. This is why Error detection is not so simple.

Of course, the second type is better in most case since it will give a chance for error recovery. But in most cases, this second type tend to be more complicated to be implemented or requires more overhead for data transfer. This is why the first type of mechanism is still being used in many applications.

What is Error Correction ? The definition is simple.. (only Algorithm is complicated :). Definition of Error Correction is to fixing the error bit (data) to normal bit (data).

Whatever you do, there is no way to prevent any error. The only thing you can do for those errors is to come out with the various methods of detecting and fixing those errors. For this detection/correction, method we need to go through roughly following procedures.

i) Convert (organize) the original data into a special structure in such a way that the reciever can easily detect the error. (This happens on Transmitter side).

iv) Check if there is any error in the received data. This is called Error Detection and happens in the reciever side.

v) If errors are found in step iv), ask for retransmission (ARQ case) or try to recover(fix) the error (FEC or HARQ case). This happens in reciever side.

If you convert data into binary stream and count the number of '1' in the data, it would be only one of two cases.. the total count of '1' is Even or Odd. In Parity Check method, transmitter reorganize the original data so that the total number of '1' is only Even (Even Parity) or only Odd (Odd Parity). Following is the example process for 'Even Parity' algorithm.

This is very simple and still being used in some simple data communication like RS 232 Serial communication. But this is detection only algorithm and it cannot correct error. Even for detection, there are many cases where this algorithm fail to detect errors. (Try think of those cases where this algorithm fails)

In Checksum algorithm, we calculate a special number called 'checksum' value from the original data and add the checksum data to the transmitted data. When the reciever get the data, it calculate the checksum value from the received data and compares the calculated value with the received checksum value.

What a system (two communicating parties) do if the reciever find (detect) an error ? We see roughly three different mode of operations depending on what kind of error handling mechanism the system uses as listed below.

In ARQ, the reciever ask for retransmission of exactly the same data by sending Nack or by skipping any Ack to the transmitter. If the transmitter does get Nack or does not get Ack within a certain time frame, it automatically retransmit the exactly the same data that was transmitted before. The advantage of this mechanism would be that it is simple to implement and it only has to implement
error detection algorithm and does not implement the error correction algorithm. The disadvantage would be that the transmiter would have to send the same data so many times if the channel condition is bad and the reciever keep detecting errors. Most common examples for this mechanism would be IP data or RLC layer transmission in WCDMA, LTE.

In FEC, transmitter encode the data before transmitssion in such a way that the reciever not only detect the error but also recover the error unless the amount of the error exceeds a certain level. In this case, the reciever does not request retransmission, in stead it recover (correct) errors from the redundancy bits and specially designed structure contained in the received data itself.
The advantage of this mechanis is obvious. It is that we don't need retransmission even when there is error. The disadvantage is that it can recover the error up to only a certain level, if there is more errors exceeding the specific level it is impossible to recover error. In order to enable more capability of error correction, we have to put more redundency bits in the transmitted data, meaning it would increase overhead.

HARQ has the property of both ARQ and FEC. It is a kind of Hybrid algorithm and it is where the name come from. It is Hybrid of ARQ and FEC. When the reciever got a data with error, furst it tries to recover (correct) the error with FEC algorithm. If the error correct was successful, it send Ack to the sender. If it fails, it sends Nack to sender. When the sender got the Nack (or no response)
from the reciever, it retransmit the data but when it retransmit the data, it usually send a little bit different sets of the original data (we call it 'different redundency version') and the reciever combines the previous copy and the retransmitted copy to increase probability of error recovery. The advantage of this algorithm is that it adopts the advantage of both ARQ and FEC and reducing the disadvantage of FEC and ARQ. But this would be more complicated to implement than simple ARQ and FEC. One common example
of this mechanism is Physical layer communication in HSDPA and LTE. For further details, refer to LTE HARQ page.

question: What is error correction?
gold_answer: fixing the error bit (data) to normal bit
passage: Error correction is a process used in data communication and storage to identify and fix errors that occur during the transmission or writing of data. An error is defined as any difference between the transmitted data and the received data. The error correction mechanism involves several steps: first, the original data is organized into a special structure that allows the receiver to easily detect errors. This is followed by error detection, where the receiver checks the received data for any discrepancies. If errors are found, the system can either request a retransmission of the data (as in Automatic Repeat reQuest, or ARQ) or attempt to correct the errors using Forward Error Correction (FEC) techniques. FEC allows the receiver to recover from errors without needing to request a resend, as it uses redundancy bits included in the transmitted data. Overall, error correction is essential for ensuring data integrity in communication systems.

question: Why is error handling so important?
gold_answer: most of digital data processing or communication would have not be realized if there is no mechism for error handling (error detection and correction)
passage:
Error handling is crucial in data processing and communications because it ensures the integrity and reliability of transmitted information. An error is defined as any discrepancy between the data sent and the data received, which can occur during transmission or storage. Without effective error handling mechanisms, such as error detection and correction, the functionality of digital communication systems would be severely compromised. 

Error detection allows systems to identify the presence of errors, while error correction enables the recovery of the original data without needing retransmission. These processes are essential for maintaining data accuracy, especially in environments prone to interference or data loss. Various methods, such as parity checks, checksums, and cyclic redundancy checks (CRC), are employed to detect errors, while techniques like Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) and Forward Error Correction (FEC) are used to correct them. 

In summary, error handling is vital for ensuring that data remains accurate and reliable, thereby facilitating effective communication and data processing across various applications.

question: What is CRC?
gold_answer: the transmitter calculate special number called CRC bits
passage: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) is an error-detecting code used to identify changes to raw data in digital networks and storage devices. It involves the generation of a short, fixed-length binary sequence, known as CRC bits, which is derived from the original data using a mathematical algorithm based on polynomial division. The transmitter appends these CRC bits to the data before transmission. Upon receiving the data, the receiver performs the same polynomial division on the received data (including the CRC bits) and checks if the result matches the expected value. If there is a discrepancy, it indicates that an error has occurred during transmission. CRC is widely used in various communication protocols, including Ethernet and IP, due to its effectiveness in detecting common types of errors.

What a system (two communicating parties) do if the reciever find (detect) an error ? We see roughly three different mode of operations depending on what kind of error handling mechanism the system uses as listed below.

In ARQ, the reciever ask for retransmission of exactly the same data by sending Nack or by skipping any Ack to the transmitter. If the transmitter does get Nack or does not get Ack within a certain time frame, it automatically retransmit the exactly the same data that was transmitted before. The advantage of this mechanism would be that it is simple to implement and it only has to implement
error detection algorithm and does not implement the error correction algorithm. The disadvantage would be that the transmiter would have to send the same data so many times if the channel condition is bad and the reciever keep detecting errors. Most common examples for this mechanism would be IP data or RLC layer transmission in WCDMA, LTE.

In FEC, transmitter encode the data before transmitssion in such a way that the reciever not only detect the error but also recover the error unless the amount of the error exceeds a certain level. In this case, the reciever does not request retransmission, in stead it recover (correct) errors from the redundancy bits and specially designed structure contained in the received data itself.
The advantage of this mechanis is obvious. It is that we don't need retransmission even when there is error. The disadvantage is that it can recover the error up to only a certain level, if there is more errors exceeding the specific level it is impossible to recover error. In order to enable more capability of error correction, we have to put more redundency bits in the transmitted data, meaning it would increase overhead.

HARQ has the property of both ARQ and FEC. It is a kind of Hybrid algorithm and it is where the name come from. It is Hybrid of ARQ and FEC. When the reciever got a data with error, furst it tries to recover (correct) the error with FEC algorithm. If the error correct was successful, it send Ack to the sender. If it fails, it sends Nack to sender. When the sender got the Nack (or no response)
from the reciever, it retransmit the data but when it retransmit the data, it usually send a little bit different sets of the original data (we call it 'different redundency version') and the reciever combines the previous copy and the retransmitted copy to increase probability of error recovery. The advantage of this algorithm is that it adopts the advantage of both ARQ and FEC and reducing the disadvantage of FEC and ARQ. But this would be more complicated to implement than simple ARQ and FEC. One common example
of this mechanism is Physical layer communication in HSDPA and LTE. For further details, refer to LTE HARQ page.

question: In ARQ, what happens when the transmitter does not get Nack or Ack?
gold_answer: it automatically retransmit the exactly the same data that was transmitted before
passage: In Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) protocols, when the transmitter does not receive a Negative Acknowledgment (Nack) or an Acknowledgment (Ack) from the receiver within a specified time frame, it assumes that the transmitted data may not have been successfully received. Consequently, the transmitter will automatically retransmit the same data that was sent previously. This mechanism is designed to ensure data integrity by allowing for the possibility of errors in transmission, as the receiver may not have been able to confirm receipt of the data due to various issues such as poor channel conditions. The simplicity of this approach is one of its advantages, although it can lead to increased overhead if the channel conditions are consistently poor, resulting in multiple retransmissions of the same data.

question: What is the disadvantage of parity check?
gold_answer: this is detection only algorithm and it cannot correct error.
passage: The primary disadvantage of the parity check method is its inability to correct errors; it can only detect them. Parity checks can fail to identify certain types of errors, particularly when an even number of bits are altered, as this can result in the same parity outcome. For example, if two bits are flipped, the parity remains unchanged, leading to undetected errors. This limitation makes parity checks less reliable for critical applications where error correction is necessary. Additionally, while parity checks are simple to implement, they do not provide information about the location of the error, which can complicate the recovery process.

question: What does Error mean?

To manage errors, systems implement mechanisms for error detection and correction, which are essential for ensuring data integrity and reliability in communication processes.

question: What does the checksum algorithm do?
gold_answer: calculate a special number called 'checksum' value from the original data and add the checksum data to the transmitted data
passage: The checksum algorithm is a method used for error detection in data transmission. It works by calculating a special numerical value, known as the checksum, from the original data before transmission. This checksum is then appended to the transmitted data. Upon receiving the data, the receiver recalculates the checksum from the received data and compares it to the checksum that was sent. If the two values match, it indicates that the data was likely transmitted without errors. If they do not match, it suggests that an error occurred during transmission. While the checksum algorithm is more robust than simpler methods like parity checks, it is still primarily a detection-only algorithm and does not correct errors. It is commonly used in various communication protocols, including IP transmission.

question: What are the cons of the ARQ algorithm?
gold_answer: the transmiter would have to send the same data so many times if the channel condition is bad and the reciever keep detecting errors
passage: The Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) algorithm, while effective for error handling in data communication, has several notable disadvantages. One major con is the potential for increased latency, as the need for retransmission of data can lead to delays, especially in poor channel conditions where errors are frequent. This can significantly impact the overall throughput of the communication system. Additionally, ARQ can lead to inefficient use of bandwidth, as the same data may be sent multiple times if errors persist, resulting in wasted resources. Furthermore, ARQ relies heavily on the assumption that the channel conditions will improve, which may not always be the case, leading to repeated failures in data transmission. Lastly, ARQ does not correct errors; it only detects them and requests retransmission, which means that it may not be suitable for real-time applications where timely delivery is critical.

question: How does checksum work?
gold_answer: calculate a special number called 'checksum' value from the original data and add the checksum data to the transmitted data. When the reciever get the data, it calculate the checksum value from the received data and compares the calculated value with the received checksum value
passage: Checksum is a method used for error detection in data transmission. It works by calculating a special numerical value, known as the checksum, from the original data before it is transmitted. This checksum value is then appended to the data being sent. Upon receiving the data, the receiver recalculates the checksum from the received data and compares it to the checksum value that was sent along with the data. If the two checksum values match, it indicates that the data was likely transmitted without errors. If they do not match, it suggests that an error occurred during transmission. While checksum is effective for detecting errors, it does not provide a mechanism for correcting them, making it primarily a detection-only algorithm. This method is commonly used in various communication protocols, including IP transmission.

question: What should we do when an error occurred?
gold_answer: come out with the various methods of detecting and fixing those errors
passage:
When an error occurs in data transmission or processing, it is essential to implement an effective error handling mechanism. The first step is to detect the error, which can be achieved through various methods such as parity checks, checksums, or cyclic redundancy checks (CRC). Once an error is detected, the system can take appropriate action based on the error handling strategy in place.

There are three primary approaches to handle errors: Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ), Forward Error Correction (FEC), and Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ). In ARQ, the receiver requests a retransmission of the erroneous data, ensuring that the correct information is received. FEC allows the receiver to correct certain errors without needing retransmission by using redundancy in the transmitted data. HARQ combines both ARQ and FEC, where the receiver first attempts to correct the error and, if unsuccessful, requests a retransmission of modified data.

By employing these mechanisms, systems can effectively manage errors, ensuring data integrity and reliable communication.

The advantage of this algorithm is that it adopts the advantage of both ARQ and FEC and reducing the disadvantage of FEC and ARQ. But this would be more complicated to implement than simple ARQ and FEC. One common example
of this mechanism is Physical layer communication in HSDPA and LTE. For further details, refer to LTE HARQ page.

question: How can one detect data bit error?
passage: To detect data bit errors, various error detection mechanisms are employed in data communication and storage systems. One common method is the Parity Check, where the original data is organized to ensure that the total number of '1's is either even (Even Parity) or odd (Odd Parity). While simple, this method can fail to detect certain errors. Another approach is the Checksum algorithm, which calculates a checksum value from the original data and appends it to the transmitted data. Upon receipt, the receiver recalculates the checksum and compares it to the received value to check for discrepancies. A more robust method is the Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC), which involves generating a CRC value based on the data and comparing it upon receipt. If an error is detected, systems may employ Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) to request retransmission of the data, or Forward Error Correction (FEC) to attempt to correct the error without retransmission. These methods are essential for ensuring data integrity in communication systems.

question: In which case is attempts made to fix the error?
passage: In the context of error handling in data communication, attempts to fix errors occur primarily in two mechanisms: Forward Error Correction (FEC) and Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ). In FEC, the transmitter encodes the data in such a way that the receiver can detect and correct errors without needing to request retransmission. This is achieved through redundancy bits and a specially designed structure within the transmitted data. On the other hand, HARQ combines the features of both FEC and Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ). In HARQ, when the receiver detects an error, it first attempts to correct it using FEC. If the correction fails, it then requests a retransmission of the data, often sending a different version to improve the chances of successful recovery. Thus, both FEC and HARQ involve attempts to fix errors, with FEC doing so directly and HARQ utilizing a combination of correction and retransmission strategies.

question: What is HMD?
passage: HMD stands for Head-Mounted Display, which is a device worn on the head that completely replaces the user's field of view with a simulated visual component. It is commonly used in virtual reality (VR) applications to immerse users in a digitally created environment. Along with audio provided through headphones, HMDs allow users to interact with the virtual world by tracking their head movements, enabling them to look around in three-dimensional space. This technology is essential for delivering an engaging VR experience, as it facilitates the perception of depth and spatial awareness within the virtual environment.

12.4.3	Virtual Reality Profiles for Streaming Media

Summary based on the input provided by Qualcomm Incorporated in SP-180746.

This summary reports on the normative specification progress accomplished during the course of the VRStream work item [1]. Primarily, the "Virtual Reality Profiles for Streaming Media" specification in TS.26.118 [2] was developed to support Virtual Reality (VR) in streaming applications. In addition, the media capabilities are enabled in Packet Switched Streaming (PSS) Services and Multimedia Broadcast Multicast Service (MBMS) by updates of the specifications TS 26.234 [3] and TS 26.346 [4], respectively. The characterization results for audio media profile proponents are documented in TR 26.818 [5].

Based on the findings in TR 26.918 [6], the work item developed the first set of Virtual Reality Profiles for Streaming Media. Virtual Reality (VR) is the ability to be virtually present in a space created by the rendering of natural and/or synthetic image and sound correlated by the movements of the immersed user allowing interacting with that world. Virtual reality typically assumes a user to wear a head mounted display (HMD), to completely replace the user's field of view with a simulated visual component, and to wear headphones, to provide the user with the accompanying audio. In the first set of technologies defined in TS 26.118, VR users are expected to be able to look around from a single observation point in 3D space, also referred to as three degrees of freedom (3DoF). It allows the user to (i) tilt side to side (Rolling), (ii) tilt forward and backward (Pitching), and (iii) turning left and right (Yawing). The specification defines a 3GPP 3DOF reference and coordinate system as well as an end-to-end architecture. In the reference client, it is assumed that pose information, i.e. the position derived by the head tracking sensor expressed by (azimuth; elevation; tilt angle), is continuously available to the VR renderer in order to render the viewport. Based on the system model, video and audio technologies are defined including system technologies (DASH and file format), suitable codecs and rendering technologies.

Specifically on video, three operation points (combination of elementary stream and rendering metadata) and three corresponding media profiles are defined, namely:

For PSS, all three profiles are added, the first one is mandatory ( 'shall'), the second one recommended ('should') and the third one allowed ('may'). For MBMS, the first two profiles are added, the first one is mandatory ( 'shall'), the second one is recommended ( 'should') and constrained to non-viewport adaptive streaming.

For audio, one solution was selected and is documented in TS 26.118, namely MPEG-H 3D Audio Baseline profile. This technology enables the distribution of channel, object and scene-based 3D audio. Additional interesting technologies enabling the distribution of channel, object and scene-based 3D audio were considered, and the characterization results of all proposed technologies are documented in TR 26.818 [5].

In addition to media specific metadata, system metadata is added to TS 26.118 to support rendering of 360 experiences on 2D screens, including the aspects of rendering without pose information. Basic requirements for a full audio-visual experience are documented under the umbrella of VR Presentations.

The completion of the work item provides a set of consistent technologies for Virtual Reality in Rel-15 for 5G Phase 1. It is providing a response to the demand identified during the successful joint 3GPP/VR-IF Workshop on Virtual Reality that took place in December 2017 [7], which was an integral part of the development of 3GPP Virtual Reality Profiles for Streaming Applications.

question: What are PSS Services?
passage: PSS Services, or Packet Switched Streaming Services, are designed to facilitate the streaming of media content over packet-switched networks. In the context of Virtual Reality (VR), PSS Services enable the delivery of immersive audio and video experiences by supporting specific media profiles that enhance the streaming quality and interactivity for VR applications. The specifications for PSS Services have been updated to include capabilities for streaming VR content, allowing users to experience three degrees of freedom (3DoF) in a virtual environment. This includes mandatory, recommended, and allowed profiles for video streaming, as well as advanced audio technologies like MPEG-H 3D Audio, which provide a rich audio experience. Overall, PSS Services play a crucial role in delivering high-quality VR content in 5G networks, responding to the growing demand for immersive media experiences.
