2G/3G: eCall

What is 'eCall' ? In other words, you may ask 'what does the letter 'e' stands for ? Does it mean 'emergency' ? or 'electronic' ? or something else ?

Even though I haven't seen any formal documents that explicitely defines the letter 'e' in eCall, I think it would not be wrong if you say the 'e' mean 'emergency', i.e, 'eCall' would mean 'emergency Call'. But this interpretation would confuse a lot of people. Then, how does eCall differ from what we normally call 'Emergency Call (like 911)' ?

I will explain on the details of this difference later, but simply put, the biggest difference would be the usual 'Emergency call' is a kind of voice call between a human and Emergency Call Center (usually another person in Emergency Call Center)' but 'eCall' is a call between a machine (called IVS : In Vehicle System within an automobile) and Emergency Center;.

For the persons who likes formal definition, I would quote some descriptions from a couple of international standards as follows :

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

Before we talk of the technical details of eCall, let's take a 10000-feet overview (high level view) on how eCall go through. You may find a lot of illustrations, cartoons on eCall from internet and following is my own version of illustration. I put the number labels on each of the steps and I would put a short descriptions on what's happening at each step.

(2) eCall is triggered. eCall can be triggered in many ways. It can be triggered automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors. Or a person (e.g, driver) in the car can push the emergency button in the car to trigger the eCall.

(3) The eCall device installed in the car (called IVS : In-Vehicle System) go through Emergency Voice Call setup process to establish the voice call channel. Once the voice call channel is established, the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point)

(4) Once the eCall Data(MSD) is received by PSAP, the information would show up automatically on the screen at PSAP center.

(5) The personnel at PSAP center may try voice contact to the person in the car if possible. But there would be many cases where this is not possible when person in the car is injured badly.

For those who came from Cellular protocol and new to eCall, it would be a little confusing on figuring out the difference between eCall and another type of Emergency Call (like 911 in North America) which we are familiar with in daily life. For those people, I think it would be easier / clearer to explain the difference in terms of overall protocol sequence. Following is my understanding (the image formed in my brain when I first got trained about this).

As you see here in the following illustration, there is common portions and different portions between eCall and Emergency Call.

NOTE : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

eCall Higher Layer Application Protocol (HLAP) is very simple (at least comparting to Cellular Protocol). Actually there is only one critical data to be transferred. The critical data is called MSD(Minimal Set of Data). All the remaining part is just to get MSD delivered to PSAP (Emergency Call Center) with reliability.

As in Cellular Voice Call, in HLAP there are two different type of call mode depending on who (IVS or PSAP) initiates call. The eCall initiated by IVS is called 'PUSH mode' and this is similar concept as MO(Mobile Originating) call in cellular voice call.

The eCall initiated by PSAP is called 'PULL mode' and this is similar concept as MT(Mobile Terminating) call in cellular voice call.

The two illustrations in this section is based on ETSI 103.428 Figure 2. The ETSI diagram is a single diagram showing both PUSH and PULL mode in single sequence. It looked a little confusing to me, so I split the digram into two separate diagram as shown below.

NOTE 1 : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

NOTE 2 : PSAP stands for Public Safety Answering Point. This is a kind of Emergency Call Center.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MO call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by IVS (the mobile unit installed inside the car). I think in most case of eCall, the eCall goes in PUSH mode as illustrated below.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MT call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by PSAP (the call center). If you compare this with PUSH mode sequence, you would notice that most of the part are same. The only difference is the SEND-MSD (START) signal before the Initiation signal. This is also very much like cellular protocol. If you compare the MO Call and MT Call sequence in cellular protocol, you would notice that most part of the two are almost same. The main difference is that in MT Call the cellular network send 'Paging' (a kind of trigger for UE to initiate the call).

Another sequence that illustrate the eCall process with a little low layer point of view (especially in terms of LL/HL ACK operation) is shown below. This applies to both PUSH and PULL model.

< ETSI TR 126.969 - Figure 1: Timeline of eCall with IVS initiated signalling and HL-ACK in normal operation >

There are various timers in eCall protocol which should be met in order to guarantee the normal functionality of the eCall. Some of these timers are an important criterial of testing eCall functionality.

As mentioned above, the only one fundamental goal for eCall is to deliver MSD(Minimal Set of Data) with reliability. Then you may ask what kind of information is in the MSD. High level description of the imformation in MSD can be find from following description. As you see, the most important information in the MSD is the location data and vehicle information.

The eCall modem allows to transfer a data message from the IVS over the cellular network to the PSAP which is denoted as eCall MSD. The MSD can include, e.g. vehicle location information, time stamp, number of passengers, Vehicle Identification Number (VIN), and other relevant accident information

The Minimum Set of Data forming the data component of an eCall sent from a vehicle to a Public Safety Answering Point or other designated emergency call centre. The MSD has a maximum size of 140 bytes and includes, for example, vehicle identity, location information and time-stamp.

Before we think of this, let's think of why we need to care of this. We should care of this because eCall signaling message and data are delivered in the form of Voice call data of GSM or WCDMA cellular network.

In GSM / WCDMA, various different types of codecs are used. Basically the codec selection is a job for the specific Radio Access Network equipment(RAN Equipment) that is communicating with the eCall device. The RAN Equipment (Network) would select the codec that would give the best performance in a specific situation. 'Performance' mean 'How fast the eCall data can be delivered' and 'How reliably it can be delivered under a specific channel condition'. It would be too much (or too boring) to present the full details on these performance here. If you are really interested in the details, refer to ETSI TR 126.969 and it would give you a lot of test data for various different Codecs.

In theory, you can use a live network and PSAP Simulator to test your eCall Device (IVS). But theory is just a theory. You would come across a lot of issues to overcome if you go for this option even though I cannot say it is impossible.

Another way of testing the eCall device is to construct test setup as described in ETSI 103.428 section 6 Test Configurations. In this document, it is described to use a private cellular network for various Interoperability and Conformance Testing.

The most practical solution (Test setup) that will be used in the industry would be to use Cellular Network Simulator and PSAP simulator as illustrated below.

Assuming that you have a test setup and you need to determine what to test. As in most of other wireless and cellular device device, you may think of general test that tend to happen during the development or system integration stage. We often call these test in various different name such as function test, integration test or smoke test etc. Usually test specification / procedure tend not to be clearly defined or the procedure changes often depending on situations. Also those test procedure / test item may vary depending on manufacturer. Therefore, it would not be easy to clearly define on what to test for this stage. However, if you just take a close look at the overall eCall protocol, you would easily guess high level test items even without looking into any specification. My personal version of the guess work about the first level test are shown below. You may come up with different idea, but I don't think there would be any big difference between your idea and my idea.

Once you complete the general function test during development and system integration level and have a stable device, you would forward the device to conformance test. Once you are at the stage of conformance test, you don't have to worry about what to test because a lot of other people (standard body) put a lot of effort and energy and came out with well defined document. In 3GPP/ETSI, those test procedures are defined in ETSI TS 103.428.

After completing the conformance, if you are trying to sell the device (acutually Automakers trying to sell cars) in a specific region (e.g, Europe, Asia, America etc), you may need to go through a specific set of test cases specified by the regulatory body in that specific region.

Followings are the examples of how eCall is being testing during the development or for conformance test before commercialization.

Followings are the list of the specifications for eCall. I think the most fundamental specifications are CEN documents. But it is not free to get those spec. Recently 3GPP / ETSI has released various specifications. I think most part of the 3GPP specification are based on CEN specification.

: Describes mostly on physical/transport layer design and process of transmitter and reciever.

: This documents describes on API and parameter descriptions of eCall modem protocol stack. It describes on overall software architecture and API prototype but not show the function body. Unless you are developing the protocol stack, you would not need to read this spec.

: This documents describes general logics on eCall Test, but it does not specifies any specific test cases or details of protocol sequence. If you are interested in physical / transport layer level testing, this document would help you to catch the overall test concept.

: If you are interested in high level protocol and function test, this document would help a lot. It shows overall protocol sequence of eCall and decfines specific test sequences. Most of the test in this document (as of V1.1.1 (2016-06)) are based on CEN EN 16062:2015

question: What is HLAP?
passage: eCall Higher Layer Application Protocol (HLAP) is a communication protocol used in the eCall system, which facilitates emergency calls from vehicles to Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs). HLAP is designed to transfer a critical piece of data known as the Minimal Set of Data (MSD), which includes essential information such as vehicle location, time stamp, and vehicle identification. The protocol operates in two modes: 'PUSH mode', where the In-Vehicle System (IVS) initiates the call, and 'PULL mode', where the PSAP initiates the call. The primary goal of HLAP is to ensure the reliable delivery of the MSD to emergency services, thereby improving response times in critical situations.

question: Where can a description of the construction of an eCall test setup be found?
passage: A description of the construction of an eCall test setup can be found in the ETSI 103.428 document, specifically in section 6, which outlines Test Configurations. This document details the use of a private cellular network for various interoperability and conformance testing of eCall devices. Additionally, it suggests utilizing a Cellular Network Simulator and a PSAP simulator as part of the practical test setup commonly used in the industry. For further insights into the testing procedures and requirements, the ETSI TS 103.428 specification provides comprehensive guidelines.

The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

question: What is the difference between eCall and 911 in North America?
passage:
eCall and 911 serve different purposes in emergency response systems. eCall is an automated emergency call system specifically designed for vehicles, which can be triggered manually by the driver or automatically by the vehicle's sensors (such as airbags). It establishes a connection between the vehicle's In-Vehicle System (IVS) and a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP), transmitting critical data such as the vehicle's location, time of the incident, and other relevant information (known as the Minimum Set of Data or MSD) alongside a voice call. This allows emergency services to respond more quickly and effectively.

In contrast, 911 is a traditional emergency call service in North America that relies on a human operator receiving a voice call from an individual in distress. The caller provides information about the emergency, and the operator dispatches the appropriate services. While both systems aim to facilitate emergency assistance, eCall enhances the process by providing automated data that can expedite response times, especially in situations where the caller may be incapacitated or unable to communicate effectively.

What is 'eCall' ? In other words, you may ask 'what does the letter 'e' stands for ? Does it mean 'emergency' ? or 'electronic' ? or something else ?

Even though I haven't seen any formal documents that explicitely defines the letter 'e' in eCall, I think it would not be wrong if you say the 'e' mean 'emergency', i.e, 'eCall' would mean 'emergency Call'. But this interpretation would confuse a lot of people. Then, how does eCall differ from what we normally call 'Emergency Call (like 911)' ?

I will explain on the details of this difference later, but simply put, the biggest difference would be the usual 'Emergency call' is a kind of voice call between a human and Emergency Call Center (usually another person in Emergency Call Center)' but 'eCall' is a call between a machine (called IVS : In Vehicle System within an automobile) and Emergency Center;.

For the persons who likes formal definition, I would quote some descriptions from a couple of international standards as follows :

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

question: How can eCall be initiated?
passage: eCall can be initiated in two primary ways: automatically or manually. Automatic initiation occurs when the vehicle's internal sensors, such as those triggered by an airbag deployment, detect a crash and automatically send an emergency call. Alternatively, a driver or passenger can manually trigger the eCall by pressing an emergency button located in the vehicle. Once initiated, the eCall system, known as the In-Vehicle System (IVS), establishes a voice call with the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) and transmits a Minimal Set of Data (MSD) that includes critical information such as the vehicle's location and identification details.

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

Before we talk of the technical details of eCall, let's take a 10000-feet overview (high level view) on how eCall go through. You may find a lot of illustrations, cartoons on eCall from internet and following is my own version of illustration. I put the number labels on each of the steps and I would put a short descriptions on what's happening at each step.

(2) eCall is triggered. eCall can be triggered in many ways. It can be triggered automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors. Or a person (e.g, driver) in the car can push the emergency button in the car to trigger the eCall.

(3) The eCall device installed in the car (called IVS : In-Vehicle System) go through Emergency Voice Call setup process to establish the voice call channel. Once the voice call channel is established, the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point)

(4) Once the eCall Data(MSD) is received by PSAP, the information would show up automatically on the screen at PSAP center.

(5) The personnel at PSAP center may try voice contact to the person in the car if possible. But there would be many cases where this is not possible when person in the car is injured badly.

For those who came from Cellular protocol and new to eCall, it would be a little confusing on figuring out the difference between eCall and another type of Emergency Call (like 911 in North America) which we are familiar with in daily life. For those people, I think it would be easier / clearer to explain the difference in terms of overall protocol sequence. Following is my understanding (the image formed in my brain when I first got trained about this).

As you see here in the following illustration, there is common portions and different portions between eCall and Emergency Call.

NOTE : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

eCall Higher Layer Application Protocol (HLAP) is very simple (at least comparting to Cellular Protocol). Actually there is only one critical data to be transferred. The critical data is called MSD(Minimal Set of Data). All the remaining part is just to get MSD delivered to PSAP (Emergency Call Center) with reliability.

As in Cellular Voice Call, in HLAP there are two different type of call mode depending on who (IVS or PSAP) initiates call. The eCall initiated by IVS is called 'PUSH mode' and this is similar concept as MO(Mobile Originating) call in cellular voice call.

The eCall initiated by PSAP is called 'PULL mode' and this is similar concept as MT(Mobile Terminating) call in cellular voice call.

The two illustrations in this section is based on ETSI 103.428 Figure 2. The ETSI diagram is a single diagram showing both PUSH and PULL mode in single sequence. It looked a little confusing to me, so I split the digram into two separate diagram as shown below.

NOTE 1 : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

NOTE 2 : PSAP stands for Public Safety Answering Point. This is a kind of Emergency Call Center.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MO call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by IVS (the mobile unit installed inside the car). I think in most case of eCall, the eCall goes in PUSH mode as illustrated below.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MT call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by PSAP (the call center). If you compare this with PUSH mode sequence, you would notice that most of the part are same. The only difference is the SEND-MSD (START) signal before the Initiation signal. This is also very much like cellular protocol. If you compare the MO Call and MT Call sequence in cellular protocol, you would notice that most part of the two are almost same. There are various timers in eCall protocol which should be met in order to guarantee the normal functionality of the eCall. Some of these timers are an important criterial of testing eCall functionality.

As mentioned above, the only one fundamental goal for eCall is to deliver MSD(Minimal Set of Data) with reliability. Then you may ask what kind of information is in the MSD. High level description of the imformation in MSD can be find from following description. As you see, the most important information in the MSD is the location data and vehicle information.

The eCall modem allows to transfer a data message from the IVS over the cellular network to the PSAP which is denoted as eCall MSD. The MSD can include, e.g. vehicle location information, time stamp, number of passengers, Vehicle Identification Number (VIN), and other relevant accident information

The Minimum Set of Data forming the data component of an eCall sent from a vehicle to a Public Safety Answering Point or other designated emergency call centre. The MSD has a maximum size of 140 bytes and includes, for example, vehicle identity, location information and time-stamp.

Before we think of this, let's think of why we need to care of this. We should care of this because eCall signaling message and data are delivered in the form of Voice call data of GSM or WCDMA cellular network.

In GSM / WCDMA, various different types of codecs are used. Basically the codec selection is a job for the specific Radio Access Network equipment(RAN Equipment) that is communicating with the eCall device. The RAN Equipment (Network) would select the codec that would give the best performance in a specific situation. 'Performance' mean 'How fast the eCall data can be delivered' and 'How reliably it can be delivered under a specific channel condition'. It would be too much (or too boring) to present the full details on these performance here. If you are really interested in the details, refer to ETSI TR 126.969 and it would give you a lot of test data for various different Codecs.

In theory, you can use a live network and PSAP Simulator to test your eCall Device (IVS). But theory is just a theory. You would come across a lot of issues to overcome if you go for this option even though I cannot say it is impossible.

Another way of testing the eCall device is to construct test setup as described in ETSI 103.428 section 6 Test Configurations. In this document, it is described to use a private cellular network for various Interoperability and Conformance Testing.

The most practical solution (Test setup) that will be used in the industry would be to use Cellular Network Simulator and PSAP simulator as illustrated below.

Assuming that you have a test setup and you need to determine what to test. As in most of other wireless and cellular device device, you may think of general test that tend to happen during the development or system integration stage. We often call these test in various different name such as function test, integration test or smoke test etc. Usually test specification / procedure tend not to be clearly defined or the procedure changes often depending on situations. Also those test procedure / test item may vary depending on manufacturer. Therefore, it would not be easy to clearly define on what to test for this stage. However, if you just take a close look at the overall eCall protocol, you would easily guess high level test items even without looking into any specification. My personal version of the guess work about the first level test are shown below. You may come up with different idea, but I don't think there would be any big difference between your idea and my idea.

Once you complete the general function test during development and system integration level and have a stable device, you would forward the device to conformance test. Once you are at the stage of conformance test, you don't have to worry about what to test because a lot of other people (standard body) put a lot of effort and energy and came out with well defined document. In 3GPP/ETSI, those test procedures are defined in ETSI TS 103.428.

After completing the conformance, if you are trying to sell the device (acutually Automakers trying to sell cars) in a specific region (e.g, Europe, Asia, America etc), you may need to go through a specific set of test cases specified by the regulatory body in that specific region.

question: How many eCalls are triggered?
passage: eCalls can be triggered in two primary ways: automatically or manually. Automatic triggering occurs when the vehicle's internal sensors, such as those in the airbag system, detect a collision or significant impact. In contrast, a manual trigger allows a person, typically the driver, to initiate the eCall by pressing an emergency button located in the vehicle. This dual mechanism ensures that eCalls can be activated in various emergency situations, enhancing the chances of timely assistance from emergency services.

question: What is IVS?
passage: IVS stands for In-Vehicle System, which is a critical component of the eCall system used in automobiles. The IVS is responsible for initiating emergency calls (eCalls) to Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs) in the event of an accident. It can be triggered automatically by vehicle sensors, such as airbags, or manually by the driver. The IVS transmits a Minimal Set of Data (MSD) that includes vital information such as the vehicle's location, time stamp, and other relevant details to assist emergency services in responding quickly and effectively. This system enhances the efficiency of emergency response by providing accurate data directly from the vehicle involved in an incident.

question: What happens once the eCall device has established the voice call channel?
gold_answer: the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point
passage: Once the eCall device has established the voice call channel, it sends the Minimal Set of Data (MSD) to the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). This data transmission occurs over the same voice channel used for the emergency voice call, allowing for reliable communication of critical information such as vehicle location, time stamp, and other relevant accident details. The MSD is designed to provide emergency services with essential information quickly, enabling them to respond more effectively to the incident. After the MSD is received by the PSAP, it appears automatically on the screen at the emergency center, facilitating a prompt response from emergency personnel.

2G/3G: eCall

What is 'eCall' ? In other words, you may ask 'what does the letter 'e' stands for ? Does it mean 'emergency' ? or 'electronic' ? or something else ?

Even though I haven't seen any formal documents that explicitely defines the letter 'e' in eCall, I think it would not be wrong if you say the 'e' mean 'emergency', i.e, 'eCall' would mean 'emergency Call'. But this interpretation would confuse a lot of people. Then, how does eCall differ from what we normally call 'Emergency Call (like 911)' ?

I will explain on the details of this difference later, but simply put, the biggest difference would be the usual 'Emergency call' is a kind of voice call between a human and Emergency Call Center (usually another person in Emergency Call Center)' but 'eCall' is a call between a machine (called IVS : In Vehicle System within an automobile) and Emergency Center;.

For the persons who likes formal definition, I would quote some descriptions from a couple of international standards as follows :

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

Before we talk of the technical details of eCall, let's take a 10000-feet overview (high level view) on how eCall go through. You may find a lot of illustrations, cartoons on eCall from internet and following is my own version of illustration. I put the number labels on each of the steps and I would put a short descriptions on what's happening at each step.

(2) eCall is triggered. eCall can be triggered in many ways. It can be triggered automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors. Or a person (e.g, driver) in the car can push the emergency button in the car to trigger the eCall.

(3) The eCall device installed in the car (called IVS : In-Vehicle System) go through Emergency Voice Call setup process to establish the voice call channel. Once the voice call channel is established, the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point)

(4) Once the eCall Data(MSD) is received by PSAP, the information would show up automatically on the screen at PSAP center.

(5) The personnel at PSAP center may try voice contact to the person in the car if possible. But there would be many cases where this is not possible when person in the car is injured badly.

For those who came from Cellular protocol and new to eCall, it would be a little confusing on figuring out the difference between eCall and another type of Emergency Call (like 911 in North America) which we are familiar with in daily life. For those people, I think it would be easier / clearer to explain the difference in terms of overall protocol sequence. Following is my understanding (the image formed in my brain when I first got trained about this).

As you see here in the following illustration, there is common portions and different portions between eCall and Emergency Call.

NOTE : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

eCall Higher Layer Application Protocol (HLAP) is very simple (at least comparting to Cellular Protocol). Actually there is only one critical data to be transferred. The critical data is called MSD(Minimal Set of Data). All the remaining part is just to get MSD delivered to PSAP (Emergency Call Center) with reliability.

As in Cellular Voice Call, in HLAP there are two different type of call mode depending on who (IVS or PSAP) initiates call. The eCall initiated by IVS is called 'PUSH mode' and this is similar concept as MO(Mobile Originating) call in cellular voice call.

The eCall initiated by PSAP is called 'PULL mode' and this is similar concept as MT(Mobile Terminating) call in cellular voice call.

The two illustrations in this section is based on ETSI 103.428 Figure 2. The ETSI diagram is a single diagram showing both PUSH and PULL mode in single sequence. It looked a little confusing to me, so I split the digram into two separate diagram as shown below.

NOTE 1 : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

NOTE 2 : PSAP stands for Public Safety Answering Point. This is a kind of Emergency Call Center.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MO call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by IVS (the mobile unit installed inside the car). I think in most case of eCall, the eCall goes in PUSH mode as illustrated below.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MT call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by PSAP (the call center). If you compare this with PUSH mode sequence, you would notice that most of the part are same. The only difference is the SEND-MSD (START) signal before the Initiation signal. This is also very much like cellular protocol. If you compare the MO Call and MT Call sequence in cellular protocol, you would notice that most part of the two are almost same. The main difference is that in MT Call the cellular network send 'Paging' (a kind of trigger for UE to initiate the call).

High level description of the imformation in MSD can be find from following description. As you see, the most important information in the MSD is the location data and vehicle information.

The eCall modem allows to transfer a data message from the IVS over the cellular network to the PSAP which is denoted as eCall MSD. The MSD can include, e.g. vehicle location information, time stamp, number of passengers, Vehicle Identification Number (VIN), and other relevant accident information

The Minimum Set of Data forming the data component of an eCall sent from a vehicle to a Public Safety Answering Point or other designated emergency call centre. The MSD has a maximum size of 140 bytes and includes, for example, vehicle identity, location information and time-stamp.

Basically the codec selection is a job for the specific Radio Access Network equipment(RAN Equipment) that is communicating with the eCall device. The RAN Equipment (Network) would select the codec that would give the best performance in a specific situation. 'Performance' mean 'How fast the eCall data can be delivered' and 'How reliably it can be delivered under a specific channel condition'. It would be too much (or too boring) to present the full details on these performance here. question: Where in the car are the eCall module installed in most cases?
passage: The eCall module, known as the In-Vehicle System (IVS), is typically installed within the telematics module of a car. This placement allows the eCall system to effectively communicate with emergency services by automatically or manually initiating emergency calls and transmitting critical data, such as the vehicle's location and identification information, in the event of an accident. The integration of the eCall module within the telematics system ensures that it can leverage existing cellular networks for reliable communication with Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs).

2G/3G: eCall

What is 'eCall' ? In other words, you may ask 'what does the letter 'e' stands for ? Does it mean 'emergency' ? or 'electronic' ? or something else ?

Even though I haven't seen any formal documents that explicitely defines the letter 'e' in eCall, I think it would not be wrong if you say the 'e' mean 'emergency', i.e, 'eCall' would mean 'emergency Call'. But this interpretation would confuse a lot of people. Then, how does eCall differ from what we normally call 'Emergency Call (like 911)' ?

I will explain on the details of this difference later, but simply put, the biggest difference would be the usual 'Emergency call' is a kind of voice call between a human and Emergency Call Center (usually another person in Emergency Call Center)' but 'eCall' is a call between a machine (called IVS : In Vehicle System within an automobile) and Emergency Center;.

For the persons who likes formal definition, I would quote some descriptions from a couple of international standards as follows :

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

Before we talk of the technical details of eCall, let's take a 10000-feet overview (high level view) on how eCall go through. You may find a lot of illustrations, cartoons on eCall from internet and following is my own version of illustration. I put the number labels on each of the steps and I would put a short descriptions on what's happening at each step.

(2) eCall is triggered. eCall can be triggered in many ways. It can be triggered automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors. Or a person (e.g, driver) in the car can push the emergency button in the car to trigger the eCall.

(3) The eCall device installed in the car (called IVS : In-Vehicle System) go through Emergency Voice Call setup process to establish the voice call channel. Once the voice call channel is established, the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point)

(4) Once the eCall Data(MSD) is received by PSAP, the information would show up automatically on the screen at PSAP center.

(5) The personnel at PSAP center may try voice contact to the person in the car if possible. But there would be many cases where this is not possible when person in the car is injured badly.

question: Who receives the eCall Data MSD
passage: The eCall Data, known as the Minimal Set of Data (MSD), is received by the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). When an eCall is triggered, the In-Vehicle System (IVS) in the vehicle establishes a voice call with the PSAP and simultaneously transmits the MSD. This data includes critical information such as the vehicle's location, time stamp, number of passengers, and Vehicle Identification Number (VIN). The PSAP personnel can then use this information to respond more effectively to the emergency situation.

question: What is RAN Equipment?
passage: RAN Equipment, or Radio Access Network Equipment, refers to the hardware and software components that facilitate wireless communication between mobile devices and the core network in cellular systems. This equipment is responsible for managing radio resources, establishing connections, and ensuring efficient data transmission. In the context of eCall, RAN Equipment plays a crucial role in selecting the appropriate codecs for voice and data communication, which impacts the speed and reliability of emergency calls initiated from vehicles. The performance of RAN Equipment is vital for the effective delivery of the Minimal Set of Data (MSD) during an eCall, as it directly influences how quickly and reliably this critical information reaches the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP).

Following is my understanding (the image formed in my brain when I first got trained about this).

As you see here in the following illustration, there is common portions and different portions between eCall and Emergency Call.

NOTE : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

eCall Higher Layer Application Protocol (HLAP) is very simple (at least comparting to Cellular Protocol). Actually there is only one critical data to be transferred. The critical data is called MSD(Minimal Set of Data). All the remaining part is just to get MSD delivered to PSAP (Emergency Call Center) with reliability.

As in Cellular Voice Call, in HLAP there are two different type of call mode depending on who (IVS or PSAP) initiates call. The eCall initiated by IVS is called 'PUSH mode' and this is similar concept as MO(Mobile Originating) call in cellular voice call.

The eCall initiated by PSAP is called 'PULL mode' and this is similar concept as MT(Mobile Terminating) call in cellular voice call.

The two illustrations in this section is based on ETSI 103.428 Figure 2. The ETSI diagram is a single diagram showing both PUSH and PULL mode in single sequence. It looked a little confusing to me, so I split the digram into two separate diagram as shown below.

NOTE 1 : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

NOTE 2 : PSAP stands for Public Safety Answering Point. This is a kind of Emergency Call Center.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MO call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by IVS (the mobile unit installed inside the car). I think in most case of eCall, the eCall goes in PUSH mode as illustrated below.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MT call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by PSAP (the call center). If you compare this with PUSH mode sequence, you would notice that most of the part are same. The only difference is the SEND-MSD (START) signal before the Initiation signal. This is also very much like cellular protocol. If you compare the MO Call and MT Call sequence in cellular protocol, you would notice that most part of the two are almost same. The main difference is that in MT Call the cellular network send 'Paging' (a kind of trigger for UE to initiate the call).

Another sequence that illustrate the eCall process with a little low layer point of view (especially in terms of LL/HL ACK operation) is shown below. This applies to both PUSH and PULL model.

< ETSI TR 126.969 - Figure 1: Timeline of eCall with IVS initiated signalling and HL-ACK in normal operation >

There are various timers in eCall protocol which should be met in order to guarantee the normal functionality of the eCall. Some of these timers are an important criterial of testing eCall functionality.

As mentioned above, the only one fundamental goal for eCall is to deliver MSD(Minimal Set of Data) with reliability. Then you may ask what kind of information is in the MSD. High level description of the imformation in MSD can be find from following description. As you see, the most important information in the MSD is the location data and vehicle information.

The eCall modem allows to transfer a data message from the IVS over the cellular network to the PSAP which is denoted as eCall MSD. The MSD can include, e.g. vehicle location information, time stamp, number of passengers, Vehicle Identification Number (VIN), and other relevant accident information

The Minimum Set of Data forming the data component of an eCall sent from a vehicle to a Public Safety Answering Point or other designated emergency call centre. The MSD has a maximum size of 140 bytes and includes, for example, vehicle identity, location information and time-stamp.

Before we think of this, let's think of why we need to care of this. We should care of this because eCall signaling message and data are delivered in the form of Voice call data of GSM or WCDMA cellular network.

In GSM / WCDMA, various different types of codecs are used. Basically the codec selection is a job for the specific Radio Access Network equipment(RAN Equipment) that is communicating with the eCall device. The RAN Equipment (Network) would select the codec that would give the best performance in a specific situation. 'Performance' mean 'How fast the eCall data can be delivered' and 'How reliably it can be delivered under a specific channel condition'. It would be too much (or too boring) to present the full details on these performance here. If you are really interested in the details, refer to ETSI TR 126.969 and it would give you a lot of test data for various different Codecs.

In theory, you can use a live network and PSAP Simulator to test your eCall Device (IVS). But theory is just a theory. You would come across a lot of issues to overcome if you go for this option even though I cannot say it is impossible.

Another way of testing the eCall device is to construct test setup as described in ETSI 103.428 section 6 Test Configurations. In this document, it is described to use a private cellular network for various Interoperability and Conformance Testing.

The most practical solution (Test setup) that will be used in the industry would be to use Cellular Network Simulator and PSAP simulator as illustrated below.

Assuming that you have a test setup and you need to determine what to test. As in most of other wireless and cellular device device, you may think of general test that tend to happen during the development or system integration stage. We often call these test in various different name such as function test, integration test or smoke test etc. Usually test specification / procedure tend not to be clearly defined or the procedure changes often depending on situations. Also those test procedure / test item may vary depending on manufacturer. Therefore, it would not be easy to clearly define on what to test for this stage. However, if you just take a close look at the overall eCall protocol, you would easily guess high level test items even without looking into any specification. My personal version of the guess work about the first level test are shown below. You may come up with different idea, but I don't think there would be any big difference between your idea and my idea.

Once you complete the general function test during development and system integration level and have a stable device, you would forward the device to conformance test. Once you are at the stage of conformance test, you don't have to worry about what to test because a lot of other people (standard body) put a lot of effort and energy and came out with well defined document. In 3GPP/ETSI, those test procedures are defined in ETSI TS 103.428.

After completing the conformance, if you are trying to sell the device (acutually Automakers trying to sell cars) in a specific region (e.g, Europe, Asia, America etc), you may need to go through a specific set of test cases specified by the regulatory body in that specific region.

question: What is the eCall initiated by IVS called?
passage: The eCall initiated by the In-Vehicle System (IVS) is referred to as "PUSH mode." This mode is characterized by the eCall being triggered automatically by the vehicle's sensors, such as an airbag deployment, or manually by the driver pressing an emergency button. In this mode, the IVS establishes a voice call with the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) and transmits the Minimal Set of Data (MSD) to provide critical information about the accident, such as vehicle location and type. This contrasts with the "PULL mode," where the PSAP initiates the call to the IVS.

2G/3G: eCall

What is 'eCall' ? In other words, you may ask 'what does the letter 'e' stands for ? Does it mean 'emergency' ? or 'electronic' ? or something else ?

Even though I haven't seen any formal documents that explicitely defines the letter 'e' in eCall, I think it would not be wrong if you say the 'e' mean 'emergency', i.e, 'eCall' would mean 'emergency Call'. But this interpretation would confuse a lot of people. Then, how does eCall differ from what we normally call 'Emergency Call (like 911)' ?

I will explain on the details of this difference later, but simply put, the biggest difference would be the usual 'Emergency call' is a kind of voice call between a human and Emergency Call Center (usually another person in Emergency Call Center)' but 'eCall' is a call between a machine (called IVS : In Vehicle System within an automobile) and Emergency Center;.

For the persons who likes formal definition, I would quote some descriptions from a couple of international standards as follows :

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

Before we talk of the technical details of eCall, let's take a 10000-feet overview (high level view) on how eCall go through. You may find a lot of illustrations, cartoons on eCall from internet and following is my own version of illustration. I put the number labels on each of the steps and I would put a short descriptions on what's happening at each step.

(2) eCall is triggered. eCall can be triggered in many ways. It can be triggered automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors. Or a person (e.g, driver) in the car can push the emergency button in the car to trigger the eCall.

(3) The eCall device installed in the car (called IVS : In-Vehicle System) go through Emergency Voice Call setup process to establish the voice call channel. Once the voice call channel is established, the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point)

(4) Once the eCall Data(MSD) is received by PSAP, the information would show up automatically on the screen at PSAP center.

(5) The personnel at PSAP center may try voice contact to the person in the car if possible. But there would be many cases where this is not possible when person in the car is injured badly.

question: What is PSAP?
passage: PSAP stands for Public Safety Answering Point. It is a type of emergency call center that receives and processes emergency calls, such as those made through the eCall system. In the context of eCall, PSAP is the destination for the emergency data and voice communication initiated by the In-Vehicle System (IVS) in a vehicle during an emergency situation. The PSAP receives the Minimal Set of Data (MSD) sent from the IVS, which includes critical information such as the vehicle's location and identification, enabling emergency services to respond more effectively and quickly to accidents.

question: What is RAN?
passage: RAN stands for Radio Access Network. It is a crucial component of mobile telecommunications systems, responsible for connecting individual devices, such as smartphones and tablets, to the core network. The RAN facilitates wireless communication by managing radio frequencies and ensuring that data is transmitted efficiently between the user equipment and the network. It encompasses various technologies, including GSM, UMTS, and LTE, and plays a vital role in determining the quality of service, coverage, and capacity of mobile networks.

Even though I haven't seen any formal documents that explicitely defines the letter 'e' in eCall, I think it would not be wrong if you say the 'e' mean 'emergency', i.e, 'eCall' would mean 'emergency Call'. But this interpretation would confuse a lot of people. Then, how does eCall differ from what we normally call 'Emergency Call (like 911)' ?

I will explain on the details of this difference later, but simply put, the biggest difference would be the usual 'Emergency call' is a kind of voice call between a human and Emergency Call Center (usually another person in Emergency Call Center)' but 'eCall' is a call between a machine (called IVS : In Vehicle System within an automobile) and Emergency Center;.

For the persons who likes formal definition, I would quote some descriptions from a couple of international standards as follows :

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

Before we talk of the technical details of eCall, let's take a 10000-feet overview (high level view) on how eCall go through. You may find a lot of illustrations, cartoons on eCall from internet and following is my own version of illustration. I put the number labels on each of the steps and I would put a short descriptions on what's happening at each step.

(2) eCall is triggered. eCall can be triggered in many ways. It can be triggered automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors. Or a person (e.g, driver) in the car can push the emergency button in the car to trigger the eCall.

(3) The eCall device installed in the car (called IVS : In-Vehicle System) go through Emergency Voice Call setup process to establish the voice call channel. Once the voice call channel is established, the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point)

(4) Once the eCall Data(MSD) is received by PSAP, the information would show up automatically on the screen at PSAP center.

(5) The personnel at PSAP center may try voice contact to the person in the car if possible. But there would be many cases where this is not possible when person in the car is injured badly.

For those who came from Cellular protocol and new to eCall, it would be a little confusing on figuring out the difference between eCall and another type of Emergency Call (like 911 in North America) which we are familiar with in daily life. For those people, I think it would be easier / clearer to explain the difference in terms of overall protocol sequence. Following is my understanding (the image formed in my brain when I first got trained about this).

As you see here in the following illustration, there is common portions and different portions between eCall and Emergency Call.

NOTE : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

eCall Higher Layer Application Protocol (HLAP) is very simple (at least comparting to Cellular Protocol). Actually there is only one critical data to be transferred. The critical data is called MSD(Minimal Set of Data). All the remaining part is just to get MSD delivered to PSAP (Emergency Call Center) with reliability.

As in Cellular Voice Call, in HLAP there are two different type of call mode depending on who (IVS or PSAP) initiates call. The eCall initiated by IVS is called 'PUSH mode' and this is similar concept as MO(Mobile Originating) call in cellular voice call.

The eCall initiated by PSAP is called 'PULL mode' and this is similar concept as MT(Mobile Terminating) call in cellular voice call.

The two illustrations in this section is based on ETSI 103.428 Figure 2. The ETSI diagram is a single diagram showing both PUSH and PULL mode in single sequence. It looked a little confusing to me, so I split the digram into two separate diagram as shown below.

NOTE 1 : IVS stands for In-Vehicle System. It is the eCall / Cellular module that are installed within Car (within Telematics module in most case). In terms of testing, this is a DUT

NOTE 2 : PSAP stands for Public Safety Answering Point. This is a kind of Emergency Call Center.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MO call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by IVS (the mobile unit installed inside the car). I think in most case of eCall, the eCall goes in PUSH mode as illustrated below.

PSAP PUSH Mode Call is like MT call in celluar terminology. This is the call initiated by PSAP (the call center). If you compare this with PUSH mode sequence, you would notice that most of the part are same. The only difference is the SEND-MSD (START) signal before the Initiation signal. This is also very much like cellular protocol. If you compare the MO Call and MT Call sequence in cellular protocol, you would notice that most part of the two are almost same. The main difference is that in MT Call the cellular network send 'Paging' (a kind of trigger for UE to initiate the call).

Another sequence that illustrate the eCall process with a little low layer point of view (especially in terms of LL/HL ACK operation) is shown below. This applies to both PUSH and PULL model.

< ETSI TR 126.969 - Figure 1: Timeline of eCall with IVS initiated signalling and HL-ACK in normal operation >

There are various timers in eCall protocol which should be met in order to guarantee the normal functionality of the eCall. Some of these timers are an important criterial of testing eCall functionality.

As mentioned above, the only one fundamental goal for eCall is to deliver MSD(Minimal Set of Data) with reliability. Then you may ask what kind of information is in the MSD. High level description of the imformation in MSD can be find from following description. As you see, the most important information in the MSD is the location data and vehicle information.

The eCall modem allows to transfer a data message from the IVS over the cellular network to the PSAP which is denoted as eCall MSD. The MSD can include, e.g. vehicle location information, time stamp, number of passengers, Vehicle Identification Number (VIN), and other relevant accident information

The Minimum Set of Data forming the data component of an eCall sent from a vehicle to a Public Safety Answering Point or other designated emergency call centre. The MSD has a maximum size of 140 bytes and includes, for example, vehicle identity, location information and time-stamp.

Before we think of this, let's think of why we need to care of this. We should care of this because eCall signaling message and data are delivered in the form of Voice call data of GSM or WCDMA cellular network.

In GSM / WCDMA, various different types of codecs are used. Basically the codec selection is a job for the specific Radio Access Network equipment(RAN Equipment) that is communicating with the eCall device. The RAN Equipment (Network) would select the codec that would give the best performance in a specific situation. 'Performance' mean 'How fast the eCall data can be delivered' and 'How reliably it can be delivered under a specific channel condition'. It would be too much (or too boring) to present the full details on these performance here. If you are really interested in the details, refer to ETSI TR 126.969 and it would give you a lot of test data for various different Codecs.

In theory, you can use a live network and PSAP Simulator to test your eCall Device (IVS). But theory is just a theory. You would come across a lot of issues to overcome if you go for this option even though I cannot say it is impossible.

Another way of testing the eCall device is to construct test setup as described in ETSI 103.428 section 6 Test Configurations. In this document, it is described to use a private cellular network for various Interoperability and Conformance Testing.

The most practical solution (Test setup) that will be used in the industry would be to use Cellular Network Simulator and PSAP simulator as illustrated below.

Assuming that you have a test setup and you need to determine what to test. As in most of other wireless and cellular device device, you may think of general test that tend to happen during the development or system integration stage. We often call these test in various different name such as function test, integration test or smoke test etc. Usually test specification / procedure tend not to be clearly defined or the procedure changes often depending on situations. Also those test procedure / test item may vary depending on manufacturer. Therefore, it would not be easy to clearly define on what to test for this stage. However, if you just take a close look at the overall eCall protocol, you would easily guess high level test items even without looking into any specification. My personal version of the guess work about the first level test are shown below. You may come up with different idea, but I don't think there would be any big difference between your idea and my idea.

Once you complete the general function test during development and system integration level and have a stable device, you would forward the device to conformance test. Once you are at the stage of conformance test, you don't have to worry about what to test because a lot of other people (standard body) put a lot of effort and energy and came out with well defined document. In 3GPP/ETSI, those test procedures are defined in ETSI TS 103.428.

After completing the conformance, if you are trying to sell the device (acutually Automakers trying to sell cars) in a specific region (e.g, Europe, Asia, America etc), you may need to go through a specific set of test cases specified by the regulatory body in that specific region.

Followings are the examples of how eCall is being testing during the development or for conformance test before commercialization.

Followings are the list of the specifications for eCall. I think the most fundamental specifications are CEN documents. But it is not free to get those spec. Recently 3GPP / ETSI has released various specifications. I think most part of the 3GPP specification are based on CEN specification.

: Describes mostly on physical/transport layer design and process of transmitter and reciever.

: This documents describes on API and parameter descriptions of eCall modem protocol stack. It describes on overall software architecture and API prototype but not show the function body. Unless you are developing the protocol stack, you would not need to read this spec.

: This documents describes general logics on eCall Test, but it does not specifies any specific test cases or details of protocol sequence. If you are interested in physical / transport layer level testing, this document would help you to catch the overall test concept.

: If you are interested in high level protocol and function test, this document would help a lot. It shows overall protocol sequence of eCall and decfines specific test sequences. Most of the test in this document (as of V1.1.1 (2016-06)) are based on CEN EN 16062:2015

Road transport and traffic telematics eSafety eCall minimum set of data - Draft EN 081018

Intelligent transport systems eSafety - Pan European eCall - Operating requirements

question: How can eCall be triggered?
gold_answer: automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors
passage: eCall can be triggered in two primary ways: automatically or manually. Automatic triggering occurs when the vehicle's internal sensors, such as those in the airbag system, detect a collision or significant impact. In contrast, manual triggering allows a person, typically the driver or a passenger, to initiate the eCall by pressing an emergency button located within the vehicle. This dual mechanism ensures that emergency services can be alerted promptly in the event of an accident, enhancing the chances of a timely response.

question: What is MSD?
passage: The Minimal Set of Data (MSD) is a crucial component of the eCall system, which is designed to enhance emergency response in the event of a vehicle accident. The MSD is a data package that is automatically or manually transmitted from a vehicle's In-Vehicle System (IVS) to a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) when an eCall is initiated. This data set typically includes vital information such as the vehicle's location, time stamp, number of passengers, and Vehicle Identification Number (VIN). The MSD has a maximum size of 140 bytes and is intended to provide emergency services with essential details that can help them respond more effectively and quickly to accidents, potentially saving lives.

question: In what form are eCall signaling message and data delivered?
gold_answer: Voice call data of GSM or WCDMA cellular network
passage: The eCall signaling message and data are delivered in the form of voice call data over GSM or WCDMA cellular networks. Specifically, the eCall system utilizes the existing voice channel to transmit the Minimal Set of Data (MSD) alongside the emergency voice call. This allows for reliable full-duplex data communication between the In-Vehicle System (IVS) and the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). The eCall modem employs various codecs selected by the Radio Access Network (RAN) equipment to optimize the performance of data delivery, ensuring that the MSD, which includes critical information such as vehicle location and identity, is transmitted effectively during an emergency situation.

What is 'eCall' ? In other words, you may ask 'what does the letter 'e' stands for ? Does it mean 'emergency' ? or 'electronic' ? or something else ?

Even though I haven't seen any formal documents that explicitely defines the letter 'e' in eCall, I think it would not be wrong if you say the 'e' mean 'emergency', i.e, 'eCall' would mean 'emergency Call'. But this interpretation would confuse a lot of people. Then, how does eCall differ from what we normally call 'Emergency Call (like 911)' ?

I will explain on the details of this difference later, but simply put, the biggest difference would be the usual 'Emergency call' is a kind of voice call between a human and Emergency Call Center (usually another person in Emergency Call Center)' but 'eCall' is a call between a machine (called IVS : In Vehicle System within an automobile) and Emergency Center;.

For the persons who likes formal definition, I would quote some descriptions from a couple of international standards as follows :

eCall is a manually or automatically initiated emergency call, (TS12 : teleServiceCode 12) from a vehicle, supplemented with a minimum set of emergency related data (MSD), as defined under the EU Commission's eSafety initiative

eCall provides reliable full-duplex data communications between IVS and PSAP in addition to emergency voice call (E112) via the cellular network, and can be initiated either automatically or manually. The eCall In-band Modem uses the same voice channel as used for the emergency voice call. eCall allows reliable transmission of MSD alternating with a speech conversation through the existing voice communication paths in cellular mobile phone systems. The expected benefit is that emergency services will be made aware of accidents much more rapidly, will get precise information on location, vehicle type etc. and therefore will be able to reach accident victims faster, with the potential to save many lives annually.

You may find a lot of illustrations, cartoons on eCall from internet and following is my own version of illustration. I put the number labels on each of the steps and I would put a short descriptions on what's happening at each step.

(2) eCall is triggered. eCall can be triggered in many ways. It can be triggered automatically by Air Bag or internal sensors. Or a person (e.g, driver) in the car can push the emergency button in the car to trigger the eCall.

(3) The eCall device installed in the car (called IVS : In-Vehicle System) go through Emergency Voice Call setup process to establish the voice call channel. Once the voice call channel is established, the IVS send eCall Data (MSD : Minimal Set of Data) to PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point)

(4) Once the eCall Data(MSD) is received by PSAP, the information would show up automatically on the screen at PSAP center.

(5) The personnel at PSAP center may try voice contact to the person in the car if possible. But there would be many cases where this is not possible when person in the car is injured badly.

question: What is meant by "active pending"?
gold_answer: The state of an activated trace is called Active Pending in a particular NE when the subscriber or equipment being traced is not registered in that NE
passage: "Active pending" refers to the state of an activated trace in a network element (NE) when the subscriber or equipment being traced is not currently registered in that NE. This state indicates that while the trace has been activated and is ready to collect data, it cannot do so until the relevant subscriber or equipment registers in the network.

3	Definitions and abbreviations

3.1	Definitions

For the purposes of the current TS, the following definitions apply:

activation of a trace: An action taken at the OSF through MMI commands to allow a trace record to be produced for a particular IMSI or IMEI when an Invocation Event occurs. This equates to "activation of a trace" in TS 29.002 [6].

active pending: The state of an activated trace is called Active Pending in a particular NE when the subscriber or equipment being traced is not registered in that NE.

invocation of a trace: An event relating to a particular IMSI or IMEI that occurs in the network that causes data to be collected in a trace record in circumstances where trace has been activated for that IMSI or IMEI. This equates to "tracing subscriber activity" in TS 29.002 [6] and "Trace Invocation" in TS 48.008 [4]. It is possible that an event relating to the IMSI/IMEI may still be active when another event or events relating to the same IMSI/IMEI occurs which requires additional information to be collected. These additional events are termed parallel events. This additional trace information for parallel events is collected in the same trace record as the first event.

trace record: In the NEF a trace record is a set of traceable data collected as determined by the trace type. The trace record is collected under the trace record criteria specified by the OSF and transferred to the OSF.

3.2	Abbreviations

For all abbreviations used in the current TS, refer to TS 21.905 [1].

question: What is a trace record?
gold_answer: a set of traceable data collected as determined by the trace type
passage: A trace record is a set of traceable data collected in a network element function (NEF) as determined by the specific trace type. It is generated when a trace has been activated for a particular International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) or International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) and is based on the criteria specified by the Operations Support Function (OSF). The trace record is then transferred to the OSF for further analysis.

question: What is IMEI?
passage: The International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) is a unique identifier assigned to mobile devices, particularly those that connect to cellular networks. It serves as a means to identify and authenticate devices on the network, allowing operators to track and manage devices effectively. The IMEI is crucial for various network management functions, including tracing and monitoring device activity, as it can be linked to specific events in the network. When a trace is activated for a particular IMEI, it enables the collection of data related to that device's activity, which can be essential for security and operational purposes.

3	Definitions and abbreviations

3.1	Definitions

For the purposes of the current TS, the following definitions apply:

activation of a trace: An action taken at the OSF through MMI commands to allow a trace record to be produced for a particular IMSI or IMEI when an Invocation Event occurs. This equates to "activation of a trace" in TS 29.002 [6].

active pending: The state of an activated trace is called Active Pending in a particular NE when the subscriber or equipment being traced is not registered in that NE.

invocation of a trace: An event relating to a particular IMSI or IMEI that occurs in the network that causes data to be collected in a trace record in circumstances where trace has been activated for that IMSI or IMEI. This equates to "tracing subscriber activity" in TS 29.002 [6] and "Trace Invocation" in TS 48.008 [4]. It is possible that an event relating to the IMSI/IMEI may still be active when another event or events relating to the same IMSI/IMEI occurs which requires additional information to be collected. These additional events are termed parallel events. This additional trace information for parallel events is collected in the same trace record as the first event.

trace record: In the NEF a trace record is a set of traceable data collected as determined by the trace type. The trace record is collected under the trace record criteria specified by the OSF and transferred to the OSF.

question: What is converged charging?
gold_answer: a process where online and offline charging are combined
passage: Converged charging is a process that integrates both online and offline charging mechanisms within a network. This approach allows for the simultaneous use of charging information by a Charging Control System (CCS) to manage services that require both quota management and those that do not. In converged charging, the network can generate charging information records while effectively monitoring resource usage in real-time, thus providing a comprehensive charging solution that enhances flexibility and efficiency in billing processes. This integration enables operators to offer a seamless experience to subscribers, accommodating various service types and usage patterns.
