question: What is time domain scheduling?
gold_answer: Determine when to transmit and how long it transmit
passage:
Time domain scheduling refers to the process of allocating transmission opportunities in the time domain for communication systems, particularly in wireless networks. In the context of LTE (Long Term Evolution) and its unlicensed variants like LTE-U and LAA (Licensed Assisted Access), time domain scheduling is crucial for managing how and when devices transmit data to avoid interference with other users, especially in environments where multiple devices share the same frequency band, such as Wi-Fi networks.

In LTE-based systems, time domain scheduling is typically centralized and deterministic, managed by the base station, which dictates when each user equipment (UE) can transmit. However, in unlicensed bands, where devices operate under protocols like CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance), there is no central control. Therefore, time domain scheduling becomes more complex, requiring algorithms that determine when a device can transmit based on the current usage of the channel by other devices.

The fundamental principle of time domain scheduling in this context is to ensure that a device listens to the channel before transmitting (Listen Before Talk - LBT) to minimize interference with ongoing communications. This involves assessing the channel's availability through mechanisms like Clear Channel Assessment (CCA) and adapting transmission durations to fit within available time slots, thereby enhancing coexist

How long CCA perform ED before it make decision ? It depends on higher layer technology (e.g, 802.11 FHSS, 802.11 OFDM, LBT). However, the minimum time span is 18 us sec.

What is the threshold energy level to make decision whether the channel is being used by some other device or not ? This also varies depending on power class of the device and reciever antenna gain. However, the base threshold is -70 dBm.

NOTE : Refer to 802.11 specification and ETSI EN 300 328 if you want to get full details and requirement for CCA.

LBT: LBT stands for Listen Before Talk. According to ETSI EN 300 328, LBT is defined as 'mechanism by which an equipment applies clear channel assessment (CCA) before using the channel' (In this document, you can find a couple of variations of LBT depending on different situations). As you see in the terminology itself, 'Listen Before Talk' indicate two major process, the first one is 'Listen' and the second part is 'Talk'. The meaning of 'Talk' is obvious. It means 'Transmit Data'. The tricky part is 'what does it exactly mean by 'Listen''. In more technical definition, 'Listen' mean 'perform CCA(Clear Channel Assessment)'. You can find a more detailed description on LBT in IEEE P802.19-08/0034r0 (The specific value (i.e, transmission time, threshold value may vary depending on application, but I think this explains overal LBT mechanism in easier way than other documents).

CSAT : CSAT stands for Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission. CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]). Unlike other techiques described in this section (defined with focus on 802.11 technology), CSAT is defined by LTE-U Forum with focus on 3GPP technology.

In LTE, every transmission within a specified spectrum is well managed/scheduled both for downlink and uplink. So Network can figure out exactly when to transmit something and when UE will transmit something.. but in Unlicensed band transmission and reception by the existing WiFi device is not as predictable as in LTE. Basically anybody can transmit in anytime as long as it complies with
CSMA/CA procedure.

In this kind of situation, how LTE network can schedule transmission in Unlicensed band ?

One method is for LTE cell to perform a special channel selection procedure and allocate the channel only when it is clean. 
In channel selection process, network measures the energy level within the allowed band and use those area in which the energy level is under a certain threshold (e.g, -62 dBm over 20 Mhz BW).

The Cell performs this kind of channel selection algorithm in on-going mode and if needed it will select more suitable channel and switch to it.

What if you (a Cell) fail to find any clean channel at the initial channel selection process ?

In this case, the cell use another mechanism called CSAT (Carrier-Sensing Adaptive Transmission). Technically, CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]).

According to Reference [5], there seems to be roughly three levels of Coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U. Most of these techniques are already mentioned in previous section, but let me rewrite in a little bit different words.

Channel Selection : This says "Use WiFi band only when it is not being used (i.e, the band is clean)". To figure out whether it is being used or not, you have to measure the engergy level of the target band as described above.

Time-domain coexistence techniques : Even when it fail to find any clean channel in channel selection stage, there is still some chance. Even though there is no clean channel at the point of channel selection, there might be some empty slots if you look at the time domain scheduling with relatively high granularity.
To find out this kind of time domain opportunity and in order not to make an interference at any time, they are considering several different technology like CSAT, eCSAT, LBT. My personal question were 'do we have to support all these technology everywhere (every devices)?'. This question was answered by Reference [5] as follows.

For non listen-before-talk (LBT) markets such as the US, South Korea, China and India, CSAT (Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission) can be used without changing Rel-10 Carrier Aggregation protocols for co-channel coexistence. For LBT markets such as Europe and Japan, Rel-13 LAA will enable channel sharing with Wi-Fi by performing clear channel assessment (CCA) based channel availability sensing and adapting the transmission duration on a fine timescale, ranging from 1ms-10ms

Opportunistic SCell operation : To me, this sounds like a rule (not a technology). Basically this says "Use the unlicensed band only when it is really necessary (e.g, in real demand on high throughput or when the primary cell is overloaded). Release the unlicensenced and fall back to anchor carrier when
the demand for unlicenced band is not critical.

Interplay of these coexistance technical components are well illustrated as follows in Ref [2].

When it comes to scheduling, Time Domain resource allocation tend to be more important.

However, in 802.11 based technology(i.e LAN, Wireless LAN etc) there is no central controling master in terms of scheduling. In this case, there is always possibility that transmission signal from one device interfere with communication of other devices. Basic idea is 'Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others' and the basic logic is 'Before you transmit anything, check if the chennel(medium) is already being used by others'. question: What happens if a cell fail to find any clear channel at the initial channel selection process?
gold_answer: the cell use another mechanism called CSAT
passage: If a cell fails to find any clear channel during the initial channel selection process, it will resort to using a mechanism called Carrier-Sensing Adaptive Transmission (CSAT). CSAT operates similarly to other channel access methods like Listen Before Talk (LBT) or Carrier Sensing Multiple Access (CSMA), but it monitors the medium for a longer duration, typically ranging from tens of milliseconds to 200 milliseconds. This extended sensing period helps ensure that the cell does not interfere with ongoing transmissions from Wi-Fi devices, thereby maintaining coexistence in the unlicensed spectrum. By employing CSAT, the cell can still attempt to utilize the unlicensed band effectively, even in the absence of a clear channel at the outset.

In every wireless communication, the communicating parties (transmitter and reciever) need to allocatie a certain amount of resources in both time domain and frequency domain. However, we don't have much control over frequency domain resource allocation because those resources are fixed permanently or semi-statically. So it is usually not in the scope of scheduling. When it comes to scheduling, Time Domain resource allocation tend to be more important.

In 3GPP based technology (i.e, Cellular Communication Technology like LTE), the time domain scheduling is obvious and determinstic even when there are many devices are in communication because all of the time domain resources determined by the central master (Base Station /Node B/eNode B). However, in 802.11 based technology(i.e LAN, Wireless LAN etc) there is no central controling master in terms of scheduling. In this case, there is always possibility that transmission signal from one device interfere with communication of other devices. To prevent (or at least reduce) this situation, we need a special algorithm for Time Domain Scheduling. Time Domain Scheduling in this case mean 'Determine when to transmit and how long it transmit'.

Then why we need to care of this kind of thing in LTE-Unlicensed technology ? Basically LTE Unlicensed technology (e.g, LTE-U, LAA etc) refer to a technology in which LTE operates in 802.11 frequency region. So LTE need to keep the rule set by 802.11 in order not to prevent the communiction between existing 802.11 devices.

There are many variations of the time domain scheduling, but the basic idea and logic is same. Basic idea is 'Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others' and the basic logic is 'Before you transmit anything, check if the chennel(medium) is already being used by others'. This logic can be illustrated as follows.

Then you may have some questions as follows : How to check (i.e, how to figure out) whether the channel (medium) is being used by other ? and how long the device need to check before it make any decision ?

I tried to list up those confusing words and how these are related to each other in following illustration. In this technology, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of voltage and compares the measured voltage with a specified value (threshold value). ED stands for Energy Detection. it is more frequently used in wireless/cellular technology. In this method, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of Power and compares the measured power with a specified value (threshold value)

CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA : As the term CSMA(Carrier Sensing Multiple Access) implies, these are technology of figuring out whether a channel is available or not based on CS method. You don't need to know the details of thechnology under the context of LTE-Unlicensed technology, but if you are really interested in thses method refer to CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA page.

CCA : CCA stands for Clear Channel Assessment. As the word implies, this is a method to figure out the channel is clear (i.e, nobody is using the channel). CCA perform ED(Energy Detection) for a certain period of time and make a decision whether the channel is clear or not. It is a common method being used in 802.11 (WLAN) technology.

How long CCA perform ED before it make decision ? It depends on higher layer technology (e.g, 802.11 FHSS, 802.11 OFDM, LBT). However, the minimum time span is 18 us sec.

What is the threshold energy level to make decision whether the channel is being used by some other device or not ? This also varies depending on power class of the device and reciever antenna gain. However, the base threshold is -70 dBm.

question: What is mptcp?
passage: Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is an extension of the traditional Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) that allows the simultaneous use of multiple paths for data transmission between two endpoints. This capability is particularly beneficial in environments where network conditions may vary, as it enhances reliability and throughput by enabling data packets to be sent over different network interfaces (such as Wi-Fi and cellular) concurrently. MPTCP is designed to improve the performance of applications that require a stable and high-bandwidth connection, making it suitable for scenarios like LTE-WLAN aggregation, where it can effectively combine the strengths of both LTE and Wi-Fi networks. The architecture of MPTCP includes a key component known as the Multipath Proxy, which manages the distribution of data across the available paths, ensuring efficient and seamless communication.

As of Jun 2016, I don't see/hear anything about LTE-R.. but I saw the drastic evolution of unlicensed LTE that created several different technologies (names) to the list. It started with LTE-U and evolved to LAA, eLAA and recently we are hearing of new branches like MulteFire and LWA. I don't know how many other technologies are waiting to be newly evolved and which of these technologies
will survive to the end.. some of them are now pretty well defined but there are a lot of other features to be defined technically. I will keep following them up and try to write down whatever has been clarified.

Followings are the brief descriptions for each of these technologies. I will put further details under separate section if more technical details are published. Followings are the list of topics that gives you further details of various LTE-Unlicensed technologies.

In every wireless communication, the communicating parties (transmitter and reciever) need to allocatie a certain amount of resources in both time domain and frequency domain. However, we don't have much control over frequency domain resource allocation because those resources are fixed permanently or semi-statically. So it is usually not in the scope of scheduling. When it comes to scheduling, Time Domain resource allocation tend to be more important.

In 3GPP based technology (i.e, Cellular Communication Technology like LTE), the time domain scheduling is obvious and determinstic even when there are many devices are in communication because all of the time domain resources determined by the central master (Base Station /Node B/eNode B). However, in 802.11 based technology(i.e LAN, Wireless LAN etc) there is no central controling master in terms of scheduling. In this case, there is always possibility that transmission signal from one device interfere with communication of other devices. To prevent (or at least reduce) this situation, we need a special algorithm for Time Domain Scheduling. Time Domain Scheduling in this case mean 'Determine when to transmit and how long it transmit'.

Then why we need to care of this kind of thing in LTE-Unlicensed technology ? Basically LTE Unlicensed technology (e.g, LTE-U, LAA etc) refer to a technology in which LTE operates in 802.11 frequency region. So LTE need to keep the rule set by 802.11 in order not to prevent the communiction between existing 802.11 devices.

There are many variations of the time domain scheduling, but the basic idea and logic is same. Basic idea is 'Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others' and the basic logic is 'Before you transmit anything, check if the chennel(medium) is already being used by others'. This logic can be illustrated as follows.

Then you may have some questions as follows : How to check (i.e, how to figure out) whether the channel (medium) is being used by other ? and how long the device need to check before it make any decision ?

In the effort to answer these questions, you will come across many terms that may confuse you for so long. I tried to list up those confusing words and how these are related to each other in following illustration. If you are new to this area, I would suggest you to understand 'what is CS and ED ?' first and then try to understand how CS / ED is used in higher level technology like CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA, CCS, LBT, CSAT etc. Already feel headache ? :)

CS / ED : CS stands for Carrier Sensing and ED stands for Energy Detection. The fundamental concept is same. The term CS is more frequently used in 802.11 area especially for Wired LAN Area. In this technology, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of voltage and compares the measured voltage with a specified value (threshold value). ED stands for Energy Detection. it is more frequently used in wireless/cellular technology. In this method, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of Power and compares the measured power with a specified value (threshold value)

CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA : As the term CSMA(Carrier Sensing Multiple Access) implies, these are technology of figuring out whether a channel is available or not based on CS method. You don't need to know the details of thechnology under the context of LTE-Unlicensed technology, but if you are really interested in thses method refer to CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA page.

CCA : CCA stands for Clear Channel Assessment. As the word implies, this is a method to figure out the channel is clear (i.e, nobody is using the channel). CCA perform ED(Energy Detection) for a certain period of time and make a decision whether the channel is clear or not. It is a common method being used in 802.11 (WLAN) technology.

How long CCA perform ED before it make decision ? It depends on higher layer technology (e.g, 802.11 FHSS, 802.11 OFDM, LBT). However, the minimum time span is 18 us sec.

What is the threshold energy level to make decision whether the channel is being used by some other device or not ? This also varies depending on power class of the device and reciever antenna gain. However, the base threshold is -70 dBm.

NOTE : Refer to 802.11 specification and ETSI EN 300 328 if you want to get full details and requirement for CCA.

LBT: LBT stands for Listen Before Talk. According to ETSI EN 300 328, LBT is defined as 'mechanism by which an equipment applies clear channel assessment (CCA) before using the channel' (In this document, you can find a couple of variations of LBT depending on different situations). As you see in the terminology itself, 'Listen Before Talk' indicate two major process, the first one is 'Listen' and the second part is 'Talk'. The meaning of 'Talk' is obvious. It means 'Transmit Data'. The tricky part is 'what does it exactly mean by 'Listen''. In more technical definition, 'Listen' mean 'perform CCA(Clear Channel Assessment)'. You can find a more detailed description on LBT in IEEE P802.19-08/0034r0 (The specific value (i.e, transmission time, threshold value may vary depending on application, but I think this explains overal LBT mechanism in easier way than other documents).

CSAT : CSAT stands for Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission. CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]). Unlike other techiques described in this section (defined with focus on 802.11 technology), CSAT is defined by LTE-U Forum with focus on 3GPP technology.

In LTE, every transmission within a specified spectrum is well managed/scheduled both for downlink and uplink. So Network can figure out exactly when to transmit something and when UE will transmit something.. but in Unlicensed band transmission and reception by the existing WiFi device is not as predictable as in LTE. Basically anybody can transmit in anytime as long as it complies with
CSMA/CA procedure.

In this kind of situation, how LTE network can schedule transmission in Unlicensed band ?

One method is for LTE cell to perform a special channel selection procedure and allocate the channel only when it is clean. 
In channel selection process, network measures the energy level within the allowed band and use those area in which the energy level is under a certain threshold (e.g, -62 dBm over 20 Mhz BW).

The Cell performs this kind of channel selection algorithm in on-going mode and if needed it will select more suitable channel and switch to it.

What if you (a Cell) fail to find any clean channel at the initial channel selection process ?

In this case, the cell use another mechanism called CSAT (Carrier-Sensing Adaptive Transmission). Technically, CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]).

According to Reference [5], there seems to be roughly three levels of Coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U. Most of these techniques are already mentioned in previous section, but let me rewrite in a little bit different words.

Channel Selection : This says "Use WiFi band only when it is not being used (i.e, the band is clean)". To figure out whether it is being used or not, you have to measure the engergy level of the target band as described above.

Time-domain coexistence techniques : Even when it fail to find any clean channel in channel selection stage, there is still some chance. Even though there is no clean channel at the point of channel selection, there might be some empty slots if you look at the time domain scheduling with relatively high granularity.
To find out this kind of time domain opportunity and in order not to make an interference at any time, they are considering several different technology like CSAT, eCSAT, LBT. My personal question were 'do we have to support all these technology everywhere (every devices)?'. This question was answered by Reference [5] as follows.

For non listen-before-talk (LBT) markets such as the US, South Korea, China and India, CSAT (Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission) can be used without changing Rel-10 Carrier Aggregation protocols for co-channel coexistence. For LBT markets such as Europe and Japan, Rel-13 LAA will enable channel sharing with Wi-Fi by performing clear channel assessment (CCA) based channel availability sensing and adapting the transmission duration on a fine timescale, ranging from 1ms-10ms

Opportunistic SCell operation : To me, this sounds like a rule (not a technology). Basically this says "Use the unlicensed band only when it is really necessary (e.g, in real demand on high throughput or when the primary cell is overloaded). Release the unlicensenced and fall back to anchor carrier when
the demand for unlicenced band is not critical.

Interplay of these coexistance technical components are well illustrated as follows in Ref [2].

LTE-U stands for LTE-Unlicensed. This is the first real implementation of the whole LTE-Unlicensed family as far as I remember. Since this is already implemented and tested relatively widely and a lot of details are known, I thought I got enough information to write this subject in a separate page. Refer to LTE-U page for the details.

In other LTE-Unlincensed technology, LTE borrow only radio spectrum from WLAN and all the transmission/reception technology except radio spectrum purely based on LTE. However, in LWA LTE borrows not only WLAN radio spectrum but also WLAN Access Point for transmitting data. This key difference is illustrated as below. To implement this key difference, we would need to implement many other
technical components. The most important part would be to implmenet special interface between LTE eNB and WLAN AP. Then you may ask.. at which layer the eNB and WLAN will be connected ? It would be quicker to interact if they can get connected at lower layer (e.g, PHY/MAC), but LTE PHY/MAC and WLAN PHY/MAC is completely different.. so hard to make any connection at this layer. So they will use higher layer (specifically PDCP) for this connection. As you know, there is no PDCP layer in WLAN. So connecting at PDCP
layer might be a little bit misleading. More accruately speaking, LTE PDCP packet will be encapsulated into WLAN MAC frame.

Now LWA is defined in 3GPP specification and I created a separate page for 3GPP LWA because it will be a long story. Refer to LWA page for the 3GPP details.

Around the end of 2016, I start hearing of implementing this both on UE modem and Network, UE testing equipment side. Now (as of early 2017) I am hearing of testing this feature on real UE. So I decided to create separate page for this. Read LAA page for the details.

Putting very simple way, Multipath Aggregation (more formally Multipath TCP Aggregation : mptcp) is LTE-WLAN aggregation at TCP level as illustrated below. The key component in this architecture would be MP Proxy (Multipath Proxy) and this part is being defined in IETF (Ref [12] )

question: What is CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA?
gold_answer: technology of figuring out whether a channel is available or not based on CS method
passage:
CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) and CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance) are network protocols used to manage how devices on a shared communication medium access the channel. 

CSMA/CD is primarily used in wired networks, such as Ethernet, where devices listen to the channel before transmitting. If a collision is detected (i.e., two devices transmit simultaneously), the devices stop transmitting and wait for a random period before attempting to transmit again.

On the other hand, CSMA/CA is used in wireless networks, such as Wi-Fi. It also involves listening to the channel before transmitting, but it employs a strategy to avoid collisions by using techniques like waiting for a clear channel and sending a request to send (RTS) before actual data transmission. This helps to minimize the chances of collisions in a wireless environment where multiple devices may be trying to communicate simultaneously. 

Both protocols are essential for efficient network communication, ensuring that devices can share the medium without excessive interference.

question: At which layer will the eNB and WLAN be connected?
gold_answer: they will use higher layer (specifically PDCP) for this connection
passage: The eNB (evolved Node B) and WLAN (Wireless Local Area Network) will be connected at the higher layer, specifically at the Packet Data Convergence Protocol (PDCP) layer. Although the LTE PHY (Physical) and MAC (Medium Access Control) layers are fundamentally different from those of WLAN, the connection is established by encapsulating LTE PDCP packets into WLAN MAC frames. This approach allows for interaction between the two systems while accommodating their distinct layer architectures.

If you are new to this area, I would suggest you to understand 'what is CS and ED ?' first and then try to understand how CS / ED is used in higher level technology like CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA, CCS, LBT, CSAT etc. Already feel headache ? :)

CS / ED : CS stands for Carrier Sensing and ED stands for Energy Detection. The fundamental concept is same. The term CS is more frequently used in 802.11 area especially for Wired LAN Area. In this technology, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of voltage and compares the measured voltage with a specified value (threshold value). ED stands for Energy Detection. it is more frequently used in wireless/cellular technology. In this method, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of Power and compares the measured power with a specified value (threshold value)

CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA : As the term CSMA(Carrier Sensing Multiple Access) implies, these are technology of figuring out whether a channel is available or not based on CS method. You don't need to know the details of thechnology under the context of LTE-Unlicensed technology, but if you are really interested in thses method refer to CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA page.

CCA : CCA stands for Clear Channel Assessment. As the word implies, this is a method to figure out the channel is clear (i.e, nobody is using the channel). CCA perform ED(Energy Detection) for a certain period of time and make a decision whether the channel is clear or not. It is a common method being used in 802.11 (WLAN) technology.

How long CCA perform ED before it make decision ? It depends on higher layer technology (e.g, 802.11 FHSS, 802.11 OFDM, LBT). However, the minimum time span is 18 us sec.

What is the threshold energy level to make decision whether the channel is being used by some other device or not ? This also varies depending on power class of the device and reciever antenna gain. However, the base threshold is -70 dBm.

NOTE : Refer to 802.11 specification and ETSI EN 300 328 if you want to get full details and requirement for CCA.

LBT: LBT stands for Listen Before Talk. According to ETSI EN 300 328, LBT is defined as 'mechanism by which an equipment applies clear channel assessment (CCA) before using the channel' (In this document, you can find a couple of variations of LBT depending on different situations). As you see in the terminology itself, 'Listen Before Talk' indicate two major process, the first one is 'Listen' and the second part is 'Talk'. The meaning of 'Talk' is obvious. It means 'Transmit Data'. The tricky part is 'what does it exactly mean by 'Listen''. In more technical definition, 'Listen' mean 'perform CCA(Clear Channel Assessment)'. You can find a more detailed description on LBT in IEEE P802.19-08/0034r0 (The specific value (i.e, transmission time, threshold value may vary depending on application, but I think this explains overal LBT mechanism in easier way than other documents).

CSAT : CSAT stands for Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission. CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]). Unlike other techiques described in this section (defined with focus on 802.11 technology), CSAT is defined by LTE-U Forum with focus on 3GPP technology.

In LTE, every transmission within a specified spectrum is well managed/scheduled both for downlink and uplink. So Network can figure out exactly when to transmit something and when UE will transmit something.. but in Unlicensed band transmission and reception by the existing WiFi device is not as predictable as in LTE. Basically anybody can transmit in anytime as long as it complies with
CSMA/CA procedure.

In this kind of situation, how LTE network can schedule transmission in Unlicensed band ?

One method is for LTE cell to perform a special channel selection procedure and allocate the channel only when it is clean. 
In channel selection process, network measures the energy level within the allowed band and use those area in which the energy level is under a certain threshold (e.g, -62 dBm over 20 Mhz BW).

The Cell performs this kind of channel selection algorithm in on-going mode and if needed it will select more suitable channel and switch to it.

What if you (a Cell) fail to find any clean channel at the initial channel selection process ?

In this case, the cell use another mechanism called CSAT (Carrier-Sensing Adaptive Transmission). Technically, CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]).

According to Reference [5], there seems to be roughly three levels of Coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U. Most of these techniques are already mentioned in previous section, but let me rewrite in a little bit different words.

Channel Selection : This says "Use WiFi band only when it is not being used (i.e, the band is clean)". To figure out whether it is being used or not, you have to measure the engergy level of the target band as described above.

Time-domain coexistence techniques : Even when it fail to find any clean channel in channel selection stage, there is still some chance. Even though there is no clean channel at the point of channel selection, there might be some empty slots if you look at the time domain scheduling with relatively high granularity.
To find out this kind of time domain opportunity and in order not to make an interference at any time, they are considering several different technology like CSAT, eCSAT, LBT. My personal question were 'do we have to support all these technology everywhere (every devices)?'. This question was answered by Reference [5] as follows.

For non listen-before-talk (LBT) markets such as the US, South Korea, China and India, CSAT (Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission) can be used without changing Rel-10 Carrier Aggregation protocols for co-channel coexistence. For LBT markets such as Europe and Japan, Rel-13 LAA will enable channel sharing with Wi-Fi by performing clear channel assessment (CCA) based channel availability sensing and adapting the transmission duration on a fine timescale, ranging from 1ms-10ms

Opportunistic SCell operation : To me, this sounds like a rule (not a technology). Basically this says "Use the unlicensed band only when it is really necessary (e.g, in real demand on high throughput or when the primary cell is overloaded). Release the unlicensenced and fall back to anchor carrier when
the demand for unlicenced band is not critical.

Interplay of these coexistance technical components are well illustrated as follows in Ref [2].

Since this is already implemented and tested relatively widely and a lot of details are known, I thought I got enough information to write this subject in a separate page. Refer to LTE-U page for the details.

In other LTE-Unlincensed technology, LTE borrow only radio spectrum from WLAN and all the transmission/reception technology except radio spectrum purely based on LTE. However, in LWA LTE borrows not only WLAN radio spectrum but also WLAN Access Point for transmitting data. This key difference is illustrated as below. To implement this key difference, we would need to implement many other
technical components. The most important part would be to implmenet special interface between LTE eNB and WLAN AP. Then you may ask.. at which layer the eNB and WLAN will be connected ? It would be quicker to interact if they can get connected at lower layer (e.g, PHY/MAC), but LTE PHY/MAC and WLAN PHY/MAC is completely different.. so hard to make any connection at this layer. So they will use higher layer (specifically PDCP) for this connection. As you know, there is no PDCP layer in WLAN. So connecting at PDCP
layer might be a little bit misleading. More accruately speaking, LTE PDCP packet will be encapsulated into WLAN MAC frame.

Now LWA is defined in 3GPP specification and I created a separate page for 3GPP LWA because it will be a long story. Refer to LWA page for the 3GPP details.

Around the end of 2016, I start hearing of implementing this both on UE modem and Network, UE testing equipment side. Now (as of early 2017) I am hearing of testing this feature on real UE. So I decided to create separate page for this. Read LAA page for the details.

question: What is Multipath Aggregation?
passage: Multipath Aggregation, more formally known as Multipath TCP (MPTCP) Aggregation, refers to the technique of combining multiple network paths for data transmission at the TCP level. This approach allows devices to utilize both LTE and WLAN connections simultaneously, enhancing throughput and reliability. The key component in this architecture is the Multipath Proxy (MP Proxy), which manages the distribution of data packets across the different paths. By leveraging the strengths of both LTE and WLAN, Multipath Aggregation aims to provide a seamless and efficient user experience, particularly in environments where network conditions may vary. This technology is particularly relevant in the context of LTE-Unlicensed (LTE-U) and other unlicensed spectrum technologies, where efficient resource utilization is crucial.

question: What is CSAT?
passage: CSAT, or Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission, is a technology used in LTE-Unlicensed (LTE-U) systems to manage transmission in unlicensed frequency bands, such as those used by Wi-Fi. It operates by monitoring the communication medium for a longer duration (typically tens of milliseconds to 200 milliseconds) compared to traditional Wi-Fi methods like CSMA (Carrier Sensing Multiple Access). This extended sensing period allows CSAT to avoid interfering with ongoing Wi-Fi data transmissions and other sporadic signals. The primary goal of CSAT is to ensure that LTE transmissions do not disrupt the quality of service for existing Wi-Fi users, thereby facilitating coexistence between LTE and Wi-Fi networks in shared frequency bands.

question: How many levels of coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U are there?
passage:
There are roughly three levels of coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U. These strategies include:

1. **Channel Selection**: This strategy involves using the WiFi band only when it is not being utilized, which requires measuring the energy level of the target band to determine if it is clear.

2. **Time-domain Coexistence Techniques**: Even if a clean channel is not found during the channel selection phase, there may still be opportunities in the time domain. This involves looking for empty slots in the time domain scheduling and utilizing techniques such as Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission (CSAT), enhanced CSAT (eCSAT), and Listen Before Talk (LBT) to minimize interference.

3. **Opportunistic SCell Operation**: This strategy suggests using the unlicensed band only when necessary, such as during high throughput demands or when the primary cell is overloaded, and reverting to the anchor carrier when the demand for the unlicensed band is not critical.

These coexistence strategies are essential for ensuring that LTE-U can operate effectively alongside existing WiFi networks without causing significant interference.

In this case, there is always possibility that transmission signal from one device interfere with communication of other devices. Time Domain Scheduling in this case mean 'Determine when to transmit and how long it transmit'.

Basic idea is 'Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others' and the basic logic is 'Before you transmit anything, check if the chennel(medium) is already being used by others'. question: What is 802.11 based technology?
passage: 802.11 based technology refers to a set of standards developed by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) for wireless local area networks (WLANs). These standards define the protocols for implementing wireless networking in various frequency bands, primarily the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. The most common implementation of 802.11 technology is Wi-Fi, which allows devices to connect to the internet and communicate with each other wirelessly. Unlike 3GPP-based technologies, such as LTE, which utilize a centralized control mechanism for scheduling and resource allocation, 802.11 operates in a decentralized manner. This means that devices must contend for access to the shared medium, leading to potential interference and the need for algorithms like Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA) to manage transmissions and minimize conflicts. Overall, 802.11 technology plays a crucial role in enabling wireless connectivity in homes, businesses, and public spaces.

question: What is the meaning of the talk process?
passage: The talk process, in the context of wireless communication, refers to the sequence of actions that occur when a device prepares to transmit data over a communication channel. Specifically, it involves two main steps: "Listen" and "Talk." The "Listen" phase, often associated with mechanisms like Clear Channel Assessment (CCA) or Listen Before Talk (LBT), requires the device to monitor the channel to determine if it is clear of other transmissions before proceeding to transmit its own data. This is crucial in environments where multiple devices share the same frequency, such as in LTE-Unlicensed technologies, to minimize interference and ensure efficient communication. The "Talk" phase is the actual transmission of data once the channel is deemed clear. This process is essential for maintaining the integrity of communications in shared frequency bands, particularly in systems that operate alongside existing technologies like Wi-Fi.

Followings are the list of topics that gives you further details of various LTE-Unlicensed technologies.

In every wireless communication, the communicating parties (transmitter and reciever) need to allocatie a certain amount of resources in both time domain and frequency domain. However, we don't have much control over frequency domain resource allocation because those resources are fixed permanently or semi-statically. So it is usually not in the scope of scheduling. When it comes to scheduling, Time Domain resource allocation tend to be more important.

In 3GPP based technology (i.e, Cellular Communication Technology like LTE), the time domain scheduling is obvious and determinstic even when there are many devices are in communication because all of the time domain resources determined by the central master (Base Station /Node B/eNode B). However, in 802.11 based technology(i.e LAN, Wireless LAN etc) there is no central controling master in terms of scheduling. In this case, there is always possibility that transmission signal from one device interfere with communication of other devices. To prevent (or at least reduce) this situation, we need a special algorithm for Time Domain Scheduling. Time Domain Scheduling in this case mean 'Determine when to transmit and how long it transmit'.

Then why we need to care of this kind of thing in LTE-Unlicensed technology ? Basically LTE Unlicensed technology (e.g, LTE-U, LAA etc) refer to a technology in which LTE operates in 802.11 frequency region. So LTE need to keep the rule set by 802.11 in order not to prevent the communiction between existing 802.11 devices.

There are many variations of the time domain scheduling, but the basic idea and logic is same. Basic idea is 'Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others' and the basic logic is 'Before you transmit anything, check if the chennel(medium) is already being used by others'. This logic can be illustrated as follows.

Then you may have some questions as follows : How to check (i.e, how to figure out) whether the channel (medium) is being used by other ? and how long the device need to check before it make any decision ?

In the effort to answer these questions, you will come across many terms that may confuse you for so long. I tried to list up those confusing words and how these are related to each other in following illustration. If you are new to this area, I would suggest you to understand 'what is CS and ED ?' first and then try to understand how CS / ED is used in higher level technology like CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA, CCS, LBT, CSAT etc. Already feel headache ? :)

CS / ED : CS stands for Carrier Sensing and ED stands for Energy Detection. The fundamental concept is same. The term CS is more frequently used in 802.11 area especially for Wired LAN Area. In this technology, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of voltage and compares the measured voltage with a specified value (threshold value). ED stands for Energy Detection. it is more frequently used in wireless/cellular technology. In this method, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of Power and compares the measured power with a specified value (threshold value)

CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA : As the term CSMA(Carrier Sensing Multiple Access) implies, these are technology of figuring out whether a channel is available or not based on CS method. You don't need to know the details of thechnology under the context of LTE-Unlicensed technology, but if you are really interested in thses method refer to CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA page.

CCA : CCA stands for Clear Channel Assessment. As the word implies, this is a method to figure out the channel is clear (i.e, nobody is using the channel). CCA perform ED(Energy Detection) for a certain period of time and make a decision whether the channel is clear or not. It is a common method being used in 802.11 (WLAN) technology.

How long CCA perform ED before it make decision ? It depends on higher layer technology (e.g, 802.11 FHSS, 802.11 OFDM, LBT). However, the minimum time span is 18 us sec.

What is the threshold energy level to make decision whether the channel is being used by some other device or not ? This also varies depending on power class of the device and reciever antenna gain. However, the base threshold is -70 dBm.

NOTE : Refer to 802.11 specification and ETSI EN 300 328 if you want to get full details and requirement for CCA.

LBT: LBT stands for Listen Before Talk. According to ETSI EN 300 328, LBT is defined as 'mechanism by which an equipment applies clear channel assessment (CCA) before using the channel' (In this document, you can find a couple of variations of LBT depending on different situations). As you see in the terminology itself, 'Listen Before Talk' indicate two major process, the first one is 'Listen' and the second part is 'Talk'. The meaning of 'Talk' is obvious. It means 'Transmit Data'. The tricky part is 'what does it exactly mean by 'Listen''. In more technical definition, 'Listen' mean 'perform CCA(Clear Channel Assessment)'. You can find a more detailed description on LBT in IEEE P802.19-08/0034r0 (The specific value (i.e, transmission time, threshold value may vary depending on application, but I think this explains overal LBT mechanism in easier way than other documents).

CSAT : CSAT stands for Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission. CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]). Unlike other techiques described in this section (defined with focus on 802.11 technology), CSAT is defined by LTE-U Forum with focus on 3GPP technology.

In LTE, every transmission within a specified spectrum is well managed/scheduled both for downlink and uplink. So Network can figure out exactly when to transmit something and when UE will transmit something.. but in Unlicensed band transmission and reception by the existing WiFi device is not as predictable as in LTE. Basically anybody can transmit in anytime as long as it complies with
CSMA/CA procedure.

In this kind of situation, how LTE network can schedule transmission in Unlicensed band ?

One method is for LTE cell to perform a special channel selection procedure and allocate the channel only when it is clean. 
In channel selection process, network measures the energy level within the allowed band and use those area in which the energy level is under a certain threshold (e.g, -62 dBm over 20 Mhz BW).

The Cell performs this kind of channel selection algorithm in on-going mode and if needed it will select more suitable channel and switch to it.

What if you (a Cell) fail to find any clean channel at the initial channel selection process ?

In this case, the cell use another mechanism called CSAT (Carrier-Sensing Adaptive Transmission). Technically, CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]).

According to Reference [5], there seems to be roughly three levels of Coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U. Most of these techniques are already mentioned in previous section, but let me rewrite in a little bit different words.

Channel Selection : This says "Use WiFi band only when it is not being used (i.e, the band is clean)". To figure out whether it is being used or not, you have to measure the engergy level of the target band as described above.

Time-domain coexistence techniques : Even when it fail to find any clean channel in channel selection stage, there is still some chance. Even though there is no clean channel at the point of channel selection, there might be some empty slots if you look at the time domain scheduling with relatively high granularity.
To find out this kind of time domain opportunity and in order not to make an interference at any time, they are considering several different technology like CSAT, eCSAT, LBT. My personal question were 'do we have to support all these technology everywhere (every devices)?'. This question was answered by Reference [5] as follows.

For non listen-before-talk (LBT) markets such as the US, South Korea, China and India, CSAT (Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission) can be used without changing Rel-10 Carrier Aggregation protocols for co-channel coexistence. For LBT markets such as Europe and Japan, Rel-13 LAA will enable channel sharing with Wi-Fi by performing clear channel assessment (CCA) based channel availability sensing and adapting the transmission duration on a fine timescale, ranging from 1ms-10ms

Opportunistic SCell operation : To me, this sounds like a rule (not a technology). Basically this says "Use the unlicensed band only when it is really necessary (e.g, in real demand on high throughput or when the primary cell is overloaded). Release the unlicensenced and fall back to anchor carrier when
the demand for unlicenced band is not critical.

technical components. The most important part would be to implmenet special interface between LTE eNB and WLAN AP. Then you may ask.. at which layer the eNB and WLAN will be connected ? It would be quicker to interact if they can get connected at lower layer (e.g, PHY/MAC), but LTE PHY/MAC and WLAN PHY/MAC is completely different.. so hard to make any connection at this layer. So they will use higher layer (specifically PDCP) for this connection. As you know, there is no PDCP layer in WLAN. So connecting at PDCP
layer might be a little bit misleading. More accruately speaking, LTE PDCP packet will be encapsulated into WLAN MAC frame.

question: What is the basic idea of time domain scheduling?
gold_answer: Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others
passage: The basic idea of time domain scheduling is to manage when and how long a device can transmit data to minimize interference with other devices sharing the same communication medium. In wireless communication, particularly in unlicensed bands where multiple devices may operate simultaneously, it is crucial to ensure that transmissions do not disrupt ongoing communications. Time domain scheduling involves assessing the channel's availability before transmitting, which is often achieved through mechanisms like Carrier Sensing (CS) and Clear Channel Assessment (CCA). These methods allow a device to "listen" to the channel to determine if it is clear before proceeding with transmission. The goal is to optimize the use of available time slots for transmission while adhering to the rules set by existing technologies, such as Wi-Fi, to maintain coexistence and reduce interference.

question: What is MP Proxy?
passage: MP Proxy, or Multipath Proxy, is a key component in the architecture of Multipath TCP Aggregation (MPTCP), which facilitates the aggregation of LTE and WLAN connections at the TCP level. This technology allows for more efficient use of network resources by enabling simultaneous data transmission over multiple paths, thereby improving throughput and reliability. The MP Proxy acts as an intermediary that manages the distribution of data packets across these different paths, ensuring that the communication remains seamless and efficient. This concept is being defined and standardized by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), highlighting its significance in the evolution of network management and connectivity solutions.

In this case, there is always possibility that transmission signal from one device interfere with communication of other devices. To prevent (or at least reduce) this situation, we need a special algorithm for Time Domain Scheduling. Time Domain Scheduling in this case mean 'Determine when to transmit and how long it transmit'.

Then why we need to care of this kind of thing in LTE-Unlicensed technology ? Basically LTE Unlicensed technology (e.g, LTE-U, LAA etc) refer to a technology in which LTE operates in 802.11 frequency region. So LTE need to keep the rule set by 802.11 in order not to prevent the communiction between existing 802.11 devices.

There are many variations of the time domain scheduling, but the basic idea and logic is same. Basic idea is 'Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others' and the basic logic is 'Before you transmit anything, check if the chennel(medium) is already being used by others'. This logic can be illustrated as follows.

Then you may have some questions as follows : How to check (i.e, how to figure out) whether the channel (medium) is being used by other ? and how long the device need to check before it make any decision ?

In the effort to answer these questions, you will come across many terms that may confuse you for so long. I tried to list up those confusing words and how these are related to each other in following illustration. If you are new to this area, I would suggest you to understand 'what is CS and ED ?' first and then try to understand how CS / ED is used in higher level technology like CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA, CCS, LBT, CSAT etc. Already feel headache ? :)

CS / ED : CS stands for Carrier Sensing and ED stands for Energy Detection. The fundamental concept is same. The term CS is more frequently used in 802.11 area especially for Wired LAN Area. In this technology, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of voltage and compares the measured voltage with a specified value (threshold value). ED stands for Energy Detection. it is more frequently used in wireless/cellular technology. In this method, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of Power and compares the measured power with a specified value (threshold value)

CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA : As the term CSMA(Carrier Sensing Multiple Access) implies, these are technology of figuring out whether a channel is available or not based on CS method. You don't need to know the details of thechnology under the context of LTE-Unlicensed technology, but if you are really interested in thses method refer to CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA page.

CCA : CCA stands for Clear Channel Assessment. As the word implies, this is a method to figure out the channel is clear (i.e, nobody is using the channel). CCA perform ED(Energy Detection) for a certain period of time and make a decision whether the channel is clear or not. It is a common method being used in 802.11 (WLAN) technology.

How long CCA perform ED before it make decision ? It depends on higher layer technology (e.g, 802.11 FHSS, 802.11 OFDM, LBT). However, the minimum time span is 18 us sec.

What is the threshold energy level to make decision whether the channel is being used by some other device or not ? This also varies depending on power class of the device and reciever antenna gain. However, the base threshold is -70 dBm.

NOTE : Refer to 802.11 specification and ETSI EN 300 328 if you want to get full details and requirement for CCA.

LBT: LBT stands for Listen Before Talk. According to ETSI EN 300 328, LBT is defined as 'mechanism by which an equipment applies clear channel assessment (CCA) before using the channel' (In this document, you can find a couple of variations of LBT depending on different situations). As you see in the terminology itself, 'Listen Before Talk' indicate two major process, the first one is 'Listen' and the second part is 'Talk'. The meaning of 'Talk' is obvious. It means 'Transmit Data'. The tricky part is 'what does it exactly mean by 'Listen''. In more technical definition, 'Listen' mean 'perform CCA(Clear Channel Assessment)'. You can find a more detailed description on LBT in IEEE P802.19-08/0034r0 (The specific value (i.e, transmission time, threshold value may vary depending on application, but I think this explains overal LBT mechanism in easier way than other documents).

CSAT : CSAT stands for Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission. CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]). Unlike other techiques described in this section (defined with focus on 802.11 technology), CSAT is defined by LTE-U Forum with focus on 3GPP technology.

In LTE, every transmission within a specified spectrum is well managed/scheduled both for downlink and uplink. So Network can figure out exactly when to transmit something and when UE will transmit something.. but in Unlicensed band transmission and reception by the existing WiFi device is not as predictable as in LTE. Basically anybody can transmit in anytime as long as it complies with
CSMA/CA procedure.

In this kind of situation, how LTE network can schedule transmission in Unlicensed band ?

One method is for LTE cell to perform a special channel selection procedure and allocate the channel only when it is clean. 
In channel selection process, network measures the energy level within the allowed band and use those area in which the energy level is under a certain threshold (e.g, -62 dBm over 20 Mhz BW).

The Cell performs this kind of channel selection algorithm in on-going mode and if needed it will select more suitable channel and switch to it.

What if you (a Cell) fail to find any clean channel at the initial channel selection process ?

In this case, the cell use another mechanism called CSAT (Carrier-Sensing Adaptive Transmission). Technically, CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]).

According to Reference [5], there seems to be roughly three levels of Coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U. Most of these techniques are already mentioned in previous section, but let me rewrite in a little bit different words.

Channel Selection : This says "Use WiFi band only when it is not being used (i.e, the band is clean)". To figure out whether it is being used or not, you have to measure the engergy level of the target band as described above.

Time-domain coexistence techniques : Even when it fail to find any clean channel in channel selection stage, there is still some chance. Even though there is no clean channel at the point of channel selection, there might be some empty slots if you look at the time domain scheduling with relatively high granularity.
To find out this kind of time domain opportunity and in order not to make an interference at any time, they are considering several different technology like CSAT, eCSAT, LBT. My personal question were 'do we have to support all these technology everywhere (every devices)?'. This question was answered by Reference [5] as follows.

For non listen-before-talk (LBT) markets such as the US, South Korea, China and India, CSAT (Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission) can be used without changing Rel-10 Carrier Aggregation protocols for co-channel coexistence. For LBT markets such as Europe and Japan, Rel-13 LAA will enable channel sharing with Wi-Fi by performing clear channel assessment (CCA) based channel availability sensing and adapting the transmission duration on a fine timescale, ranging from 1ms-10ms

Opportunistic SCell operation : To me, this sounds like a rule (not a technology). Basically this says "Use the unlicensed band only when it is really necessary (e.g, in real demand on high throughput or when the primary cell is overloaded). Release the unlicensenced and fall back to anchor carrier when
the demand for unlicenced band is not critical.

Interplay of these coexistance technical components are well illustrated as follows in Ref [2].

LTE-U stands for LTE-Unlicensed. This is the first real implementation of the whole LTE-Unlicensed family as far as I remember. Since this is already implemented and tested relatively widely and a lot of details are known, I thought I got enough information to write this subject in a separate page. Refer to LTE-U page for the details.

In other LTE-Unlincensed technology, LTE borrow only radio spectrum from WLAN and all the transmission/reception technology except radio spectrum purely based on LTE. However, in LWA LTE borrows not only WLAN radio spectrum but also WLAN Access Point for transmitting data. This key difference is illustrated as below. To implement this key difference, we would need to implement many other
technical components. The most important part would be to implmenet special interface between LTE eNB and WLAN AP. Then you may ask.. at which layer the eNB and WLAN will be connected ? It would be quicker to interact if they can get connected at lower layer (e.g, PHY/MAC), but LTE PHY/MAC and WLAN PHY/MAC is completely different.. so hard to make any connection at this layer. So they will use higher layer (specifically PDCP) for this connection. As you know, there is no PDCP layer in WLAN. So connecting at PDCP
layer might be a little bit misleading. More accruately speaking, LTE PDCP packet will be encapsulated into WLAN MAC frame.

Now LWA is defined in 3GPP specification and I created a separate page for 3GPP LWA because it will be a long story. Refer to LWA page for the 3GPP details.

Around the end of 2016, I start hearing of implementing this both on UE modem and Network, UE testing equipment side. Now (as of early 2017) I am hearing of testing this feature on real UE. So I decided to create separate page for this. Read LAA page for the details.

Putting very simple way, Multipath Aggregation (more formally Multipath TCP Aggregation : mptcp) is LTE-WLAN aggregation at TCP level as illustrated below. The key component in this architecture would be MP Proxy (Multipath Proxy) and this part is being defined in IETF (Ref [12] )

question: What is PHY/MAC?
passage:
PHY (Physical Layer) and MAC (Medium Access Control) are two fundamental layers in the OSI model that play crucial roles in wireless communication systems, including LTE (Long Term Evolution) and WLAN (Wireless Local Area Network). The PHY layer is responsible for the physical transmission of data over the air, including modulation, signal encoding, and the actual radio frequency transmission. It deals with the hardware aspects of communication, such as antennas and signal strength.

On the other hand, the MAC layer is responsible for managing how data packets are placed on the physical medium. It controls access to the shared communication medium, ensuring that multiple devices can communicate without interfering with each other. This includes functions like framing, addressing, and error detection. In the context of LTE and WLAN, the MAC layer also implements protocols for channel access, such as Carrier Sensing Multiple Access (CSMA) in WLANs and scheduling algorithms in LTE.

In summary, PHY and MAC are essential for enabling efficient and reliable communication in wireless networks, with PHY focusing on the physical transmission of signals and MAC managing access to the communication medium.

question: In what way are frequency domain resource allocation fixed?
passage: In frequency domain resource allocation, the resources are considered fixed because they are allocated permanently or semi-statically, meaning that they do not change frequently or dynamically like time domain resources. This fixed nature limits the ability to schedule or reallocate frequency resources on-the-fly, as is common in time domain scheduling where a central controller, such as a base station, can manage and adjust resource allocation based on current network conditions. In contrast, frequency resources in wireless communication systems, particularly in technologies like LTE, are predetermined and must adhere to specific regulatory and operational constraints, making them less flexible and more predictable compared to time domain resources.

CSAT : CSAT stands for Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission. CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]). Unlike other techiques described in this section (defined with focus on 802.11 technology), CSAT is defined by LTE-U Forum with focus on 3GPP technology.

In LTE, every transmission within a specified spectrum is well managed/scheduled both for downlink and uplink. So Network can figure out exactly when to transmit something and when UE will transmit something.. but in Unlicensed band transmission and reception by the existing WiFi device is not as predictable as in LTE. Basically anybody can transmit in anytime as long as it complies with
CSMA/CA procedure.

In this kind of situation, how LTE network can schedule transmission in Unlicensed band ?

One method is for LTE cell to perform a special channel selection procedure and allocate the channel only when it is clean. 
In channel selection process, network measures the energy level within the allowed band and use those area in which the energy level is under a certain threshold (e.g, -62 dBm over 20 Mhz BW).

The Cell performs this kind of channel selection algorithm in on-going mode and if needed it will select more suitable channel and switch to it.

What if you (a Cell) fail to find any clean channel at the initial channel selection process ?

In this case, the cell use another mechanism called CSAT (Carrier-Sensing Adaptive Transmission). Technically, CSAT is very similar to CSMA or LBT(Listen Before Talk), the main difference is that CSAT monitors(senses) the medium for much longer duration (around tens of msec to 200 msec) comparing to normal WiFi CSMA, so that it would not interfere not only with WiFi
data transmission (QoS traffic) but also with more sporadic transmission like discovery signals (Ref [2]).

According to Reference [5], there seems to be roughly three levels of Coexistence strategy regarding LTE-U. Most of these techniques are already mentioned in previous section, but let me rewrite in a little bit different words.

Channel Selection : This says "Use WiFi band only when it is not being used (i.e, the band is clean)". To figure out whether it is being used or not, you have to measure the engergy level of the target band as described above.

Time-domain coexistence techniques : Even when it fail to find any clean channel in channel selection stage, there is still some chance. Even though there is no clean channel at the point of channel selection, there might be some empty slots if you look at the time domain scheduling with relatively high granularity.
To find out this kind of time domain opportunity and in order not to make an interference at any time, they are considering several different technology like CSAT, eCSAT, LBT. My personal question were 'do we have to support all these technology everywhere (every devices)?'. This question was answered by Reference [5] as follows.

For non listen-before-talk (LBT) markets such as the US, South Korea, China and India, CSAT (Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission) can be used without changing Rel-10 Carrier Aggregation protocols for co-channel coexistence. For LBT markets such as Europe and Japan, Rel-13 LAA will enable channel sharing with Wi-Fi by performing clear channel assessment (CCA) based channel availability sensing and adapting the transmission duration on a fine timescale, ranging from 1ms-10ms

Opportunistic SCell operation : To me, this sounds like a rule (not a technology). Basically this says "Use the unlicensed band only when it is really necessary (e.g, in real demand on high throughput or when the primary cell is overloaded). Release the unlicensenced and fall back to anchor carrier when
the demand for unlicenced band is not critical.

Interplay of these coexistance technical components are well illustrated as follows in Ref [2].

In every wireless communication, the communicating parties (transmitter and reciever) need to allocatie a certain amount of resources in both time domain and frequency domain. However, we don't have much control over frequency domain resource allocation because those resources are fixed permanently or semi-statically. So it is usually not in the scope of scheduling. When it comes to scheduling, Time Domain resource allocation tend to be more important.

In 3GPP based technology (i.e, Cellular Communication Technology like LTE), the time domain scheduling is obvious and determinstic even when there are many devices are in communication because all of the time domain resources determined by the central master (Base Station /Node B/eNode B). However, in 802.11 based technology(i.e LAN, Wireless LAN etc) there is no central controling master in terms of scheduling. In this case, there is always possibility that transmission signal from one device interfere with communication of other devices. To prevent (or at least reduce) this situation, we need a special algorithm for Time Domain Scheduling. Time Domain Scheduling in this case mean 'Determine when to transmit and how long it transmit'.

Then why we need to care of this kind of thing in LTE-Unlicensed technology ? Basically LTE Unlicensed technology (e.g, LTE-U, LAA etc) refer to a technology in which LTE operates in 802.11 frequency region. So LTE need to keep the rule set by 802.11 in order not to prevent the communiction between existing 802.11 devices.

Basic idea is 'Your transmission should not interfere with communication between others' and the basic logic is 'Before you transmit anything, check if the chennel(medium) is already being used by others'. This logic can be illustrated as follows.

ED stands for Energy Detection. it is more frequently used in wireless/cellular technology. In this method, the device measures the energy level in the channel (medium) mostly in the form of Power and compares the measured power with a specified value (threshold value)

CSMA/CD or CSMA/CA : As the term CSMA(Carrier Sensing Multiple Access) implies, these are technology of figuring out whether a channel is available or not based on CS method. You don't need to know the details of thechnology under the context of LTE-Unlicensed technology, but if you are really interested in thses method refer to CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA page.

CCA : CCA stands for Clear Channel Assessment. As the word implies, this is a method to figure out the channel is clear (i.e, nobody is using the channel). CCA perform ED(Energy Detection) for a certain period of time and make a decision whether the channel is clear or not. It is a common method being used in 802.11 (WLAN) technology.

question: What is channel selection?
gold_answer: Use WiFi band only when it is not being used (i.e, the band is clean)
passage: Channel selection refers to the process used in wireless communication systems, particularly in LTE-Unlicensed (LTE-U) technologies, to determine which frequency band to utilize for transmission. This process involves measuring the energy levels within the available frequency bands to identify "clean" channels—those that are not currently being used by other devices, such as Wi-Fi. The goal is to minimize interference with existing communications. If a clean channel is found, the LTE system can allocate that channel for its transmissions. If no clean channels are available, the system may employ additional techniques, such as Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission (CSAT), to monitor the medium for longer periods and identify potential opportunities for transmission without causing interference. This careful channel selection is crucial for ensuring coexistence with other wireless technologies operating in the same frequency range.

question: What is cellular communication technology like LTE?
passage:
Cellular communication technology like LTE (Long Term Evolution) is a standard for wireless broadband communication for mobile devices and data terminals. It is designed to provide high-speed data transmission and improved network capacity compared to previous generations of mobile technology. LTE operates on a packet-switched network, allowing for efficient data handling and reduced latency. 

One of the key features of LTE is its use of advanced modulation techniques and multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology, which enhances data rates and overall network performance. LTE also supports a wide range of frequency bands, enabling operators to deploy the technology in various spectrum allocations.

In addition to standard LTE, there are extensions like LTE-U (LTE Unlicensed) and LAA (Licensed Assisted Access), which allow LTE to operate in unlicensed frequency bands, such as those used by Wi-Fi. These technologies incorporate mechanisms like Listen Before Talk (LBT) and Carrier Sensing Adaptive Transmission (CSAT) to coexist with existing Wi-Fi networks, ensuring that LTE transmissions do not interfere with other users in the unlicensed spectrum.

Overall, LTE and its extensions represent a significant evolution in mobile communication technology, providing faster data speeds, greater capacity, and improved user experiences in a variety of environments.

Two of the technology falling into this category is LTE-U and LTE-R. LTE-U has been proposed and start being implemented in the industry for about a year and LTE-R just start being proposed as Integrated wireless railway network to be commercialized .

As of Jun 2016, I don't see/hear anything about LTE-R.. but I saw the drastic evolution of unlicensed LTE that created several different technologies (names) to the list. It started with LTE-U and evolved to LAA, eLAA and recently we are hearing of new branches like MulteFire and LWA. I don't know how many other technologies are waiting to be newly evolved and which of these technologies
will survive to the end.. some of them are now pretty well defined but there are a lot of other features to be defined technically. I will keep following them up and try to write down whatever has been clarified.

Followings are the brief descriptions for each of these technologies. I will put further details under separate section if more technical details are published. Also, I put many whitepapers and YouTube links under Reference section. I would recommend you to go through those materials when you have free time and use this page as reminder afterwards.
