All that the thick text book is trying to say is "How we can make the efficient process ?", "How do you represent it in mathemaical form ?", "How do you prove (in mathemtical way) that it is efficient and always work?"

In real work, most of engineers doesn't care about this. There are only handsful of persons who digest all those textbook issues and come out with 'what they think is efficient process' and produce 'technical specification (e.g, 3GPP)'. Around 99% of us just follows the specification. That's why we don't read the text book after we graduate from university and still can survive -:)

There would be a couple of variations of the definitions of Source Coding depending on the context. The first type of definition is 'to convert the original data(user data) into a certain binary sequence' which is illustrated as below.

(With Reference to Lec 2 | MIT 6.450 Principles of Digital Communications I, Fall 2006 (YouTube) )

Another type of definition for source coding (according to Ref [2]) is to convert a source data into a form that can minimize the bandwidth that are required to transmit the data. Simply put, it is just another name for 'Data Compression'.

Again, It doesn't look that complicated. Then why the text book about this is so thick ?

Channel Coding is a method to replace 'original data bits' with 'some other bits (normally longer than the original bits)'. For example, the simplest coding would be as follows :

Another example of coding would be addition of parity bits as in RS 232 communication

In communication system, we usually call 'the original data' as a 'message' and call the ecoded data as 'Codeword'. In all encoding process, the length of Codeword is greater than the length of 'message', in means that in coding process some additional bits are added to the original data(message) and this additional bits are called 'redundency bits'.

Most of the experts in this area would come out with something like 'Shannon's theorem'.. but let's just look at this in intuitive way rather than bringing up such a scary words.

Let's look at the simple wireless communication process that we went through in previous section. In this process, what do you think is the biggest problem ?

The answer is the 'noise' which is added by 'Channel'. As you can guess, this noise would make a lot of errors while the reciever is demodulate the received signal into the bit stream.

Which option do you prefer ? You would know that the first option would be almost impossible especially in wireless communication. If it is wired communication, at least you can make some try to reduce the noise in the channel but in wireless it is almost impossible to remove the noise directly from the channel.

It means the only option is to develop some method (algorithm) to detect and correct the error caused by the noisy channel. This is the main motivation for 'Coding'.

Main idea of Coding is to add some additional bits (we call this as redundancy bits) to original data in a very special way (not in a random/arbitrary way) so that they can be used to detect the exact location of error and correct it.

In communication chain, following two blocks are added for this purpose. 'Encoding' is the process of adding redundancy bits and 'Decoding' is the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data.

Usually Encoding/Decoding blocks locate as shown below. Encoding takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream.

Getting in further detail, this encoding often happens in two steps called Source Coding and Channel Coding, but in this post I will just describe this process as a single step.

In previous section, I said "Encoding/Decoding is mainly for detecting/correcting erros generated in communication process". It is very good and important step. But once you gain something, you would lose some other things. It is almost nature of everything including our life.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

As I said earlier, Coding is adding some redundancy bits to original data and these redundancy bits will be used to detect and correct error in decoding process. There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. But the more redudancy bit you add, the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits, not for the information that you want to send. So you have to carefully determine how many bits you would allocate for the redundancy
bits.

Fortunately in most mobile communication system, somebody else has already determined the answer to these questions. For example, in LTE or WCDMA system.. 3GPP specification specifies all the details of Encoding/Decoding process and you don't have to worry about these questions.

For example, in LTE case, 3GPP 36.212 specifies the Coding algorithm and related parameters as shown below. Chapter 5 of the specification provides all the detailed parameters to implement the coding process.

The goal is to balance the amount of redundancy added for error correction with the throughput of the system, ensuring that the communication remains effective and efficient.

question: Which is longer the codeword or the message?
passage: In communication systems, the length of the codeword is always longer than the length of the message. This is because during the encoding process, additional bits, known as redundancy bits, are added to the original data (the message) to create the codeword. The purpose of these redundancy bits is to enable error detection and correction during transmission. For example, in block coding, a message of k bits is transformed into a codeword of n bits, where n is greater than k (n > k). This ensures that the encoded data can withstand potential errors introduced by noise in the communication channel.

question: What is equivalent to source coding?
passage: Source coding is equivalent to data compression. It involves converting original user data into a binary sequence in a way that minimizes the bandwidth required for transmission. This process aims to represent the data using the least number of bits possible while ensuring that the data can be accurately reconstructed at the receiving end. Essentially, source coding is about efficiently encoding information to reduce redundancy and optimize the use of available resources in communication systems.

Most of the experts in this area would come out with something like 'Shannon's theorem'.. but let's just look at this in intuitive way rather than bringing up such a scary words.

Let's look at the simple wireless communication process that we went through in previous section. In this process, what do you think is the biggest problem ?

The answer is the 'noise' which is added by 'Channel'. As you can guess, this noise would make a lot of errors while the reciever is demodulate the received signal into the bit stream.

Which option do you prefer ? You would know that the first option would be almost impossible especially in wireless communication. If it is wired communication, at least you can make some try to reduce the noise in the channel but in wireless it is almost impossible to remove the noise directly from the channel.

It means the only option is to develop some method (algorithm) to detect and correct the error caused by the noisy channel. This is the main motivation for 'Coding'.

Main idea of Coding is to add some additional bits (we call this as redundancy bits) to original data in a very special way (not in a random/arbitrary way) so that they can be used to detect the exact location of error and correct it.

In communication chain, following two blocks are added for this purpose. 'Encoding' is the process of adding redundancy bits and 'Decoding' is the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data.

Usually Encoding/Decoding blocks locate as shown below. Encoding takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. bits.

question: Why can we still survive even if we don't read the text book after we graduate from university?

These specifications provide clear guidelines and methodologies that have been developed and vetted by experts, allowing engineers to implement efficient processes without needing to understand every detail of the theoretical framework. Consequently, while textbooks provide foundational knowledge, the day-to-day work often involves following established protocols, enabling professionals to succeed without continuous reference to academic texts.

question: What does the receiver do in a communications channel?
gold_answer: demodulate the received signal into the bit stream
passage: In a communications channel, the receiver plays a crucial role in interpreting the transmitted signals. After the sender encodes the original data into a codeword and transmits it through the channel, the receiver's primary function is to demodulate the received signal back into a bit stream. This process involves detecting and correcting any errors that may have occurred during transmission due to noise in the channel. The receiver utilizes decoding algorithms to extract the original message from the received codeword, leveraging the redundancy bits added during the encoding process to identify and correct errors. Ultimately, the receiver aims to reconstruct the original data as accurately as possible, ensuring effective communication.

question: Which has greater length codeword or message?
passage: In communication systems, the length of a codeword is always greater than the length of the original message. This is because coding processes, such as channel coding, involve adding redundancy bits to the original data (the message) to ensure error detection and correction during transmission. For instance, in block coding, a message of k bits is transformed into a codeword of n bits, where n is always greater than k (n > k). This additional length is necessary to accommodate the redundancy bits that help maintain the integrity of the data as it travels through potentially noisy channels.

Let's look at the simple wireless communication process that we went through in previous section. In this process, what do you think is the biggest problem ?

The answer is the 'noise' which is added by 'Channel'. As you can guess, this noise would make a lot of errors while the reciever is demodulate the received signal into the bit stream.

Which option do you prefer ? You would know that the first option would be almost impossible especially in wireless communication. If it is wired communication, at least you can make some try to reduce the noise in the channel but in wireless it is almost impossible to remove the noise directly from the channel.

It means the only option is to develop some method (algorithm) to detect and correct the error caused by the noisy channel. This is the main motivation for 'Coding'.

Main idea of Coding is to add some additional bits (we call this as redundancy bits) to original data in a very special way (not in a random/arbitrary way) so that they can be used to detect the exact location of error and correct it.

In communication chain, following two blocks are added for this purpose. 'Encoding' is the process of adding redundancy bits and 'Decoding' is the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data.

Usually Encoding/Decoding blocks locate as shown below. Encoding takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream.

Getting in further detail, this encoding often happens in two steps called Source Coding and Channel Coding, but in this post I will just describe this process as a single step.

In previous section, I said "Encoding/Decoding is mainly for detecting/correcting erros generated in communication process". It is very good and important step. But once you gain something, you would lose some other things. It is almost nature of everything including our life.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

As I said earlier, Coding is adding some redundancy bits to original data and these redundancy bits will be used to detect and correct error in decoding process. There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. But the more redudancy bit you add, the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits, not for the information that you want to send. So you have to carefully determine how many bits you would allocate for the redundancy
bits.

question: What is a cyclic code?
gold_answer: set of code in which a code can be generated by cyclic shift of another code in the set
passage: A cyclic code is a type of error-correcting code in which any cyclic shift of a codeword results in another codeword that is also part of the same code set. This means that if you take a codeword and shift its bits in a circular manner, the resulting sequence will still belong to the set of valid codewords. For example, if you have a codeword represented as (0 1 0 1 0 1), shifting it right by one position yields (1 0 1 0 1 0), which is also a valid codeword in the set. This property makes cyclic codes particularly useful in communication systems, as they can be efficiently encoded and decoded, allowing for effective error detection and correction in the presence of noise.

question: What protocol specifies encoding decoding process for LTE or WCDMA system?
passage: The protocol that specifies the encoding and decoding process for LTE (Long Term Evolution) and WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) systems is defined by the 3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project) specifications. Specifically, for LTE, the coding algorithms and related parameters are detailed in the 3GPP TS 36.212 document. This specification outlines the necessary encoding and decoding processes, including the use of various coding techniques such as Turbo Coding and Convolutional Coding, which are essential for error detection and correction in mobile communication systems.

Let's look at the simple wireless communication process that we went through in previous section. In this process, what do you think is the biggest problem ?

The answer is the 'noise' which is added by 'Channel'. As you can guess, this noise would make a lot of errors while the reciever is demodulate the received signal into the bit stream.

Which option do you prefer ? You would know that the first option would be almost impossible especially in wireless communication. If it is wired communication, at least you can make some try to reduce the noise in the channel but in wireless it is almost impossible to remove the noise directly from the channel.

It means the only option is to develop some method (algorithm) to detect and correct the error caused by the noisy channel. This is the main motivation for 'Coding'.

Main idea of Coding is to add some additional bits (we call this as redundancy bits) to original data in a very special way (not in a random/arbitrary way) so that they can be used to detect the exact location of error and correct it.

In communication chain, following two blocks are added for this purpose. 'Encoding' is the process of adding redundancy bits and 'Decoding' is the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data.

Usually Encoding/Decoding blocks locate as shown below. Encoding takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream.

Getting in further detail, this encoding often happens in two steps called Source Coding and Channel Coding, but in this post I will just describe this process as a single step.

In previous section, I said "Encoding/Decoding is mainly for detecting/correcting erros generated in communication process". It is very good and important step. But once you gain something, you would lose some other things. It is almost nature of everything including our life.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

As I said earlier, Coding is adding some redundancy bits to original data and these redundancy bits will be used to detect and correct error in decoding process. There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. But the more redudancy bit you add, the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits, not for the information that you want to send. So you have to carefully determine how many bits you would allocate for the redundancy
bits.

Fortunately in most mobile communication system, somebody else has already determined the answer to these questions. For example, in LTE or WCDMA system.. 3GPP specification specifies all the details of Encoding/Decoding process and you don't have to worry about these questions.

For example, in LTE case, 3GPP 36.212 specifies the Coding algorithm and related parameters as shown below. Chapter 5 of the specification provides all the detailed parameters to implement the coding process.

question: What is decoding in the communications channel?
gold_answer: the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data
passage: Decoding in a communications channel refers to the process of extracting the original message from the received coded data, which may have been altered by noise during transmission. After encoding, where redundancy bits are added to the original data to facilitate error detection and correction, decoding takes the received codeword and attempts to reconstruct the original message by identifying and correcting any errors that may have occurred. This process is crucial in ensuring that the data received at the destination is as accurate as possible, despite the potential for interference and distortion in the communication channel. Decoding algorithms are designed to interpret the redundancy bits added during encoding, allowing the receiver to detect the location of errors and correct them, thereby improving the reliability of data transmission.

question: How to eliminate noise from a communications channel?
passage: To eliminate noise from a communications channel, one effective method is to implement coding techniques, specifically error detection and correction algorithms. Since it is often impossible to remove noise directly from the channel, coding adds redundancy bits to the original data, allowing the receiver to detect and correct errors that occur during transmission. This process involves two main steps: encoding, where redundancy bits are added to the original message, and decoding, where the received data is processed to extract the corrected information. By using structured coding methods, such as block codes or convolutional codes, the system can enhance its ability to recover the original message despite the presence of noise, thus improving the overall reliability of the communication system.

There are only handsful of persons who digest all those textbook issues and come out with 'what they think is efficient process' and produce 'technical specification (e.g, 3GPP)'. Another type of definition for source coding (according to Ref [2]) is to convert a source data into a form that can minimize the bandwidth that are required to transmit the data. Simply put, it is just another name for 'Data Compression'.

Again, It doesn't look that complicated. Then why the text book about this is so thick ?

Another example of coding would be addition of parity bits as in RS 232 communication

In communication system, we usually call 'the original data' as a 'message' and call the ecoded data as 'Codeword'. In all encoding process, the length of Codeword is greater than the length of 'message', in means that in coding process some additional bits are added to the original data(message) and this additional bits are called 'redundency bits'.

Most of the experts in this area would come out with something like 'Shannon's theorem'.. but let's just look at this in intuitive way rather than bringing up such a scary words.

Let's look at the simple wireless communication process that we went through in previous section. In this process, what do you think is the biggest problem ?

The answer is the 'noise' which is added by 'Channel'. As you can guess, this noise would make a lot of errors while the reciever is demodulate the received signal into the bit stream.

Which option do you prefer ? You would know that the first option would be almost impossible especially in wireless communication. If it is wired communication, at least you can make some try to reduce the noise in the channel but in wireless it is almost impossible to remove the noise directly from the channel.

It means the only option is to develop some method (algorithm) to detect and correct the error caused by the noisy channel. This is the main motivation for 'Coding'.

Main idea of Coding is to add some additional bits (we call this as redundancy bits) to original data in a very special way (not in a random/arbitrary way) so that they can be used to detect the exact location of error and correct it.

In communication chain, following two blocks are added for this purpose. 'Encoding' is the process of adding redundancy bits and 'Decoding' is the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data.

Usually Encoding/Decoding blocks locate as shown below. Encoding takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream.

Getting in further detail, this encoding often happens in two steps called Source Coding and Channel Coding, but in this post I will just describe this process as a single step.

In previous section, I said "Encoding/Decoding is mainly for detecting/correcting erros generated in communication process". It is very good and important step. But once you gain something, you would lose some other things. It is almost nature of everything including our life.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

As I said earlier, Coding is adding some redundancy bits to original data and these redundancy bits will be used to detect and correct error in decoding process. There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. But the more redudancy bit you add, the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits, not for the information that you want to send. So you have to carefully determine how many bits you would allocate for the redundancy
bits.

question: What is encoding in the communications channel?
gold_answer: the process of adding redundancy bits
passage:
Encoding in a communications channel refers to the process of converting original data, often called a message, into a coded format known as a codeword. This process typically involves adding redundancy bits to the original data to enhance error detection and correction capabilities during transmission. The primary goal of encoding is to ensure that the data can be transmitted efficiently and accurately, even in the presence of noise and other interferences in the communication channel. 

Encoding can be broken down into two main types: Source Coding, which focuses on compressing the data to minimize bandwidth usage, and Channel Coding, which adds redundancy to the data to protect against errors. The encoded data (codeword) is usually longer than the original message due to the inclusion of these redundancy bits. This additional information allows the receiver to detect and correct errors that may occur during transmission, thereby improving the reliability of the communication system.

question: What happens if you add more redundancy bits?
gold_answer: the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits
passage: Adding more redundancy bits in a communication system enhances the error detection and correction capabilities. This means that the system can identify and correct a greater number of errors that may occur during data transmission, particularly in noisy environments. However, the trade-off for this increased reliability is a reduction in throughput. As more bits are allocated for redundancy, fewer bits are available for the actual information being transmitted. Therefore, while adding redundancy bits improves the robustness of the communication process, it also necessitates careful consideration of the balance between error correction capabilities and the efficiency of data transmission.

question: What is data compression?
gold_answer: to convert a source data into a form that can minimize the bandwidth that are required to transmit the data
passage: Data compression is the process of converting original data into a more compact binary sequence, thereby minimizing the amount of bandwidth required for transmission. This technique, also referred to as source coding, aims to represent data using fewer bits without losing essential information. By reducing the size of the data, data compression enhances the efficiency of communication systems, allowing for faster transmission and reduced storage requirements. In essence, it is a critical method used to optimize the handling and transfer of data in various applications, particularly in digital communications.

In previous section, I said "Encoding/Decoding is mainly for detecting/correcting erros generated in communication process". It is very good and important step. But once you gain something, you would lose some other things. It is almost nature of everything including our life.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

As I said earlier, Coding is adding some redundancy bits to original data and these redundancy bits will be used to detect and correct error in decoding process. There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. But the more redudancy bit you add, the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits, not for the information that you want to send. So you have to carefully determine how many bits you would allocate for the redundancy
bits.

question: What is a a generator function capable of performing?
passage: A generator function is a type of binary function used in coding, specifically for converting a message into a codeword. It operates by applying a mathematical representation, often expressed in matrix form, to the input message. The generator function typically includes an identity matrix that corresponds to the length of the message, allowing for the systematic addition of redundancy bits to enhance error detection and correction capabilities. This process is essential in communication systems, as it ensures that the transmitted data can be accurately reconstructed at the receiver's end, despite potential noise and errors introduced during transmission. The specific generator functions used are usually provided by the communication system's specifications, ensuring that the encoding process is efficient and reliable.

question: In real work, what doesn't most of engineers care about?
passage: In real work, most engineers do not concern themselves with the intricate theoretical aspects of communication coding, such as the mathematical proofs and detailed specifications found in textbooks. Instead, they primarily focus on implementing established technical specifications, like those provided by organizations such as 3GPP. This means that while a small number of experts may delve into the complexities of efficient coding processes and the underlying mathematics, the vast majority of engineers simply apply these specifications in practice without needing to understand the theoretical foundations. This practical approach allows them to effectively work within the communication systems without needing to revisit academic texts after graduation.

All that the thick text book is trying to say is "How we can make the efficient process ?", "How do you represent it in mathemaical form ?", "How do you prove (in mathemtical way) that it is efficient and always work?"

In real work, most of engineers doesn't care about this. There are only handsful of persons who digest all those textbook issues and come out with 'what they think is efficient process' and produce 'technical specification (e.g, 3GPP)'. Around 99% of us just follows the specification. That's why we don't read the text book after we graduate from university and still can survive -:)

There would be a couple of variations of the definitions of Source Coding depending on the context. The first type of definition is 'to convert the original data(user data) into a certain binary sequence' which is illustrated as below.

(With Reference to Lec 2 | MIT 6.450 Principles of Digital Communications I, Fall 2006 (YouTube) )

Another type of definition for source coding (according to Ref [2]) is to convert a source data into a form that can minimize the bandwidth that are required to transmit the data. Simply put, it is just another name for 'Data Compression'.

Again, It doesn't look that complicated. Then why the text book about this is so thick ?

Channel Coding is a method to replace 'original data bits' with 'some other bits (normally longer than the original bits)'. For example, the simplest coding would be as follows :

Another example of coding would be addition of parity bits as in RS 232 communication

In communication system, we usually call 'the original data' as a 'message' and call the ecoded data as 'Codeword'. In all encoding process, the length of Codeword is greater than the length of 'message', in means that in coding process some additional bits are added to the original data(message) and this additional bits are called 'redundency bits'.

Most of the experts in this area would come out with something like 'Shannon's theorem'.. but let's just look at this in intuitive way rather than bringing up such a scary words.

Let's look at the simple wireless communication process that we went through in previous section. In this process, what do you think is the biggest problem ?

The answer is the 'noise' which is added by 'Channel'. As you can guess, this noise would make a lot of errors while the reciever is demodulate the received signal into the bit stream.

Which option do you prefer ? You would know that the first option would be almost impossible especially in wireless communication. If it is wired communication, at least you can make some try to reduce the noise in the channel but in wireless it is almost impossible to remove the noise directly from the channel.

It means the only option is to develop some method (algorithm) to detect and correct the error caused by the noisy channel. This is the main motivation for 'Coding'.

Main idea of Coding is to add some additional bits (we call this as redundancy bits) to original data in a very special way (not in a random/arbitrary way) so that they can be used to detect the exact location of error and correct it.

In communication chain, following two blocks are added for this purpose. 'Encoding' is the process of adding redundancy bits and 'Decoding' is the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data.

Usually Encoding/Decoding blocks locate as shown below. Encoding takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream.

Getting in further detail, this encoding often happens in two steps called Source Coding and Channel Coding, but in this post I will just describe this process as a single step.

In previous section, I said "Encoding/Decoding is mainly for detecting/correcting erros generated in communication process". It is very good and important step. But once you gain something, you would lose some other things. It is almost nature of everything including our life.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

As I said earlier, Coding is adding some redundancy bits to original data and these redundancy bits will be used to detect and correct error in decoding process. There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. But the more redudancy bit you add, the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits, not for the information that you want to send. So you have to carefully determine how many bits you would allocate for the redundancy
bits.

Fortunately in most mobile communication system, somebody else has already determined the answer to these questions. For example, in LTE or WCDMA system.. 3GPP specification specifies all the details of Encoding/Decoding process and you don't have to worry about these questions.

For example, in LTE case, 3GPP 36.212 specifies the Coding algorithm and related parameters as shown below. Chapter 5 of the specification provides all the detailed parameters to implement the coding process.

question: What is block code?

This redundancy helps in error detection and correction during data transmission. For example, a block code might take 4-bit chunks of input data and convert them into 7-bit codewords, ensuring that the encoded data can be transmitted more reliably over a communication channel.

question: What does encoding do with bits in the channel?
gold_answer: takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream
passage: Encoding in a communication channel serves the critical purpose of enhancing data transmission reliability by adding redundancy bits to the original data. This process transforms the original data, referred to as the "message," into a longer sequence known as the "codeword." The additional bits, or redundancy bits, are strategically included to enable error detection and correction, which is essential in mitigating the effects of noise that can corrupt the transmitted signal. By employing various encoding techniques, such as source coding and channel coding, the system can ensure that the received data is accurate and minimizes errors, despite the challenges posed by the communication channel. Thus, encoding effectively prepares the data for transmission, making it more robust against potential errors during the communication process.

question: What is an example of channel coding?
gold_answer: addition of parity bits as in RS 232 communication
passage: An example of channel coding is the addition of parity bits, as seen in RS-232 communication. Channel coding involves replacing original data bits with a longer sequence of bits, which includes redundancy bits that help in detecting and correcting errors during data transmission. Another example is block coding, where the input data stream is divided into small blocks, and each block (message) is replaced with a longer block (codeword). question: What are redundancy bits?
passage: Redundancy bits are additional bits added to the original data during the encoding process in communication systems. These bits serve a crucial purpose: they enable the detection and correction of errors that may occur during data transmission, particularly in noisy channels. When the original data, referred to as a "message," is encoded, it is transformed into a longer sequence known as a "codeword." The length of the codeword is always greater than that of the message, as it includes these redundancy bits. By strategically adding redundancy, the system can identify the exact location of errors and correct them during the decoding process, thereby improving the reliability of data transmission.

question: Is encoding decoding enough to eliminate noise?
gold_answer: once you gain something, you would lose some other things
passage: Encoding and decoding are essential processes in communication systems designed to combat the effects of noise introduced during data transmission. While encoding adds redundancy bits to the original data, enabling error detection and correction, it is not sufficient on its own to eliminate noise completely. Noise can distort the transmitted signal, leading to errors that encoding and decoding aim to correct. However, the presence of noise in the channel can still result in some errors that may not be correctable, depending on the coding scheme used and the level of redundancy added. Therefore, while encoding and decoding significantly improve the reliability of data transmission, they do not entirely eliminate noise; they merely provide a mechanism to detect and correct errors caused by it.

question: What is the biggest problem in communication process?
passage: The biggest problem in the communication process is the presence of noise introduced by the channel. This noise can lead to errors during the demodulation of the received signal into a bit stream, making it difficult for the receiver to accurately interpret the transmitted data. In wireless communication, it is particularly challenging to eliminate this noise directly from the channel, which necessitates the development of methods and algorithms for error detection and correction. This is where coding comes into play, as it involves adding redundancy bits to the original data in a structured manner to help identify and correct errors caused by the noisy channel.

question: How does encoding happen in detail?
gold_answer: often happens in two steps called Source Coding and Channel Coding
passage:
Encoding in communication systems is a crucial process that involves converting original data (user data) into a binary sequence, which can be efficiently transmitted over a channel. This process typically occurs in two main steps: Source Coding and Channel Coding. 

Source Coding aims to minimize the bandwidth required for data transmission, often referred to as data compression. It transforms the original data into a more compact form. Channel Coding, on the other hand, adds redundancy bits to the original data to create a longer codeword. This redundancy is essential for error detection and correction, especially in noisy communication channels.

The encoding process can be visualized as taking a stream of bits (the message) and producing a coded bit stream (the codeword). The codeword is always longer than the message, as it includes additional bits that help identify and correct errors during transmission. Various coding techniques, such as Block Codes and Convolutional Codes, are employed to achieve efficient encoding. 

For instance, in Block Coding, the input data stream is divided into small blocks, each replaced by a corresponding codeword based on a predefined mapping. In Convolutional Coding, the encoding process involves a more complex relationship between the input and output, often represented mathematically through generator functions.

Again, It doesn't look that complicated. Then why the text book about this is so thick ?

Channel Coding is a method to replace 'original data bits' with 'some other bits (normally longer than the original bits)'. For example, the simplest coding would be as follows :

Another example of coding would be addition of parity bits as in RS 232 communication

In communication system, we usually call 'the original data' as a 'message' and call the ecoded data as 'Codeword'. In all encoding process, the length of Codeword is greater than the length of 'message', in means that in coding process some additional bits are added to the original data(message) and this additional bits are called 'redundency bits'.

Most of the experts in this area would come out with something like 'Shannon's theorem'.. but let's just look at this in intuitive way rather than bringing up such a scary words.

Let's look at the simple wireless communication process that we went through in previous section. In this process, what do you think is the biggest problem ?

The answer is the 'noise' which is added by 'Channel'. As you can guess, this noise would make a lot of errors while the reciever is demodulate the received signal into the bit stream.

Which option do you prefer ? You would know that the first option would be almost impossible especially in wireless communication. If it is wired communication, at least you can make some try to reduce the noise in the channel but in wireless it is almost impossible to remove the noise directly from the channel.

It means the only option is to develop some method (algorithm) to detect and correct the error caused by the noisy channel. This is the main motivation for 'Coding'.

Main idea of Coding is to add some additional bits (we call this as redundancy bits) to original data in a very special way (not in a random/arbitrary way) so that they can be used to detect the exact location of error and correct it.

In communication chain, following two blocks are added for this purpose. 'Encoding' is the process of adding redundancy bits and 'Decoding' is the process of extracting the error corrected bits from the received data.

Usually Encoding/Decoding blocks locate as shown below. Encoding takes in the bits stream and produce coded bit stream.

Getting in further detail, this encoding often happens in two steps called Source Coding and Channel Coding, but in this post I will just describe this process as a single step.

In previous section, I said "Encoding/Decoding is mainly for detecting/correcting erros generated in communication process". It is very good and important step. But once you gain something, you would lose some other things. It is almost nature of everything including our life.

What is the gain for Encoding/Decoding ? It is the received data with less or almost no error.

What is the loss ? What is downside of this process ? Following are the major issues caused by Encoding/Decoding process.

As I said earlier, Coding is adding some redundancy bits to original data and these redundancy bits will be used to detect and correct error in decoding process. There are many different Encoding/Decoding algorithms which has it's own advantage and disadvantages. So we would always have the following question when we implement Coding/Decoding Blocks.

In general, the more redundancy bits you add, you would have higher error detection/correction capability. But the more redudancy bit you add, the less throughput you would get because larger portions of transmitted bits should be allocated for the redundancy bits, not for the information that you want to send. So you have to carefully determine how many bits you would allocate for the redundancy
bits.

14	OAM improvements

14.1	Other 5G System Charging aspects

14.1.1	Service Based Interface for 5G Charging

Summary based on the input provided by Huawei Technologies France in SP-181159.

The 5G Phase 1 architecture specifies the CHF as "Charging Function". The main purpose of the CHF is to provide the Service based Interface "Nchf". This Work Item specifies the Nchf_ConvergedCharging services, operations and procedures.

The service aspects are defined in TS 32.290 while the Service API Definition and Open API are defined in TS 32.291.

TS 32.290 also defines the charging scenario (converged event based charging and converged session-based charging), charging functionalities and the	Message format of the Common Data structure of Charging Data (Request and Response). TS 32.291also defines the bindings of CDR field, Information Element and Resource Attribute.

14.1.2	Charging for IMS over 5G System Architecture Phase 1

Summary based on the input provided by Nokia Shanghai Bell in SP-181183.

This work introduces the IMS charging extensions for IMS on top of 5G Core. In this context, the IMS charging (relying on existing Diameter based Ro/Rf charging architecture) is enhanced by extension of existing parameters:

These parameters apply for both online and offline charging, including information captured in IMS CDRs.

This is defined in TS 32.260 (IMS charging); TS 32.299 (Diameter charging applications) and TS 32.298 (CDR parameter description).

14.1.3	SMS Charging in 5G System Architecture Phase 1

Summary based on the input provided by Nokia Shanghai Bell in SP-181184.

This work introduces the SMS Charging in 5G System Architecture Phase 1.

For "SMS over NAS" in 5G Core, SMS charging is specified from SMSF in the service-based charging architecture with CHF, for SMO and SMT via SMSF:

For SMS via IMS, SMS Diameter-based Rf offline charging is introduced from IP-SM-GW with new ISM-SMO and ISM-SMT CDRs and includes 5GS RAT Type and User Location.

SMS Diameter-based Rf offline charging from SMS-SC and SC-SMO/SC-SMT CDRs are extended with 5GS RAT Type and User Location.

SMS Diameter-based Ro online charging from both IP-SM-GW and SMS-SC are extended with 5GS RAT Type and User Location.

Summary based on the input provided by Ericsson, ZTE, Intel, Huawei, Nokia in SP-xxx.

This set of Work Items enhances the Management Services (MnS) specifications to support the 5G network in addition to the pre-5G network supported in previous Releases. These WIs are shown in the table below.

Management and orchestration of 5G networks and network slicing

The basic concepts for Management Services (defined in TS 28.533) are:

The generic management services concept, defined in TS 28.530, follows the management service concepts as defined in TS 28.533. The specification includes the following information:

Provisioning of 5G networks and network slicing

The following functionalities related to provisioning are defined in TS 28.531, TS 28.532 and TS 28.541:

Fault Supervision for 5G networks and network slicing

Fault Supervision is one of the fundamental functions for the management of a 5G network and its communication services. This work item specifies the following aspects of fault supervision for 5G networks and network slicing:

The stage 1 part is documented in TS 28.545 [13] and the stage 2 and stage 3 parts are documented in clause 6 and clause 9 of TS 28.532 [10].

Performance assurance for 5G networks including network slicing

The performance assurance of 5G networks and network slicing relies on a set of management services with the relevant management data (e.g. performance measurements and KPIs).

The management services in terms of performance assurance include the measurement job control service, performance data file reporting service, performance data streaming service, and management data analytics service (MDAS). The performance data includes performance measurements and KPIs for NFs, NSSIs and NSIs. The performance data of NSSI are generated based on the aggregation and calculation of performance data of NFs, and the performance data of NSIs are produced based on the aggregation and calculation of performance of data of NSSIs and NFs.

The performance assurance related management services are defined in TS 28.550 [14].

The performance measurements and KPIs for 5G networks are defined in TS 28.552 [15] and TS 28.554 [16] respectively.

Network Resource Model (NRM) for 5G networks and network slicing

To support management and orchestration of 5G network and network slicing, several Network Resource Model (NRM) related specifications were added or enhanced including TS 28.540 [17], TS 28.541 [18], TS 28.622 [19], TS 28.623 [20], TS 28.626 [21] and TS 28.658 [22]. The specifications include the following information:

5G Trace management

The work item introduced 5G system (including both NG-RAN and 5GC) Trace in following aspects:

The objective of this WI is to enhance the interactions between 3GPP management system and supporting external management systems (e.g., ETSI NFV MANO) to support the management of 5GC and NG-RAN where a gNB is split into a CU (Centralized Unit) that can be implemented as VNF, and a DU (Distributed Unit) that can be implemented as PNF, with the F1 interface between CU and DU.

question: What is CU?
passage: In the context of 5G network architecture, CU stands for Centralized Unit. It is a component of the radio access network (RAN) that is responsible for higher-layer processing functions, such as radio resource management and control signaling. The CU works in conjunction with the Distributed Unit (DU), which handles lower-layer functions. The separation of CU and DU allows for more flexible network deployment and management, enabling operators to optimize performance and resource utilization in 5G networks. The interface between the CU and DU is referred to as the F1 interface.

question: What is NRM?
passage: NRM stands for Network Resource Model. It is a framework used in telecommunications to define and manage the resources within a network, particularly in the context of the EPC (Evolved Packet Core) architecture. Summary based on the input provided by Ericsson in RP-181149.

The WI specified a new interface, namely E1, that enables interconnecting a gNB-CU-CP (control plane part of the gNB central unit) and a gNB-CU-UP (user plane part of the gNB central unit) [1]. The split of control plane and user plane via E1 interface enhances the split between gNB-CU (gNB central unit) and gNB-DU (gNB distributed unit) defined within the NR WI. It offers the possibility of:

(1) optimizing the location of different RAN functions based on the deployment scenario, (2) support efficient radio resource isolation for network slicing, (3) independent scaling of CP and UP capacity.

In the NR WI, a split of the gNB into a gNB-CU and a gNB-DU is defined. The gNB-CU hosts the RRC, SDAP and PDCP radio protocols, while the gNB-DU hosts the PHY, MAC and RLC radio protocols. The gNB-CU and the gNB-DU are connected via the F1 interface. This WI complements the split defined in the NR WI by enabling to split the gNB-CU into a gNB-CU-CP and a gNB-CU-UP. The gNB-CU-CP hosts the RRC and the instance of the PDCP protocol serving the control plane, while the gNB-CU-UP hosts the SDAP and the instance of the PDCP protocol serving the user plane. The gNB-CU-CP and the gNB-CU-UP are connected via the E1 interface. The gNB-CU-CP is connected to the gNB-DU via the control plane part of the F1 interface (F1-C), while the gNB-CU-UP is connected to the gNB-DU via the user plane part of the F1 interface (F1-U). question: What is CTF?
passage: The Charging Trigger Function (CTF) is a critical component in network management that generates charging events based on the usage of network resources. It serves as the central point for collecting information related to chargeable events from various network and service elements, assembling this data into corresponding charging events, and forwarding them to the Charging Data Function (CDF). The CTF is mandatory in all network elements that support offline charging functionality and consists of two main functional blocks. It can be distributed within network elements or service elements, and in certain service-specific scenarios, its components may be divided between the User Equipment (UE) and the network element. The operational behavior of the CTF, including the definition and matching of chargeable events, is detailed in specific technical specifications for different domains and services.

5.2.2.1.3	RACH message part

Figure 5 shows the structure of the random-access message part radio frame. The 10 ms message part radio frame is split into 15 slots, each of length Tslot = 2560 chips. Each slot consists of two parts, a data part to which the RACH transport channel is mapped and a control part that carries Layer 1 control information. The data and control parts are transmitted in parallel. A 10 ms message part consists of one message part radio frame, while a 20 ms message part consists of two consecutive 10 ms message part radio frames. The message part length is equal to the Transmission Time Interval of the RACH Transport channel in use. This TTI length is configured by higher layers.

The data part consists of 10*2k bits, where k=0,1,2,3. This corresponds to a spreading factor of 256, 128, 64, and 32 respectively for the message data part.

The control part consists of 8 known pilot bits to support channel estimation for coherent detection and 2 TFCI bits. This corresponds to a spreading factor of 256 for the message control part. The pilot bit pattern is described in table 8. The total number of TFCI bits in the random-access message is 15*2 = 30. The TFCI of a radio frame indicates the transport format of the RACH transport channel mapped to the simultaneously transmitted message part radio frame. In case of a 20 ms PRACH message part, the TFCI is repeated in the second radio frame.

question: what is the purpose of breaking down a complex system into a combination of multiple delta functions?
gold_answer: characterize the mathematical properties of the complex system from the combination of the mathematical characteristics of delta function
passage:
Breaking down a complex system into a combination of multiple delta functions serves several important purposes in signal representation and analysis. The delta function is a well-defined mathematical construct that allows for the representation of discrete signals in a simplified manner. By using delta functions, we can express any discrete value through shifts and multiplications, making it easier to analyze and manipulate signals mathematically.

This approach is particularly useful in Linear Time Invariant (LTI) systems, where the properties of the delta function are well understood. By representing a complex signal as a sum of shifted delta functions, we can leverage the known characteristics of the delta function to characterize the overall system behavior. This method facilitates the calculation of system outputs through convolution, allowing us to predict how the system will respond to various input sequences.

In essence, breaking down a complex system into delta functions transforms a potentially complicated problem into a series of simpler, manageable components, enabling clearer analysis and understanding of the system's behavior.

passage: The delta function, often denoted as δ(t), is a mathematical representation used in signal processing to describe an impulse or a discrete event. In discrete signal representation, the delta function is defined such that it equals 1 at t = 0 and 0 at all other points. For continuous signals, the delta function is conceptualized as having an infinitely small width while maintaining an area of 1 under the curve. This unique property allows the delta function to effectively represent any discrete value through shifting and scaling operations. For instance, a signal value at a specific time can be expressed as a scaled and shifted delta function, enabling the representation of complex signals as combinations of simpler delta functions. This approach is particularly useful in linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, where the characteristics of the delta function can be leveraged to analyze and predict system behavior.

As in any other field, we also use mathematical notations to represent a signal whether you like it or not -:). You should be familiar with this kind of mathematical representation since most of technical documents (especially text books) use the same expression.

The most important component of signal representation is to understand the meaning of 'delta' fuction. Delta function in discrete signal can be illustrated as below. As you see, delta function is a special function which has '1' only at t = 0 and '0' at all other points. (In case of continuous signal, Delta function is defined
as a function where the width of the function is infinitely small and the area under the function is 1).

If you sum up all of these shift-multiplied versions of delta function, you can even express a sequence of signal in simple mathematical form.

If you want to express the following sequence without using the delta function, you may have to write s(t,x) = {(-8,0),(-7,2),(-6,0),(-5,0),(-4,1),(-3,0),(-2,0),(-1,0),(0,0),(1,0),(2,1),(3,0),(4,0),(5,2),(6,0),(7,0),(8,0)}. Here, t indicate time in descrete form. x indicate the amplitude (or value) of the signal at 't'. For example, s(t,x) = (-7,2) indicate the value (the amplitude of
the signal) at time -7 is 2. s(t,x) = (2,1) indicate the value (the amplitude of the signal) at time 2 is 1.

Now let's think if we can s(t,x) using delta function. For example, how can we represent s(t,x) = (-7,2) using delta function ?

First, let's think of how we can represent t = -7. As described above, delta function has non-zero value only at n (time) = 0. Then how can we make the delta function has none-zero value at t = -7. With junior high school math, you can get the none zero value by shifting the delta function by 4 to the left. How can you represent this shift in math ? Again from junior

If you combine the result of the first and second step, you would understand s(t,x) = (-7,2) can be expressed as '2 x delta(t+7)'.

Another reason why we use delta function for signal representation is the fact that the characteristics of the delta function is well investigated. Therefore, we can easily identify the characteristics of the signal based on the characteristics of the delta function. (Again, this holds true that the system is Linear Time Invarient).

question: what is the reason the delta function is used in signal representation?
gold_answer: because we can represent any discrete value by shift and multiplication of the function
passage: The delta function is used in signal representation primarily because it allows for the concise and effective representation of discrete signals. It is a special function that takes the value of 1 at a specific point (t=0) and 0 elsewhere, making it ideal for representing individual signal values at specific time instances. By shifting and scaling the delta function, any discrete signal can be expressed as a sum of these shifted delta functions, which simplifies the mathematical representation of complex signals. This approach is particularly useful in Linear Time Invariant (LTI) systems, where the characteristics of the delta function are well understood, enabling the analysis and characterization of the system's response to various inputs. Additionally, the delta function facilitates operations such as convolution, which is essential for predicting system outputs based on known impulse responses. Overall, the delta function serves as a foundational tool in signal processing, allowing for the breakdown of complex signals into manageable components.

question: where is the delta function non-zero?
passage: The delta function is non-zero only at a specific point, which is typically at t = 0 for discrete signals. In the context of continuous signals, the delta function is defined as having an infinitely small width with an area of 1, meaning it is non-zero at a single point but integrates to 1 over its entire range. For example, a shifted delta function, such as delta(t + 7), would be non-zero at t = -7, effectively shifting the point of non-zero value to that location. Thus, the delta function serves as a mathematical representation of impulses or discrete values at specific points in time, allowing for the characterization and manipulation of signals in various applications.

question: what is LTI short for in signal representation?
passage: LTI stands for Linear Time Invariant. In the context of signal representation, a system is considered LTI if it satisfies two key properties: linearity and time invariance. Linearity means that the output of the system is directly proportional to the input, allowing for the superposition of inputs. Time invariance indicates that the system's behavior and characteristics do not change over time; thus, if an input signal is delayed, the output will also be delayed by the same amount without any alteration in shape. Understanding these properties is crucial for analyzing and predicting the behavior of systems in signal processing and communication theory.

question: How is delta function defined?
gold_answer: as a function where the width of the function is infinitely small and the area under the function is 1).
passage: The delta function, often denoted as δ(t), is a mathematical function that plays a crucial role in signal processing and systems analysis. In the context of discrete signals, the delta function is defined such that it takes the value of '1' at t = 0 and '0' at all other points. For continuous signals, the delta function is characterized as a function with an infinitely small width, yet the area under the function equals 1. This unique property allows the delta function to serve as an idealized impulse, enabling the representation of signals through shifting and scaling operations. In practical applications, particularly in Linear Time Invariant (LTI) systems, the delta function is instrumental in expressing complex signals as combinations of simpler components, facilitating analysis and understanding of system behavior.

gold_answer: the system should be LTI (Linear Time Invarient)

This means that the system's response to any input can be determined by its impulse response, which is the output when a delta function is applied as input. The delta function serves as a mathematical tool to express discrete signals, allowing for the decomposition of complex signals into simpler components. Each component can be represented as a scaled and shifted delta function, enabling the calculation of the system's output through convolution. By summing the results of these convolutions, one can predict the overall output of the system for a given input sequence. This approach leverages the well-defined properties of the delta function, facilitating the analysis and characterization of the system's behavior.

question: how is the delta function defined for continuous signal?
gold_answer: as a function where the width of the function is infinitely small and the area under the function is 1
passage:
The delta function for continuous signals, often referred to as the Dirac delta function, is defined as a function that is infinitely narrow and infinitely high at a single point, specifically at t = 0, such that the area under the function is equal to 1. Mathematically, it can be expressed as:

\[
\delta(t) = 
\begin{cases} 
\infty & \text{if } t = 0 \\
0 & \text{if } t \neq 0 
\end{cases}
\]

and the integral over the entire real line is given by:

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) \, dt = 1.
\]

This property allows the delta function to serve as an idealized representation of an impulse, making it a crucial tool in signal processing and systems analysis, particularly in the context of Linear Time Invariant (LTI) systems. The delta function can also be used to represent sampling of continuous signals, where it effectively "picks out" the value of the signal at specific points in time.

question: In what case will the GNSS receiver report its velocity?
gold_answer: If requested by the LMF and supported by the UE
passage: In the UE-based or standalone mode, the GNSS receiver will report its velocity if it is specifically requested by the Location Management Function (LMF) and if the User Equipment (UE) supports this capability. Along with the velocity, the GNSS receiver may also provide an estimate of the uncertainty associated with the velocity measurement, if available.

8.1.2.2.1.1	UE-based mode

In UE-based or standalone mode, the GNSS receiver reports the latitude, longitude and possibly altitude, together with an estimate of the location uncertainty, if available.

If requested by the LMF and supported by the UE, the GNSS receiver may report its velocity, possibly together with an estimate of the uncertainty, if available.

If requested by the LMF and supported by the UE, the GNSS receiver may report the relation between GNSS system time (where the specific GNSS is indicated by a GNSS ID; the specific GNSS system time may be selected by the UE) and NG-RAN air-interface timing. This information may be used by the LMF to assist other UEs in the network.

The UE should also report an indication of which GNSSs and possibly other location methods have been used to calculate a fix.

question: What is WEP?
passage: WEP, or Wired Equivalent Privacy, is a security protocol designed to provide a wireless local area network (WLAN) with a level of security comparable to that of a wired network. It employs a shared key for authentication and encryption, meaning that all devices on the network use the same pre-shared key. However, WEP has significant drawbacks, primarily due to its lack of key management. Since the same static key is used across all devices, it becomes cumbersome to change the key, leading to prolonged use of the same key and increased vulnerability to hacking. As a result, WEP is considered outdated and has largely been replaced by more secure protocols like WPA (WiFi Protected Access) and WPA2.

question: do you have to change key often when using WEP?
passage: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) has a significant drawback in that it lacks key management, relying instead on a shared static key for authentication and encryption across all devices and access points (APs). As a result, many devices end up using the same static key for extended periods, increasing the risk of unauthorized access and making it easier for hackers to compromise the network. Therefore, while it is technically possible to change the key, the practical challenges often lead to infrequent changes, which is not ideal for maintaining security.

question: why does no one use 'open system authentication'?
passage: Open System Authentication (OSA) is rarely used in practice because it essentially means "no authentication," which poses significant security risks. While there are specific scenarios where OSA might be employed, such as for testing purposes or in environments where additional security measures are implemented behind the Access Point (AP), it is generally not a recommended practice. Most organizations prefer more secure authentication methods, like WPA or WPA2, which provide better protection against unauthorized access and data breaches. The lack of key management and reliance on a shared key in OSA makes it cumbersome and vulnerable, leading to its decline in favor of more robust security protocols.

question: is the key changed once in WEP?
passage: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) does not change the key automatically; it uses a static shared key for all devices on the network. This means that every wireless station and access point (AP) shares the same preshared key, which must be manually distributed to each device. Consequently, changing the key is cumbersome, as it requires redistributing the new key to all devices, leading to a situation where the same key is often used for an extended period. This lack of key management increases the vulnerability of the network to attacks, as the static key can be more easily compromised by hackers.

The primary goal of WLAN security is to safeguard the network from unauthorized access and potential data breaches, thereby maintaining the overall security of the wireless communication environment.

question: what is a disadvantage of WEP?
gold_answer: every wireless station and AP has the same "preshared" key that is used during authentication and encryption
passage: A significant disadvantage of WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is its lack of key management, as it relies on a shared key for authentication and encryption. This means that all wireless stations and access points (APs) use the same pre-shared key, which must be manually distributed to each device. Consequently, changing the key becomes cumbersome, as it requires redistributing the new key to all devices. This static key usage over time increases the vulnerability of the network, making it easier for hackers to compromise the system.

question: Who or what is responsible for all call termination fees associated with call or service termination?
passage: The HPLMN (Home Public Land Mobile Network) operator is responsible for all interworking connectivity and call termination fees associated with call or service termination in the context of roaming architecture for voice over IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) with home routed traffic. 5.5.3.8	Charging Principles for roaming architecture for voice over IMS with home routed traffic

The roaming architecture for voice over IMS with home routed traffic is described in the TS 23.228 [209]. The breakout point for both the IMS signalling and media traffic is in the home network for a roaming UE, i.e. for 3GPP systems, the P-GW/GGSN/SMF-UPF for a roaming UE is in the HPLMN of the UE.

Based on GSMA BA.27 [500], the VPLMN will not have awareness of the services being used over the IMS APN and cannot support service-aware wholesale charging. Data roaming charges will apply for all traffic traversing S8 or Gp interface per the existing data roaming agreement. The HPLMN operator will be responsible for all interworking connectivity and call termination fees associated with call or service termination.

Specifically, the serving PLMN identifier of the UE is needed for the home network.

Details are described in the TS 32.260 [20].

question: What can connect both to the 5G Core Network and a 4G Core Network?
passage: The 5G Access Network (5G AN) can connect to both the 5G Core Network (5G CN) and the 4G Core Network (4G CN). This capability is part of the Non-Standalone (NSA) architecture, which allows for dual connectivity between 4G and 5G networks. Specifically, the NSA solution enables the 5G AN to operate alongside the existing LTE system, providing users with both 4G and 5G connectivity. This dual connectivity is also referred to as "EN-DC," which stands for "4G and 5G Dual Connectivity." The integration of the 5G AN with the 4G CN requires certain enhancements to the 4G network, as outlined in the relevant 3GPP specifications.

question: What does this work contribute?
gold_answer: adds the capability to perform Forward Error Correction and/or Robust Header Compression
passage: The work contributes to the enhancement of the Generic Control and Service Environment (GCSE) framework by introducing the capability to implement Forward Error Correction (FEC) and Robust Header Compression (ROHC) for Multimedia Broadcast Multicast Service (MBMS) traffic. This addition allows for improved data integrity and efficiency in the transmission of MBMS content. The FEC and ROHC functionalities can be configured through external interfaces to the Broadcast Multicast Service Center (BM-SC), specifically via the MB2 and xMB interfaces. Furthermore, the activation of these features can be managed at the service level, enabling selective application to all streams of a service or none, thereby providing flexibility in network management and service delivery.
context:
3GPP-Specs#21915-f00#70

12.4.4	FEC and ROHC Activation for GCSE over MBMS

Summary based on the input provided by Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd . in SP-180881.

As part of extensions to the GCSE framework, this work adds the capability to perform Forward Error Correction and/or Robust Header Compression.

As part of this work item, the capability to perform FEC and ROHC for MBMS traffic using the GC or the Transport delivery method are added. Both tools can be configured through the external interfaces to the BM-SC, namely the MB2 and xMB. Currently, activation at service level is allowed, so that FEC/ROHC can be applied to all streams of the service or to none of them.

question: What is used to test OTA AAS BS?
passage: The testing of OTA (Over-The-Air) AAS (Active Antenna System) Base Stations (BS) involves the use of radiated test signals, as the OTA AAS BS is designed to function without a conducted interface. This system typically includes multiple transceiver units (a minimum of 8 for E-UTRA and MSR, and 4 for UTRA) and a composite antenna. The OTA requirements ensure that the performance and protection levels of the OTA AAS BS are comparable to those of a non-AAS BS with multiple transceivers. The testing focuses on various transmitter and receiver requirements, including sensitivity and interference handling, which are evaluated based on radiated signals at the Radiated Interface Boundary (RIB). Additionally, EMC (Electromagnetic Compatibility) requirements are integrated into the RF radiated spurious emission specifications, ensuring comprehensive performance assessment of the OTA AAS BS.
context:
3GPP-Specs#21915-f00#78

12.6	Active Antenna System (AAS)

Summary based on the input provided by Huawei in RP -172345 (long version), revised in RP-182112 (shorter version, more in line with the rest of this present document).

The WI added a full set of OTA requirements to the AAS BS specification for MSR, single RAT UTRA and single RAT E-UTRA AAS BS with no conducted interface.

The OTA AAS BS is a system which contains multiple transceiver (i.e. ≥8 for E-UTRA and MSR, or ≥4 for UTRA) units and a composite antenna. Since a single OTA AAS BS is comparable to a non-AAS BS with multiple transceivers, the eAAS requirements aim to ensure that the same protection and performance is provided as a non-AAS BS with 8 transceivers for E-UTRA and MSR and with 4 transceivers for UTRA.

The previous AAS WI produced an AAS BS specification for an AAS BS which provided access to a conducted interface. Requirements were applied at both the conducted interface (the Transceiver Array Boundary) and the radiated interface. An AAS BS conforming to the release 13/14 AAS BS requirements is now referred to as a hybrid AAS BS in the release 15 specification. To enable AAS BS with larger number of transceiver units and higher frequencies, where maintaining a conducted interface may limit implementation, all OTA requirements have been developed enabling the OTA AAS BS to be treated as a black box that is tested externally using radiated test signals.

12.6.1	Architecture and interfaces

The OTA AAS BS architecture is similar to the hybrid AAS BS architecture with the removal of the conducted interface (the transceiver array boundary).

The Radiated Interface Boundary (RIB) is an interface at which the OTA requirements can be specified. As an OTA AAS BS is expected to have a large number of transceiver units, the minimum number of transceiver units is restricted to 8 for E-UTRA and MSR and to transceiver 4 for UTRA.

12.6.2	OTA requirements

Transmitter requirements

Transmitter requirements can be classified into 3 types:

Receiver requirements

With the exception of the receiver spurious emissions (which is TRP like the transmitter spurious emissions) all the receiver requirements are based on receiving a wanted signal at a specified power level, either on its own or in the presence of an interferer.

The OTA receiver requirements have 2 types of OTA sensitivity defined:

Each of the interference requirements are specified with respect to:

For in-band interference requirements (i.e. dynamic range, ACS ICS, in-band blocking, RX IMD) wanted and interferer signal are specified as having the same angle of arrival. The relative difference between the wanted signal and the interferer is the same as the conducted requirement in all cases.

Out of band blocking requirement is specified as field strength (in V/m) and is the same for all frequencies. The wanted signal is an offset from EISminSENS.

For co-location blocking tests a radiated wanted signal, based on an offset from EISminSENS, is specified in the same way as the other interference requirements. The interferer is applied via CRA, the level of the interferer is specified at the conducted input to the CRA.

EMC requirements

EMC radiated emission requirements are already OTA and are hence merged into the RF radiated spurious emission requirements. As the RF requirements are dominant, the OTA emissions are captured in the BS RF specification and this is referenced from the RAN4 BS EMC specification.

The EMC radiated immunity requirements generate much higher interferer levels than the RF blocking requirements and hence the two aspects have to be separated. As the OTA AAS BS has an intentional radiator and its wanted performance is specified by the declared RoAoA, these 2 types of RAN4 requirements are separated by a spatial mask (i.e. so called spatial exclusion) with radiated immunity requirement only specified outside the declared RoAoA.
