7.4	Call Handling for an MSP subscriber

The procedure for handling MSP calls can be divided into two areas: mobile originating call handling and mobile terminating call handling.
7.4.1	Mobile Originating (MO) call handling
The served subscriber may use the registered profile or explicitly select a provisioned profile to set up an MO call. If the profile is explicitly selected, the selection information will be included in the called party BCD number and transported to the gsmSCF. If the gsmSCF recognises that a profile has not been explicitly selected (there is no profile selection information  in the called party BCD number) then the registered profile is used. The MMI for explicitly selecting a profile is defined in 3G TS 22.030.

When the gsmSCF receives an Initial_DP message containing MO call parameters from the gsmSSF, the process MO_MSP_Call_gsmSCF will be invoked, see figure 5. All other call handling is described in 3G TS 23.018 and 3G TS 23.078.

7.4.2	Mobile Terminating (MT) call handling
The profile used for an MT call to the served subscriber is determined by the called MSISDN.
The information flow for an MT call is shown in figure 29.
When the gsmSCF receives an Initial_DP message containing MT call parameters from the gsmSSF, the process MT_MSP_Call_gsmSCF will be invoked, see figure 8. All other call handling is described in 3G TS 23.018 and 3G TS 23.078.

question: Where is the A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST included?
passage: The A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST is included in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request. This request is sent by 3G_MSCA to request a Handover Number when establishing a circuit connection after an Inter-3G_MSC UMTS to GSM handover without an existing circuit connection. The A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST is crucial for the assignment operation towards the BSS, as it contains necessary codec information and facilitates the handover process between the 3G and GSM networks.

13.2	UMTS to GSM handover

If a circuit connection has to be set up (for example for a Mobile Originated or Mobile Terminated Call Establishment) after an Inter-3G_MSC UMTS to GSM handover without circuit connection, 3G_MSCA shall request a Handover Number using a MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request, containing the A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST, on the established MAP connection. For speech calls, 3G_MSC-A shall also include the Iu Supported Codecs List to be used by MSC-B for subsequent intra-MSC-B intersystem handover to UMTS and intra-MSC-B SRNS relocation. If MSCB indicates to MSCB and to 3G_MSCA that at least one of two procedures assignment or Handover Number allocation can not be completed, then 3G_MSCA shall terminate the circuit establishment attempt. The existing connection to the UE/MS shall be maintained, if possible.
Upon receipt of the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request MSCB shall perform the requested assignment operation towards the BSS. In addition it shall retrieve a Handover Number from VLR-B. If a failure occurs in the assignment or Handover Number allocation then it shall be reflected in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER response that at least one of these two procedures has not been completed (i.e. either by a MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER result with the assignment procedure outcome and the Handover Number allocation outcome or by a MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER error).

If 3G_MSC-A supports A interface over IP, then for speech calls 3G_MSC-A may include the AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor) in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request.
If the BSS-B supports A over IP, then MSC-B shall include a Codec List (MSC preferred) in the A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST message to BSS-B. MSC-B may select the codecs for the Codec List (MSC preferred) from the channel type information and the AoIPSupported Codecs List (Anchor), if this list was provided by 3G_MSC-A in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request. For a detailed description of the handling of these codec lists by 3G_MSC-A and MSC-B see 3GPP TS 23.153. If the AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor) was not provided or MSC-B does not support the selection of codecs from the AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor), then MSC-B shall create the Codec List (MSC preferred) using the channel type information received from 3G_MSC-A in the A-ASSIGNMENT-REQUEST message included in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request.

If MSC-A provided an AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor) in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER request and MSCB selected the codecs for the Codec List (MSC preferred) from the AoIP-Supported Codecs List (Anchor), MSCB may include the AoIP-Selected Codec (Target) and AoIP-Available Codecs List (MAP) in the MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER response.
When 3G_MSCA receives a successful MAP-PREPARE-HANDOVER response, it shall establish a circuit connection to MSCB by using the appropriate network supported procedures. In figure 37 this is indicated by the IAM (Initial Address Message) and ACM (Address Complete Message). MSCB shall also send the Answer message if appropriate to the signalling system. Upon receipt of the Answer 3G_MSCA shall consider the circuit connection establishment phase complete. If a failure occurs during the circuit establishment phase then the existing connection to the UE/MS shall be maintained, if possible.

question: what is NSA?
passage: The NSA, or Non-Stand Alone architecture, is a deployment option for 5G that allows the integration of the 5G Radio Access Network (NR) with the existing 4G LTE and EPC infrastructure. This configuration enables the use of 5G technology without the need to replace the current network, providing benefits such as lower latency while still relying on 4G services. The NSA is also referred to as "E-UTRA-NR Dual Connectivity (EN-DC)" or "Architecture Option 3." In this setup, the 4G base station (eNB) acts as the Master Node, while the 5G base station (en-gNB) serves as the Secondary Node, facilitating dual connectivity through both networks. The NSA architecture is considered a transitional step towards full 5G deployment, which is achieved through the Stand-Alone (SA) architecture that operates independently of 4G infrastructure.

5.3.2	The NSA versus SA architecture

Two deployment options are defined for 5G:

-	the "Non-Stand Alone" (NSA) architecture, where the 5G Radio Access Network (AN) and its New Radio (NR) interface is used in conjunction with the existing LTE and EPC infrastructure Core Network (respectively 4G Radio and 4G Core), thus making the NR technology available without network replacement. In this configuration, only the 4G services are supported, but enjoying the capacities offered by the 5G New Radio (lower latency, etc). The NSA is also known as "E-UTRA-NR Dual Connectivity (EN-DC)" or "Architecture Option 3". See also the clause on EDCE5.

-	the "Stand-Alone" (SA) architecture, where the NR is connected to the 5G CN. Only in this configuration, the full set of 5G Phase 1 services are supported.

The NSA architecture is illustrated in the following figure.

The NSA architecture can be seen as a temporary step towards "full 5G" deployment, where the 5G Access Network is connected to the 4G Core Network. In the NSA architecture, the (5G) NR base station (logical node "en-gNB") connects to the (4G) LTE base station (logical node "eNB") via the X2 interface. The X2 interface was introduced prior to Release 15 to connect two eNBs. In Release 15, it also supports connecting an eNB and en-gNB as to provide NSA.

The NSA offers dual connectivity, via both the 4G AN (E-UTRA) and the 5G AN (NR). It is thus also called "EN-DC", for "E-UTRAN and NR Dual Connectivity".

In EN-DC, the 4G's eNB is the Master Node (MN) while the 5G's en-gNB is the Secondary Node (SN).

This is explained in detail on the dedicated section on NSA of this present document.

The SA architecture is illustrated in the following figure.

The SA architecture can be seen as the "full 5G deployment", not needing any part of a 4G network to operate.

The NR base station (logical node "gNB") connects with each other via the Xn interface, and the Access Network (called the "NG-RAN for SA architecture") connects to the 5GC network using the NG interface.

The continuation of this section refers to the SA architecture, the NSA being addressed in a subsequent, dedicated, section.

question: Can there be several GMLCs in one PLMN?
gold_answer: In one PLMN, there may be more than one GMLC
passage: Yes, there can be several Gateway Mobile Location Centres (GMLCs) in one Public Land Mobile Network (PLMN). Each GMLC serves specific functions related to location services and can handle requests from external LCS clients. The presence of multiple GMLCs allows for efficient management of location services, including privacy checks and routing information, particularly in scenarios involving roaming users or different service areas within the same PLMN.
context:
4.3.3	Gateway Mobile Location Centre, GMLC

The Gateway Mobile Location Centre (GMLC) contains functionality required to support LCS. In one PLMN, there may be more than one GMLC.
A GMLC is the first node an external LCS client accesses in a PLMN (i.e. the Le reference point is supported by the GMLC). AFs and NFs may access GMLC directly or via NEF. The GMLC may request routing information and/or target UE privacy information from the UDM via the Nudm interface. After performing authorization of an external LCS Client or AF and verifying target UE privacy, a GMLC forwards a location request to either a serving AMF using Namf interface or to a GMLC in another PLMN using the Ngmlc interface in the case of a roaming UE.
The target UE's privacy profile settings shall always be checked in the UE's home PLMN prior to delivering a location estimate.

The "Visited GMLC" (VGMLC) is the GMLC, which is associated with the serving node of the target UE.
The "Home GMLC" (HGMLC) is the GMLC residing in the target UE's home PLMN, which is responsible for the control of privacy checking of the target UE.

A GMLC is the first node an external LCS client accesses in a PLMN (i.e. the Le reference point is supported by the GMLC). AFs and NFs may access GMLC directly or via NEF. The GMLC may request routing information and/or target UE privacy information from the UDM via the Nudm interface. After performing authorization of an external LCS Client or AF and verifying target UE privacy, a GMLC forwards a location request to either a serving AMF using Namf interface or to a GMLC in another PLMN using the Ngmlc interface in the case of a roaming UE.
The target UE's privacy profile settings shall always be checked in the UE's home PLMN prior to delivering a location estimate.

The "Visited GMLC" (VGMLC) is the GMLC, which is associated with the serving node of the target UE.
The "Home GMLC" (HGMLC) is the GMLC residing in the target UE's home PLMN, which is responsible for the control of privacy checking of the target UE.

This assumption ensures that the UE can effectively manage its reception and processing of the signals, maintaining optimal performance in the presence of transmit diversity.

question: What would happen if TFO would not be active?
gold_answer: the round trip delay would be smaller
passage: If TFO (Transparent End-to-End Optimisation) is not active during an active AMR (Adaptive Multi-Rate) call, the process of downgrading the codec mode in response to poor radio link quality would be less efficient. Without TFO, when a degradation in quality is detected, the codec mode adaptation would involve a round trip delay, as the codec mode request would need to be sent from the Base Transceiver Station (BTS) to the TRAU (Transcoder and Rate Adaptation Unit) before the new codec mode is applied. This delay can significantly impact the responsiveness of the system, leading to a slower adaptation to the changing conditions. In contrast, with TFO active, the codec mode can be downgraded immediately without negotiation, allowing for a more seamless adjustment to maintain call quality.
context:
3GPP-Specs#45009-f00#24

C.1	Downgrading

For an active AMR call without TFO, the codec mode is downgraded when the quality of the radio link decreases. In that case the codec bit rate is reduced so that more throughput is left on the radio interface to add protection. The principle when TFO is active is that as soon as one side detects the need to downgrade the codec rate, it informs the other side and the codec mode is immediately downgraded. There is no negotiation before downgrading.

C.1.1	Uplink downgrading

The following figure shows the uplink adaptation due to detection by the BTS1 of a bad quality in the uplink from the MS1. In that case the round trip delay between BTS1 and BTS2 has no impact, as the uplink codec adaptation is decided immediately by BTS1 and performed by the MS1.

C.1.2	Downlink downgrading

The following figure C.1.2 shows the downlink adaptation due to detection by the MS1 of a bad quality of the downlink from the BTS1. The codec mode adaptation must be performed on the far end MS (MS2), where the source encoder is located. In that case the round trip delay before the downlink adaptation is effective has an high impact. If TFO would not be active, the round trip delay would be smaller, because the Codec Mode Request sent by the BTS1 to the TRAU1 would be immediately taken into account by the TRAU1 and the new codec mode applied in downlink: without TFO ongoing the (tandem) source encoder is located in TRAU1.

question: What is geometric?

question: What is ionospheric?
passage: The ionosphere is a region of the Earth's upper atmosphere, primarily located between about 30 miles (48 kilometers) and 600 miles (965 kilometers) above the Earth's surface, where ionization occurs due to solar radiation. This ionization affects the propagation of radio waves, causing delays and distortions in signals transmitted through this layer. In the context of GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System), ionospheric corrections are necessary to account for these dispersive effects, ensuring accurate positioning by compensating for the signal delays caused by the ionosphere.

question: How does dynamic allocation decide the bandwidth to use?
gold_answer: The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved.
passage: Dynamic allocation in 802.11ac determines the bandwidth to use through a negotiation process between the transmitter (initiator) and receiver (responder) that occurs during data transmission. This process utilizes the RTS/CTS (Request to Send/Clear to Send) mechanism, where the entire available bandwidth is divided into smaller segments (e.g., 20 MHz, 40 MHz, 80 MHz). The initiator sends RTS messages across these segments and waits for CTS responses from the receiver. If the receiver successfully acknowledges all RTS messages, the initiator can use the full bandwidth. If only some CTS responses are received, the initiator adjusts the bandwidth accordingly, using only the segments that were acknowledged as clear. This dynamic approach allows for efficient bandwidth utilization based on real-time channel conditions, enabling higher throughput and adaptability during a single session.

No new technology can be invented overnight. We all understand this. However, we don't want to wait forever until everything is ready all at once. In some technology, they call these chunk as 'Stage' (like Stage 1, Stage 2 etc) and in some technology they call them as 'Phase' (e.g, Phase 1, Phase 2 etc). In 802.11ac, they call them as Wave (e.g, Wave 1, Wave 2 etc). 802.11ac has been evolved as two Waves (at least as of now, Aug 2016) as listed below.

If you have a 802.11ac WLAN Card (device), the first thing you have to do is to figure out the Access Point (AP) around the device support 802.11ac. (Actually you don't need to figure out this, your WLAN device will figure out :).

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame. Step 3 : (In various reason, e.g, Node B failed to receive RTS due to interference or Medium is busy based on carrier sensing ) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for only two consecutive 20 Mhz blocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for the two 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that only 40Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the 40 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for the two 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

question: What is dynamic allocation?
gold_answer: Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.
passage: Dynamic allocation refers to the method of negotiating and determining bandwidth in a communication system, allowing for adjustments during an active session. In the context of 802.11ac Wi-Fi technology, dynamic allocation enables the transmitter and receiver to assess and modify the bandwidth used for data transmission at short intervals, rather than maintaining a fixed bandwidth throughout the session. This is achieved through a process where the transmitter sends multiple Request to Send (RTS) signals across various frequency blocks, and the receiver responds with Clear to Send (CTS) signals. Based on the CTS responses received, the transmitter can adaptively select the available bandwidth, optimizing the communication based on current channel conditions. This approach enhances throughput and efficiency by allowing real-time adjustments to the bandwidth used for data transmission.

passage: SU-MIMO (Single User MIMO) and MU-MIMO (Multi User MIMO) are two different techniques used in wireless communication, particularly in the context of Wi-Fi standards like 802.11ac. SU-MIMO is designed to serve a single user at a time, allowing the access point (AP) to transmit multiple data streams to one device, thereby increasing the throughput for that specific user. In contrast, MU-MIMO enables the AP to communicate with multiple users simultaneously, transmitting different data streams to several devices at once. This capability enhances overall network efficiency and throughput, especially in environments with many users. While SU-MIMO focuses on maximizing the performance for individual connections, MU-MIMO aims to optimize the performance across multiple connections, making it a significant advancement in wireless technology.

question: What does an AP broadcast to indicate that 802.11ac is supported?
passage: To indicate that 802.11ac is supported, an Access Point (AP) broadcasts a Beacon signal containing specific information about its capabilities. This Beacon signal includes details such as the Maximum MPDU Length, Supported Channel Width Set, and various VHT (Very High Throughput) capabilities. For instance, it may specify whether it supports 160 MHz channel width or short guard intervals for 160 MHz and 80+80 MHz configurations. The presence of these specific parameters in the Beacon signal allows WLAN devices to determine the AP's support for 802.11ac features, enabling them to connect and utilize the enhanced throughput capabilities of the standard.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. passage: In the context of 802.11ac, dynamic allocation occurs when the transmitter (Node A) and receiver (Node B) negotiate the bandwidth during a session based on the availability of the spectrum. An example of dynamic allocation with interference is when Node A attempts to use an 80 MHz channel divided into four 20 MHz blocks. This process allows for efficient use of available spectrum even in the presence of interference, demonstrating the flexibility of dynamic bandwidth allocation in 802.11ac.

question: What does dynamic allocation do?
gold_answer: It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.
passage: Dynamic allocation in the context of 802.11ac refers to the ability of the transmitter and receiver to negotiate and determine the bandwidth used for data transmission in real-time, even during a single communication session. Unlike static allocation, where the bandwidth is set at the beginning of the connection and remains fixed, dynamic allocation allows for adjustments based on current channel conditions. This is achieved through a process that involves sending multiple Request to Send (RTS) messages across different frequency blocks and waiting for Clear to Send (CTS) responses. If the CTS is received for all requested blocks, the full bandwidth can be utilized; if not, the bandwidth is adjusted accordingly. This flexibility enhances throughput and optimizes the use of available spectrum, making it a key feature of the 802.11ac standard.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. question: What is the purpose of Channel Sounding?
gold_answer: The fundamental purpose of this complicated process is to figure out the charateristics (nature) of radio channel between the Access Point and Devices.
passage: Channel Sounding is a process used in wireless communication, particularly in the 802.11ac standard, to assess the characteristics of the radio channel between an Access Point (AP) and devices. The primary purpose of Channel Sounding is to enable accurate beamforming, which optimizes the transmission of data to multiple users simultaneously (MU-MIMO). During this process, the AP and devices perform a sequence of measurements to determine the channel conditions, allowing the AP to extract suitable beamforming parameters. Although Channel Sounding does not convey user data and may introduce some overhead, it is essential for enhancing overall throughput by ensuring that the communication is tailored to the specific channel conditions.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame. Step 3 : (In various reason, e.g, Node B failed to receive RTS due to interference or Medium is busy based on carrier sensing ) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for only two consecutive 20 Mhz blocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for the two 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that only 40Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the 40 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for the two 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

question: What is AP?

It acts as a bridge between the wireless clients and the wired network, enabling communication and data transfer. In the context of 802.11ac, the AP broadcasts a Beacon signal that contains information about its capabilities, including support for various features such as Very High Throughput (VHT) and multiple bandwidth options. The AP also plays a crucial role in managing connections, facilitating data transmission, and optimizing performance through technologies like Multi User MIMO (MU-MIMO) and beamforming.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. 802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. question: What is static allocation?
gold_answer: Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session)
passage: Static allocation refers to a method of bandwidth allocation in communication systems where the transmitter and receiver negotiate and determine the bandwidth during the initial stages of connection setup. Once established, this bandwidth remains fixed throughout the entire communication session. In contrast to dynamic allocation, where bandwidth can change during the session based on real-time conditions, static allocation provides a consistent bandwidth that does not adapt to varying network conditions. This approach can simplify the management of network resources but may not be as efficient in utilizing available bandwidth compared to dynamic methods.

question: What is MU-MIMO?
passage: MU-MIMO, or Multi User MIMO, is a technology introduced in the 802.11ac Wi-Fi standard that allows an Access Point (AP) to transmit multiple data streams simultaneously to multiple users. Unlike traditional MIMO (Single User MIMO), which targets a single device at a time, MU-MIMO enhances network efficiency by enabling the AP to serve multiple clients concurrently. This capability is particularly beneficial in environments with many users, as it can significantly improve overall throughput and reduce latency. However, implementing MU-MIMO presents challenges, including the need for precise channel estimation and coordination among users to optimize performance. Despite these challenges, MU-MIMO represents a significant advancement in wireless communication technology, aiming to meet the growing demand for high-speed internet access in dense user scenarios.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame. Step 3 : (In various reason, e.g, Node B failed to receive RTS due to interference or Medium is busy based on carrier sensing ) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for only two consecutive 20 Mhz blocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for the two 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that only 40Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the 40 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for the two 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame. Step 3 : (In various reason, e.g, Node B failed to receive RTS due to interference or Medium is busy based on carrier sensing ) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for only two consecutive 20 Mhz blocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for the two 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that only 40Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the 40 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for the two 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

question: What is MIMO?
passage: MIMO, which stands for Multiple Input Multiple Output, is a technology used in wireless communication that employs multiple antennas at both the transmitter and receiver ends to improve communication performance. In the context of Wi-Fi, particularly with the 802.11ac standard, MIMO allows for the simultaneous transmission of multiple data streams to and from multiple users, enhancing overall throughput and efficiency. This is referred to as MU-MIMO (Multi User MIMO), which enables an access point to serve multiple devices at the same time, rather than sequentially, thereby optimizing the use of available bandwidth and improving user experience in high-density environments.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. question: What is Anritsu MT8862?
passage: The Anritsu MT8862 is a WLAN test equipment designed for testing and validating the performance of wireless LAN devices, particularly those compliant with the 802.11ac standard. It is capable of capturing detailed logs of communication between devices, including the transmission of Beacon signals that convey essential information about the capabilities of access points (APs). The MT8862 plays a crucial role in analyzing the 802.11ac features, such as Very High Throughput (VHT) and Multi-User MIMO (MU-MIMO), by providing insights into the channel conditions and performance metrics necessary for optimizing wireless communication. This equipment is essential for developers and engineers working on WLAN technology to ensure compliance and enhance the performance of their devices.

Initially, Node A splits the 80 MHz channel into four contiguous 20 MHz blocks and performs carrier sensing to check their availability. After determining that all blocks are clear, Node A sends a Request to Send (RTS) for each 20 MHz block. If Node B successfully receives all RTS messages, it responds with a Clear to Send (CTS) for each block. Upon receiving the CTS for all blocks, Node A concludes that the entire 80 MHz bandwidth is available and proceeds to transmit data using the full bandwidth. This dynamic allocation allows for efficient use of the available spectrum, adapting to the current channel conditions in real-time.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. One of the most important keywords in 802.11ac would VHT. VHT stands for Very High Throughput. You would not need any additional explanation on what this means. The meaning is obvious and self-explanatory.

The question is how to achieve VHT and what kind of new frames and protocols are introduced to implement this.

In wireshark log, you may see this framing information from Radiotap Header as shown below.

802.11ac support various types of bandwidth combination like 20 Mhz, 80 Mhz, 160 Mhz. Then the question would 'how do they allocate the bandwidth ?'. Statically or Dynamically ?

Static allocation means that Transmitter (Initiator) and Reciever(Responder) negotiate and determines the bandwidth during early stage of connection setup and keep it same until the end of communication (a session).

Dynamic allocation means that Transmitter and Reciever SOMEHOW negotiate/determine the bandwidth in very short interval even during a single session.

802.11ac picked up the dynamic allocation approach. It allows the change of the bandwidth at every transmission.

Then the question is 'HOW ?'. What kind of negotiation they use to determine/agree upon the bandwidth between Transmitter and Reciever ?

Basic Idea is simple. As you see in Data Transmission in Detail section, basic channel acquisition process for all 802.11 is based on RTS/CTS mechanism. 802.11ac use the same mechanism to determine the avaiable bandwidth dynamically. The idea is to split the whole possible 802.11ac band into multiple blocks of basic segments (e.g, 20 Mhz, 40 Mhz, 80 Mhz etc) and perform the multiple RTS/CTS simulateneously across the multiple frequency block. (It is very similary for Carrier Aggregation in LTE). First, the initiator sends multiple RTS accross the multiple frequency block and wait for CTS. If the initiator recieves CTS accross the all the blocks, it can use all the frequency blocks (very wide aggregated bandwidth). If the initiator recieves only a few CTS for the all transmitted RTS, it uses the smaller bandwidth for which CTS is recieved. (Refer to Ref [9] for the details).

Let me give you a couple of examples with illustration on how Dynamic Bandwidth goes. Here goes only two cases but there can be much more variations on this.

This is the case where there is no interference between Node A(initiator) and Node B(recipient) and the full bandwith is avaiable for both nodes. Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame and it is assumed that all of these RTS reached Node B successfully. Step 3 : (Assuming that Node B detected RTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for every 20 Mhz subblocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for all of 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that all 80Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the full 80 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for every 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

This is the case where there is some interference in some spectrum blocks within the 80 Mhz block on Node B(recipient). Of course, these nodes does not know anything about the bandwidth availability before it completes step 3. Step 0 : Right before Step 1, it is assumed that Node A split the whole 80 Mhz section into 4 contiguous 20 Mhz block and performed carrier sensing for each of these 20 Mhz block. And it is assumed that all of these 20 Mhz block turned out to be available. Step 1 : Node A wait for a certain time period called DIFS(DCF Inter Frame Space), assuming that the scheduling is done in DCF. Step 2 : Node A transmit RTS for each of 20 Mhz block to Node B using 802.11a frame. Step 3 : (In various reason, e.g, Node B failed to receive RTS due to interference or Medium is busy based on carrier sensing ) Node B transmit CTS using 802.11a frame for only two consecutive 20 Mhz blocks. Step 4 : (Assuming that Node A detected CTS for the two 20 Mhz blocks) Node A assumes that only 40Mhz BW is clear/no-interference and transmit the data in 802.11ac mode utilizing the 40 Mhz. Step 5 : (Assuming that Node B received and decoded the whole data) Node B sends Ack for the two 20 Mhz blocks (40 Mhz in total).

In 802.11ac, Following new Frame Types are added to the existing type. Most of New Frametype is for impelementing Channel Measurement and Report to perform MU-MIMO Beamforming.

This frame is used for BeamFormer (AP) to initiate Channel Measurement Process. (Refer to 802.11ac 8.3.1.20 VHT NDP Announcement frame format for the details)

It indicates the number of columns, Nc, in the Compressed Beamforming Feedback Matrix

This frame is used for BeamFormee (user) to report channel measurement result (Refer to 802.11ac 8.5.23.2 VHT Compressed Beamforming frame format for the details)

To perform proper beamforming for specific devices, it is crucial to figure out accurate channel condition between BeamFormer and BeanFormee. To figure out the channel condition, BeamFormer and BeamFormee performs a specific sequence of calibration process and this process is called Channel Measurement or Sounding process. It goes as follows.

Refer to 802.11ac 9.31.5.2 Rules for VHT sounding protocol sequences, Figure 9-41a and Figure 9-41a for the details.

NOTE : The fundamental purpose of this complicated process is to figure out the charateristics (nature) of radio channel between the Access Point and Devices. This is also called 'Channel Sounding'. During this process, no user data is conveyed. It means this process can be a kind of overhead (throughput degradation factor). If AP can best optimize the communication by extracting the most suitable BeamForming parameters from this process, this process can give a overall throughput gain. However, if AP failed to get the best BeamForming parameters from this process, this would just create unncessary overhead.

MU-MIMO stands for Multi User MIMO and this is adopted only in 802.11ac (not in 802.11n and lower). When we say MIMO(Multi Input Multi Output), it normally mean SU-MIMO(Single User MIMO), which is a MIMO targeted to only one device(user). On the contrary, MU-MIMO is the MIMO targeted to multiple user simulateneously. It mean that in MU-MIMO the transmitter (Access Point) can transmite the multiple stream of data targeted to multiple user.

It sounds fancy, right ? However, the implementation of this technology would not be as easy as it sound and real performance would not be as good as expected. Probably it would need to go through a long way of evolution. Let's think of some of the challenges and possible issues related to MU-MIMO

Putting aside the practical feasibility of this MU-MIMO, the specification is done. In most case of technology (even though it is not all the case), once the specification is issued the technology continues to evolve and get better and better.

You would have the same questions about 802.11ac. Is 802.11ac compatitle with the existing (previous) techology (e.g, 802.11a and 802.11n) ? The answer is Yes. 802.11ac is designed from beginning to be compatible with 802.11a / n both for Access point and devices.

question: What is PFCP?
passage: PFCP, or Packet Forwarding Control Protocol, is a key protocol used in the 5G Core Network (5GC) over the N4 interface. It facilitates the separation of the Control Plane and User Plane, which is essential for the efficient operation of 5G networks. PFCP is an evolution of the protocol used in the Evolved Packet Core (EPC) for Control and User Plane Separation (CUPS), with enhancements to meet the specific requirements of 5G, such as support for Ethernet traffic and Quality of Service (QoS) flows. This protocol plays a crucial role in managing data traffic and ensuring optimal performance in 5G network architectures.

Summary based on the inputs provided by China Mobile, Nokia, Ericsson, Huawei in SP-180595.

The services provided by 5G NFs are designed as a set of APIs based on the following protocol stack:

To reduce the coupling between clients and servers, the RESTful framework is applied for the APIs design as follows:

OAuth2 (as specified in IETF RFC 6749) is used for authorization of NF service access, with the NRF acting as the Authorization Server.

The Service Based Interfaces also support procedures for overload control and message prioritisation.

PFCP (Packet Forwarding Control Protocol) is used over the N4 interface for the separation of Control Plane and User Plane in the 5GC. This is the same protocol as supported for CUPS in EPC, with a few extensions to support all the 5GC requirements (e.g. Ethernet traffic, QoS flows).

GTPv2 is used over the N26 interface for mobility between EPC and the 5GC. This is the same protocol as supported over S10 in EPC, with minimal extensions to support 5GS requirements (e.g. 5GS TAI, gNB ID).

For 5G network interworking with external DNs (i.e. N6 interface), those protocols specified in TS 29.061 (IP, non-IP, DHCP, RADIUS and Diameter protocols) are still applicable between the SMF/UPF and the external DNs with possible adaptation. In addition, the Ethernet traffic is also supported by the SMF/UPF for interworking with external DN.

question: What does service based interface support?
gold_answer: procedures for overload control and message prioritisation
passage: The service-based interface in 5G networks supports a range of functionalities designed to enhance the interaction between network functions (NFs) while minimizing the coupling between clients and servers. It utilizes a RESTful framework for API design, which facilitates easier integration and communication. Key features of the service-based interface include support for authorization through OAuth2, overload control procedures, and message prioritization. Additionally, it enables the separation of control and user planes using the Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP) and supports mobility management with GTPv2. The interface also accommodates interworking with external data networks (DNs) using various protocols, including IP, non-IP, DHCP, RADIUS, and Diameter, along with Ethernet traffic support. Overall, the service-based interface is crucial for the efficient operation and management of 5G networks.

question: Where is CTPv2 used?
passage: CTPv2, or GTPv2, is used over the N26 interface for mobility management between the Evolved Packet Core (EPC) and the 5G Core (5GC). It facilitates the transfer of user sessions and mobility information, ensuring seamless connectivity as users move between different network areas. GTPv2 is an extension of the protocol previously used in EPC, specifically over the S10 interface, and has been adapted to meet the requirements of the 5G system, including support for new features such as 5G Tracking Area Identity (TAI) and gNB ID.

question: What differs CAP from Ro?

passage: The main difference between CAP (CAMEL Application Part) and Ro lies in their underlying technologies and applications within the charging architecture. While both reference points provide functionality for online charging, CAP is specifically based on CAMEL techniques, which are applicable in both Circuit Switched (CS) and Packet Switched (PS) domains. In contrast, Ro is a reference point that supports online charging without the CAMEL framework. Essentially, CAP integrates CAMEL capabilities, allowing for more advanced charging scenarios, whereas Ro serves as a more straightforward online charging interface.

question: what are the perks of MQTT?
gold_answer: very light , simple and small sized
passage: MQTT, or Message Queuing Telemetry Transport, offers several key perks that make it particularly suitable for IoT applications. Firstly, it is an extremely lightweight protocol, which minimizes the amount of data transmitted, making it ideal for low-bandwidth and low-power devices. This is crucial for systems like 6LoWPAN, where traditional protocols may generate excessive traffic. Secondly, MQTT employs a simple publish/subscribe mechanism, allowing devices to efficiently receive updates only when relevant data changes, thus reducing unnecessary communication. Additionally, its straightforward packet structure and protocol sequence facilitate easy implementation and understanding, contributing to its popularity in the IoT landscape. Overall, MQTT's efficiency, simplicity, and effectiveness in managing data flow make it a dominant choice for IoT communications.

IoT: MQTT

MQTT stands for Message Queuing Telemetry Transport. or MQ Telemetry Transport. It is extremly simple and lightweight messaging protocol based on publish / subscribe mechanism.

In case of current high bandwidth connection (like ordinary internet, WiFi, Cellular), we already have so wide varieties of protocols like http, ftp, sip etc. Most of these protocols is generating relatively large traffic even though it can be considered as almost nothing with recent broadband communication technology and it would not be a big issue even with IoT devices if the devices is based on celluar network (e.g, WCDMA or LTE). However, this kind of protocol can cause untolerable amount of traffic for the devices that is based on very low throughput and small sized packet system like 6LoWPAN. For this kind of low throughput/small packet based system, we would need very light , simple and small sized application layer protocol. MQTT is one of the most popular protocol that meets this requirement.

For learning any kind of protocol, my personal approach is almost always same. To understand the packet (or frame) structure and then following through a couple of example protol sequences line by line. Sometimes I practice decoding the captured hex stream by hand based on Packet Structure specification. I will do the same thing here.

Protocol Sequence of MQTT is very simple as illustrated below. First, Client (IoT End Device) request connection to a Broker (a kind of server). If the connection accepted, the device (client) would send 'SUBSRIBE' message saying "I want to get this and this kind of data. So please send me the data whenever those data is upadated on your side (Broker)". If this request is accepted by Broker, the broker would send the data to the device whenever any new data comes into the database. For more details on profocol sequence, see 'Protocol Sequence' section. For more details on the structure and contents of each message, refer to Packet structure section.
